div.p: "OUR CHRISTMAS CORNER."

' • BALLADE OF CHRISTMAS GHOSTS. Between the moonlight and the fire, In winter evenings long ago, What ghosts I raised at your desire, t To make your leaping blood run slow! Dow old, how grave, how wise we grow! What Christmas ghost can make us chill— Save these that troop in mournful row, The ghosts we all can raise at will? ." The beasts can talk in barn and byre On Christmas-eve, old legends know. As one by one the years retire, We men fall silent then, I trow— , Such sights has memory to show, Such voices from the distance thrill., 7 Ah me! they come with Christmas snow, The ghosts we all can raise at will. Oh, children of the village choir, • Your carols on the midnight throw! Oh, bright across the mist and mire, Ye ruddy hearths of Christmas glow! Beat back the shades, beat down the woe, 4 Renew the strength of mortal will; Be welcome, all, to come or go, The ghosts we all can raise at will. Friend, sursuna conk, soon or slow We part, like guests who've joyed their fill; Forget them not, nor mourn them so, The ghosts we all can raise at will. Magazine.

CHRISTMAS VIOLETS. Last night I found the violets You sent me once across the sea From gardens that the winter frets, In summer lands they came to me. Still fragrant of the English earth, Still humid from the frozen dew. . To me they spoke of Christmas mirth, They spoke of England, spoke of you. • The flowers are scentless, black, and sere, The perfume long has passed away; The sea whose tides are year by year Is,set between us, chill and gray. But you have reached a windless age, The haven of a happy clime; You do not dread the winter's rage, Although we missed the summer lime. And like the flower's breath over sea, Across the gulf of time and pain, To-night returns the memory Of love that lived not all in vain. -.—Harper's Magazine.

GOOD LORD DELIVER US, I went to church, and with my aunt Knelt where the richest people kneeled; I listened to the rector's chant Oft broken a' the organ pealed— " Good Lord deliver us." Stained glass, and gilt, and velvet stools, With many a saint in fresco work I saw, and thought (0 fool of foo:s!) Of our plain. white-washed vi'lage kirk— Good Lord deliver us." I whispered, " Who is yonder man Gray-haired and praying so devout?" Quick glanced tiny aunt, as woman can And said, scarce turning head about, "Good Lord deliver us." " Director—bank! " she whispered me; "Defaulted —million dollars, dear— Heads every public charity," I clutched my purse and gasped in fear, " Good Lord deliver ns." "Bat he, dear aunty, over there, Who worships with such pions look; The one with apostolic air, Who chants 80 sweetly from his book— Good Lord deliver us?" "Stock-broker, love—a Crossus, too— Appropriated funds, they say— He'd make a splendid catch for you:' I hid my country face to pray. "Good Lard deliver us." I glanced around. There must be one Good min among these wicked men. "Pray what has that fair Christian done?" If each a face knows thieving, then Good Lord deliver us.

Nov AM ENGLISHMAN.—" Yes, as a rule. the English- man is a amain ceinpanion," said an Arkansas man who had just returned from a European tour. "I boarded a train in London bound for Edinburgh, Scotland. Shortly after entering the ,compartment I saw that I was to have a travelling companion, for a full, heavy man en- tered apd took a seat apposite to me. He seemed to be nervously afraid that .I would speak to him—seemed to recognise my nationality aud to dread my questions. 1 You needn't be anxious,' thought I, as the train sped along, 'for I would see you in Jericho before I would *peak to you. Confound an Englishman, anyway.' Whenever I ventuxed to look at him he would look away, and then, —him, whenever he looked at me rd look away. I was teaching him that an American could hold his tengue. 'alloon came, and we took our luncheon bas- kets and ate in silence.. The scenery was beautiful, the grassy slopes, graceful hills, and majestic trees charmed me, and I was almost,dying to say comething, but, as an old negro mammy wed express it, I let my. 'Oh, if I only had ,you off some place where no • one could see us, I would make you speak,' I mused. At; last, late in the evening, the aram reached Edinburgh. I , felt relieved when I left the train and got ,into a cab. 1 What are you waiting foil asked the driver. " 'Nuther genlaman.' The confounded:Eaglishman, un- able, it seemed, to get another conveyance, was forced to ride with rue. This amused nxr; for I knew it nearly Jellied him. We rolled along the street without glancing at each other. 'Well, I'll swear,' I mused. The sullen fellow and I were going to stop at the same lictel. We at near each other at supper, and after the meal we hap- pened to sit near each other on the verasdah. I looked at him with a frown.—' You needn't be seared,' tie re- marked; lam not gulag to speak to you:'—' And 1 am not going to speak to you either.'—' You infernal Eng- lishmen, said he, are so particular, I thought I'd show you that an American can ride all day with yen and not talk.'—' Who's an Englishman?' Boxnaa DAY.—In consequence of the niultiplicity'of business on Christmas-day, the giving of the Christmas- boxes was postponed to the 26th, St. Stephen's Day, which became the established Boxing-day. It was a privileged, day for all sorts of beggars, when the ' bell- men, the beadles, the street-sweepers, the chimney- sweeps, the charity-boys, the lamp-lighters, and the waits—singers of more or 'less doleful carols—went about to all doors and rapped for a Christmas-box. Old Pepys relates (1668) that he was called up by drums and trumpets. "These things and boxes," he adds, "have cost me much money this Christmas, and will do more." MOZART'S INTRODUCTION TO TRH PUBLIC.--If the true artist, as some cultured critics say, will recoil with hor- ror from the sensational, what (says the Pall Mall Gazette) must Mozart have felt on his first introduction • to the public?. The programme of his first performance_ drawn up by his father at Frankfort in 1764, has lately been discovered in Germany, and according to the Gar- tenlaube runs thus:—" My daughter twelve years old and my son of seven, the son being the great Mozart, will execute the concertos of the greatest masters on several kinds of pianos, and my boy on the violin, likewise. My , son will cover the fingerboard of the piano with a cloth and play as if it were not covered. He will guess both standing near or at a distance any note any accord sounded on the piano, on a bell, or any other instrument. In conclusion, he will improvise as long as desired both on the organ or the piano, in all keys, even the most difficult, as anyone' may choose. But his rendering of organ music differs greatly from that of the piano.' A Raman MAN.—It was an rinteresting time at the house of Dobbs, and finally when .the Doctor came out inta•the hall, Dobbs was in a state of excitment equal to •an election night. "Well, doctor ?" he said inquiringly, .and grabbing the physician's coat front with both hana. "Twins," responded the doctor briefly. "How—How— How many ?" he asked in a dazed manner. "The usual number," replied the doctor, smiling. "Oh, yes—Ah— excuse me, doctor. Boys or girls ?" Boys." "-Boys ?" " Yes." "Then I'm a ruined man !" "Ruined," was the surprised answer, "what's the matter with you?" "Why, doctor, for the last twenty years- it's 'been all I could do to meet the demands of my boys for my old clothes, and now, at my time of life, to have to com- mence wearing two pairs of pants at once, in order to keep up with the procession, is more than I can-under- take, and I see ruin, with a big R, staring me square in the face, and I can't make a move to ,defend myself." The doctor gave him a dose of chloral to quiet his nerves. A Paway RETORT.—There lived in Southern Ohio, in the early days of that State, one Judge G—, eminent in his profession as a lawyer, and well known for his suavity of manner and courtly bearing. The judge having been nominated for the office of County Judge, thought to surprise an eccentric genius by the name of Sam who was mauling rails on the judge's farm, and took occasion to mention it on his first visit to the -" Hills," as he called his place, when the following con- versation ensued :—" Well, Sam, what do you think?"— "Sometimes one thing, Jedge, an' sometimes 'nother.P— -" But, Sam, they have nominated me,as County Judge." —" They might a done wuss, Jedge. Howsomenever, don't holler till yer outen the woods." The Judge was ,duly elected, and on his next visit to the Hills thereafter announced the fact unctuously to Sam, who was in the woods, maul in hand. "Well, Sam I am elected by a large majority. What do you think of that?"—" Well, Jedge, down in our parts where I was raised, when we wanted a stopper, 'n' hadn' any cork, we ginnerally took a corn cob." The Judge passed on; Sam resumed his mauling. Ma. ARCHIBALD FORBES' CHRISTMAS"DINNER IM THE KILYBER Pass.—ln the short eastern gloaming the com- mittee of arrangement gathered in the mess-tent under a solemn sense of responsibility; on its members devolved the duty of setting out the tables. Not the, in strict truth, there were any tables; that luxury was as yet unknown- in the headquarter camp. But substitutes were available in planks raised on boxes, in the lids of those boxes, and in a couple of half doors, that had been picked up somehow. These appurtenances so disposed as to bear securely the viands that presently were to be spread, the question of seats gave some trouble. The regular company had stools or chairs of their own, but there were the two French noblemen who had straggled up the Khyber with letters ef introduction to Sir Sam, and my baggage with my campstool was not up. To the Frenchmen was allotted the empty champagne crate; 'to me was assigned the beer barrel set up on its end. , The mess ante-room was the camp street outside the dining tent; and at the fashionable late hour of eight we went in" to dinner, to the strains of the "Roast Beef of Old England." It was a right jovial feast, and the most cordial good-fellowship prevailed. He would have been a cynical epicurean who would have criticised the appointments; the banquet itself was above all cavil, Rummaging among some old papers the other day, I found the menu, which deserves to be quoted "Soup—Julienne. Fish—Whitebait (fnom the Cabul River). Entrées—Cotelettes aux Champignons, Poulets la Mayonaise. Joints—Ram and fowl, roast beef, roast saddle of mutton, boiled brisket of beef, boiled leg of mutton and caper sauce. Curry—Chicken. Sweets— Lemon., jelly, blancmange, apricot tart, plu,m pudding. Grilled sardines, cheese fritters, cheese, dessert." Truth compels the avowal that there was no table-linen, nor was the board resplendent with plate or gay with flowers. Table crockery was, deficient, or to be more accurate, therewweaasenaotenne., rA All al tthheerdizmhenskw, oe ruet ooff molt agl d s, and the iron tea-cups. But it tasted none the worse on this account, and let it be recorded that there were dawnpagne glasses, while between every two guests a portly magnum reared its golden head. Except "The Queen," of course, there were but two toasts after the feast—one was "Absent Friends," drunk in a wistful silence, and the other, the caterer's health, greeted with vociferous enthusiasm.—English Illustrated illiwazine. AN ENGLISH FARMER'S CHISTMA&J 300 YEARS AGO. *si We may not get anywhere a more vivid/picture of how an English yeoman-farmer and his fabzilY spent, Christmas in the reigns of the Tudor Queetia,lary and Elizabeth; than is presented in the quaint and homely, yet witty rhymes of Thomas Tusser, Gent., of Braham Hall, in Essex, who lived there in the' time of Edward the Sixth, and wrote his "One Hundred Points of Good , Husbandry," all done in easy verse, and first priatan 1557; afterwards enlarged to "Five Hundred Points," Szc., and printed in 1577, reprinted in 1580. ,Thomas Tusser was the "Poor Richard" of his age; his -maxims of good husbandry and thrifty hbusewifery are couched in pithy rhymes, such as might be committed to memory by the young men and maids, for useful application in future clays. Tusser was a hearty stickler for keeping up all good old customs, and for the worthy celebration of feasting-times. Let us hear him tell how his genera- tion of English country-folk held festivity at Christmas: A DESCRIPTION OF THE FEAST OF THE BIRTH OF CHRIST, COMMONLY CALLED CHRISTMAS.

Of Christ cometh Christmas, the name with the feast, A time full of joie to the greatest and least; At Christmas was Christ, our Saviour borne, The world through sinne altogether forlorne. At Christmas the dales coo begin to take length, Of Christ cloth religion eheefiy'take strength. As Christmas is onely a figure or trope, Bo onely in Christ is the strength of our hope. At Christmas we banket [banquet], the rich with the poore, Who then (but the miser) bat openeth his doore ? At Christmas of Christ 111141117 Carols we sing, , And give many gifts in the joy of that King. At Christmas of Christ we rejoice and be glad, As onely of whom our comfort is had At Christmas we joy altogether with mirth, For litt sake that joyed us all with his birth.

her doll* You see, he had changed his mind about cut- ting oft the scalp of her head. But when the nails were stuck in the bonnet, and he had raised the hammer to strike a blow that would have killed her, dear good pussy came into the room, and said, "Please, sir, pray let An* live!. I know she will be a good girl, and be kind-th everybody t" Annie cried and wept, and said, "Yes, indeed I will, for ever and ever !' And they begged and prayed for mercy, the sweet black cat fawn- ing upon the Master Dolly, and rubbing her head against his knees, until his sawdust heart was touched with pity. He stood up grandly, like a conquering hero in tfie act of forgiving his enemy, and said," Well, Annie, I will let you go! Be kind, be good, be free, be happy !" Most of the other Dolls said this was quite right Annie took good care of them all Eta long as they lived, but she never had any more new ones.

* * * At Christmas good husbands have corne on the ground In barne, and in Boller, worth many a pound, With plentie of other things, cattle and sheepe, All sent them (no doubt on) good houses to keepe. At Christmas the hardness of winter doth rage, A griper of all things and specially age: Then lightly poorepeople, the yqung with the old, Be sorest oppressed with hunger and cold. At Christmas. by labour is little to get, That wanting the poorest in danger are set, What season then better, of all the whole years, Thy needie poor neighbour to comfort and cheere? Surely the spirit of these lines, both in piety and in charity, is such as well accords with the event which is signalised by a Christian Christmas. But let us hear, in another piece, what was the sort of fare English far- mers feasted their families and guests upon during Christmas-tide, when Thomas Tusser wrote, nearly 330 years since. It was, we shall see, substantially what Christmas fare is now. The fashion in eating and drink- ing does not change with the centuries so much as that of dress does, though there are variations in cookery and new articles imported from abroad have within the last century 'been added to our dietary. Cmusrass HUSBANDLIE PARE. Good husband and huswife now cheefly be glad, Things handsom to have, as they ought to be bad; They both doo provide against Christmas doo come, To welcome good neighbour, good cheere to have some. Good bread and good drinke, a good tier in the hall, Brawn:, pudding, and souse, and good mustard withall. Beefs, mutton, and porke, shred pies of the best, Pig, veale, goose, and capon, and turkey well dresty Cheese, apples and nuts; jolly Carols to heare ; As then in the countrie is counted good cheere. What cost to good husband is any of this? Good household provision onely it is. Of other the like I doo leave out a menie, That costeth the husbandman never a penie. Did our yeoman ancestors fare amiss at Christmas, with the dishes quick following enumerated by good Thomas Tusser ? We wot not. This was the style of feasting in Essex and Suffolk then. Was Lancashire behindhand Evidence might be raked up that, if money was scarce in these Northern Counties in the sixteenth century, fat beeves, and pigs, turkeys, geese, and capons were plenti- ful. Our Lancashire bowmen could not have fought as they did at Flodden, and in other battles of the period, if they had not been both well bred and well fed. And despite the incalculable increase of England's wealth that-we are always boasting of, one might be fain to think that in every homestead in the country parts of Lancashire in 1884 the supply of Christmas edibles in- cluded, besides "good bread,' " brawne, pudding, and souse," "beefe' mutton; porke, shred pies" (or their modern equivalent, mince pies), "a pig, veale, goose, capon, and turkey," and for dessert, "cheese, apples, and nuts." At any rate, each bne of these Christmas dishes and dainties in vogue in L 557 may be had now by any English family whose head has the money to buy them withal. But honest Thomas Tusser has something more to say of Christmas. In a series of seasonable rhymes for each month of the year, full of "sage advices," come these under "Christmas" : CHRISTMAS. Get Joys and hull, woman, deck up thyne house; And take this sane bmwne, for to seeth and to souse. Provide us good cheere, for thou knowst the old guise ; • Old customes, that good be, let no man despise.' At Christmas be mery, and thank God of all. And feast thy pore neighbours, the great with the small. Yea, all the yere long, have an eie to the poore, And God sbal,l send luck, to keep open the doore. - Gond fruite and good, plenty, riotb well in thy, loft, Then lay for an orcharde, and cherishe it oft. Thy profet is mickell. the pleasure is muteh, At pleasure with profet, few wise men will gruteh. For plantes and for stoekes, lay &forehand to cost; But set or remove them, while twelvetide doe last. Set one from another, full twenty fete square, The better and greater they yerely will bare. A glossary of a new edition of Tusser's "Points of Good Husbandne " explains that "brawne," which occurs twice in the lines we have quoted, meant anciently the flesh of the wild boar; later, used for flesh generally. "Shred pies" were what we call mince pies, the meat being cut into shreds. "Souse" means "pig's feet and ears pickled." "bye and hull" to deck the house at Christmas, wear, ivy and holly. " Stocks "to be set or removed at " Twelvetide," mean young trees.

div.head: DOLLY'S REVENGE.
div.p: DOLLY'S REVENGE.

Once there was a little girl, who had too marl. dolls. She ought to have been a kind Mamma or a kind Nurse to all of them. But lam sorry to say, she was not , She threw them about, and trod upon them; she knocked!' them against the wall; she crammed the big one intb a doll's-house that was meant for the small ones; their arms and legs were torn off, and she did not send thei& to the Doctor to be mended. When she played at wash- ing and dressing them she did it so roughly that the paint was washed qf their pretty faces antbthe big comb tore off their flaxen hair. One cold day in winter, this cruel child put a poor little Dolly out in the garden. It was soon covered with snow, and the gardener swept , it up with his broom. He brought it to the kitchen, and when the careless little girl saw it, she was afraid it would die. The maids in the kitchen said if it died she would be tried for murder. So she held it to the fire, and then it got so hot that the wax of its body melted, and and they said it had'got a fever. When it was bed-time, this naughty child lay down, in her little white bed. She• had eaten her piece of Christmas,pudding and two mince pies, and an orange, and three figs, and some nuts and preserved fruit. But though she had had all these good things, Annie could not sleep. s She lay and tossed and kicked, and tumbled all the bed-clothes, and thought how wicked she had been to her poor little dolls. In the middle of the night, when she was not quite asleep, but only dreaming, she knew they were all dead, and it was she who had killed them. All their ghosts came at once ' to her bedside, crying out, "Here she is! Annie! Annie ! Annie !" Then they said, "„We are children now, ' and you are only a Doll! Your Papa and Mamma have I I taken us to live with them instead of you, and the gover- ness and servants will let us do whatever we like." They made Annie get up out of her bed; and the tall one, 1 with the wooden head and hands, and with the long naked I body and legs, made of white cotton stuffed with bran, took Annie all over the house. She coeld not run away, or fight, or scream, because she was now only a dal herself. At first she was rudely washed in a tub in the scullery, and her nice hair was pulled nearly off her head, while the broken points of the old comb stuck in her skin and hurt her very much. And her face was wiped with a dirty old dish-clout, and the soap got into her eyes, mouth, and nose. The tall Doll, which!had become a Savage because Annie had stripped off its clothes, and was almost bald like a Red Indian, told 1 Annie she was going to be scalped, but she must first be tortured, and frozen, and burnt. She thought, now they will carry me away into the wilderness, and she cried, "No, let me be in my own home !" Then the big Doll said," This is your house," and ptished-her into the doll's house, which was a small box, so that her arms and. legs stuck- out .;:,f the four windows. All the other Dolls laughed to see Annie shut up in prison. After that she I was taken out, and whirled round and round, until she came to the nursery window. Outside the snow lay on I the ground, and they threw her out. There she felt very cold, and cried until pussy, who had been hunting the , robins, came to take her part. When pussy mewed and squalled, the Dolls feared that people would come; so they brought Annie into the house. There were no ser- vants in the kitchen, but a fire was burning on the hearth. The little girl said, "Oh, lam so cold," and they held her a long time in front of the fire, so that she was quite scorched. There was a Plate and knife and bread and butter on the table, but the Dolls never gave her a' bit. She did not see if they ate any of it themselves; but she remembered that she had never given them any- thing to eat, nor a drop of tea. She was now very sorry and ashamed that she had treated them so badly. She, asked their pardon; but the toll Dolly, who was their leader and commander, said," Annie, why did you break ourdimbs ? why did you bruise our heads? Come and see, you cruel, wicked, girl," They made her go to a box called the Dolls' Hospital, which she had never cared to visit. It was full of arms and legs and battered heads; crushed waxen faces, with the eyes picked out, and cloth bodies with holes and wounds that let out half the sawdust. "Look at the dying and the dead !" said this angry Dolly, "and don't you know that you drove a nail into my skull last Tuesday week? Why shouldn't Ido the same with you? Than he got a hammer and two big nails, and was going to do it, but first he thought he 1 wculd put Annie's bonnet on her head, so as to fasten it on with the hail, which she had tried to do with one of

div.head: NOCTURNAL ADVENTURE.
div.p: A NOCTURNAL ADVENTURE.
BY Sitlit.

It is about ten years since I first made the acquaintance of Mr. Wilson, then of Osbaldeston Hall. It matters not how the acquaintance had been formed, but I had found out during the short time I had known him, previous to the date . . . .

I am now writing about, that he was as genial a man as one could wish to meet with. I had also been introduced to Mrs. Wilson, and I think I could not better describe her than by saying that she was a fitting' wife for a good hus- band. She seemed to me to be the very perfection of what one likes to imagine a farmer's wife ought to be. It was the morning after Christmas-day, and I was lying awake in bed, Wondering what to do with myself for the next two days. I had had what I considered a good Christmas. and I had now two days on my hands totally unengaged, and I was somewhat undecided as to the spend- ing of them. Some of my friends had gone to Preesall, a village near Fleetwood, where there were some shooting and some fishing to be had, and they had pressed me hard ago with them the day before Christmas; but as I like to have my 'Christmas dinner at home, I had declined, and I did not now care to follow. This and one or two more invitations had been disposed of, and I had decided to avail myself of Mr. Wilasn's of invitation to go to his house at Osbaldeston and spend a few days with him, amusing my- self by thinning his rabbits, and so on. When I had finally decided to go I at once jumped out of bed and began to prepare. Having dispased of an early breakfast, I put a ferret in a bag, half-a-dozen rabbit nets and a few dead lines in my pocket, and set out to walk the distance, six or seven miles. How well I remember the exhilarating effect the brisk walk in the clear frosty air had upon use that morning as I made my way over Mellor, down by the Bay Horse, and on towards Osbaldeston. What beautiful and fantastic shapes the tree and hedgerows assumad, with their covering of pare white anew; forming all sort, of patterns of diamond bejewelled tracery and festoons—and what a pleasant sounding, crisp crunching my feet made every step I took. How snag looked some of the cottages and farm-houses, with their snow-clad roofs and eaves, beautifully ornamented with glittering ley stalactites. As I got nearer my destination I was gratified with a sight of a rabbit or a hare now and then, skurrying into the wood. Suddenly as I came to the crest of a hill a large panorama bursts upon my view, with the Ribble and Osbal- deston Hall lying at the bottom of the decline, about a quarter of a mile away; and in five minutes more I am at the end of my journey. Osbaldeston is situated on the left bank of the Ribble, about a mile below the ancient Raman city of Rib- cheater, which is on the opposite bank. It was once a place of some consequence; and remains of its moat are still to be seen. It has attached to it a well wooded farm of 300 acres, and at the time I am writing of one field of what is called the park was used as a breeding ground for pheasants. I had capital sport, for Mr. Wilson's sheep dog had the best nose of any dog I was ever out with. If he marked a burrow or a hole there was invariably a rabbit or a rat; and he wasted no time over untenanted retreats. When it got dark and the sport was ended I felt heartily tired, and in good form for the substantial five o'clock tea we partook of. About eight o'clock we had supper, and then we passed the hours till bedtime in the seasonable pastime of story- telling; sitting around a fireplace of the old arched type, with a chimney up which a cart might have been drawn. Since the introduction of coal, however, a somewhat modern kitchen range had been built in, but so large was it that it was capable of accommodating on the fire two large pans side by side. Being more or less of an antiquarian, I made some inquiries from my host respecting the age and former owners of the hall and demesne, but found that he knew next to nothing about The place, as be was not interested in its past history. The only information that I could get was that there was an old lintel over one of the new shippon doors with some initials and the date 1593 on It; that he understood the place had originally belonged to the Osbal- destons, a powerful family, and that it had subsequently fallen into the hands of a monastic body. A little before twelve I suggested bed and was given a candle and shown up a flight of oaken stairs, into a room which was large enough for a ballroom. The very size of it gave me the shivers. It was so very large that, hesitating for a moment as I did just inside the doorway to take a survey, I was surprised to notice that I could, by the light of the candle, only just see nay bed in the distance. I found, too, that the door had no hasp on it, and would not keep closed. The room had a very antiquated appearance. The chimney breast, and mantelshelf, and the ceiling were orna- mented with a beautiful plaster and carved scroll. On the chimney breast were some initials relating to the Osbaldes- sons ; and on the pi,Nrs Aupporting the mantelshelf were two raised carved figured of females, whose nether limbs ,ended in more scrollwork. The walls were wainscotted all round with panels of dark oak in various geometrical figures which gave the room a very gloomy 'appearance. On the right and near the door was a large closet built of oak, the use for which 1 could not make out until I saw that on one side there was a square piece cat out of the panelling, and then I concluded that it had been used as a confessional. On the Booth side was the window, which was mullioned and tran- somed, and extended nearly the full width of the room. It was glazed the old fashioned way with small squares of glass fixed with lead. In looking through the window I saw that the snow had again begun to fall, and was being drifted against it by the wind, which was rising. The furniture of this wilderness consisted of a ponderous old mahogany four- poster bedstead, hung with dark crimson damask; a few cane chairs, a small table under the window, with a small swing mirror on it, some carpeting round the bed and a Brussels hearthrug in front of the fire-grate. I don't know how long I should have continued my ex- plorations had I not been warned by the falling of the wick of my candle that it was time to desist, seeing which I made all the despatch I could and got into bed. I do not know how long I had been asleep, but that I had been asleep there was no doubt, because I awoke with a start. I wondered what had awakened me, but could arrive at no satisfactory conclusion. The wind was soughing and moaning amongst the trees, and I could, or fancied I could just hear the snow as it was driven against the windows. I couldalso hear a gentle, irregular tapping at the window, which, though not very reassuring, in a strange place, I at last decided must be caused by the wind somehow. How- ever, after lying quiet and listening for some time I came to the conclusion that I must have been having an unpleasant dream, which had startled me out of my sleep. Partly satis- fied with this solution I was again composing myself when I heard something which completely upset my calculations. As I lay there in that big lonely room I became conscious that there was someone there besides myself. I could distinctly hear someone breathing, and breathing as if they were out of breath. I listened for a few seconds, and then I said " Who's there ?" There was no response to my ques- tion, but the breathing ceased. This did not exactly inspire me with confidence, but I really could not tell what to do next, and in my indecision I awaited fotther developments. In about two minutes, which seemed an hour to me, the breathing recommenced, and then, horror! I heard a sound as of two mortals in deadly conflict on the room floor. I listened till my ears nearly cracked. The roots of my hair felt as if they were creeping all over my head. A cold clammy perspiration began to ooze from every pore, and I felt that I was either in the presence of some awful tragedy, or that my unbelief in ghosts was being painfully shattered. The tension of my nerves was such that it was impossible for me to remain a passive listener for long, and though having an awful dread upon me of what I might possibly see, I sat up in bed and glared around as well as the dark- ness would permit. I could see nothing on the side the window was at, but when I turned my eyes to the other side of the bed I was nearly petrified, for there, not more than three yards away, and close to the floor, I could discern two eyes blazing in the darkness, nearly as plainly as I now see the paper upon which I write. Suddenly they vanished, and now commenced such a struggle about that room as I think never mortal in similar circumstances listened to. Now the combatants seemed to be in the middle of the room, now near the window, now under the bed, then they receded and got to the other end of the room; and all the time a heavy, quick breathing could be heard, and occasionally a kind of a gurgle, as if someone was being choked. Once a chair was knocked over. Now they begin to approach the bed again; nearer and nearer they come, until they get so close I can stand it no longer, and making up my mind to get out of the room I shout, "Whatever is there in the room ?" and jump out of bed and rush towards the door, but have not got more than three paces when I fall over a living body, and hear such An unearthly yell as nearly made my hair stand on end, and precipitated my movements con- siderably. Recovering my feet I ran towards the entrance to the room as fast as my legs could carry me, but finding the wall instead, I grope my way along it till I find the doorway, bolt through it and close the door. It would be easier to imagine my feelings than describe them as I stood there in my shirt on that cold winter's morning. I have been in some strange positions, but never in one to equal that. And what made it worse it was darker than the bedroom I had quitted, and though I was dreadfully frightened at the time, it struck me as strange, because I had noticed that there was a window on the landing and I could not now see it. I was also afraid to move lest I should fall downstairs, and, taken altogether, my position was worse than awful. My suspense was soon ended, for a few seconds after I had got out of the room I could hear a match being struck, and directly after I heard Mr. Wilson's voice close to me asking where I was. I said, " l'm here." He said," Where? I cannot see yen." I said. "Here on the landing," but he, judging from the sound where I was, opened the door, and then I discovered that instead of being on the landing I had got into the confessional. He said, "Whatever was that noise; and what are you doing out of bed 2" I said, "There's something dreadful happened in this room ; th9.e's somebody either killed or very near it." " Somebody killed," he ejaculated ; "whatever do you

Not one in all the hundreds assembled drank a cup more full of pleasure than did George Sefton. He had heard this noble epic in music of the Messianic Advent many a time before, but now as the alternating recit, air and chorus came round with their beautions and inspiring imagery, their pas- sages of soothing tenderness, their pathetic appeals, and their joyous triumph, the infinite depth of love and passionate yearning of that divinest of songs," He shall feed His flock like a shepherd," the accumulating fervour and grandeur of the choruses, his heart was filled wills a strangely mistic glow he had not felt for many a day. It hardly comports with my purpose to follow further the course of the masic. My business is with George Sefton I and the young lady who sits a few yards to his right; to both these individuals this evening was fated to be the most eventful in their lives. During this first half of the performance he had spied Miss Foster, whom he had met ones or twice before. He remembered her as a gentle-mannered girl of modest ex- pression and quiet grace of mien, but with a quick shooting eye betokening rapid perception and judgment, but beyond a soft and transient twitter of pleasure at these former meetings; of a short half-hour be was utterly uncon- scious of any regard. He took a chair beside her, and both plunged into conver- sation upon the performance. "Who are those people there," said she, "with a big music book apiece?" "Oh, they are the great musical critics of the town." "I don't think they are very well behaved."

"How so?" "They have made such a fuss, and chattered shame- fully." "Oh, I dare say. Maybe you're of my opinion about them and the ilk of them." "What is your opinion?" she asked. "That they are a set of hurdy-girdies—contemptible handle-turners." ' "Of what P " said Miss Foster, with a comical smile, and a strong rising inflection. "Music churners," retorted be, "if you like it better; a trio of tune folk nabs and upstart humbugs." To this she answered by the merriest rippling laugh, and inclined her head in assent. "Yes," he continued, "they are right in myline of sight, and I couldn't help being witness to their stupidity. These people are abject slaves to staves and bars, and haven't as much soul as a well-drilled drum-stick. Did you see them all get into quite a flutter of nudging head-poking scribble and giggle when that new contralto nervously slipped and mangled a bar in 'He shall feed His flock?' but she strug- gled right, and nearly all the song was a genuine and beau- tiful rendering. The girl has got a heart below her throat, and that's what these fellows haven't. Her musical instinct brcught her in touch with the spirit of the composer, and despite her lapses in the mechanism she was really a more truthful interpreter of both poet and composer than some of your stars I have heard who are mere musical machinists, whose hope is to be created with a barrel over their windpipe, spiked to a tune. They may starch and furbelow themselves into musical dandies to boot, and cheat themselves and their like into the illusion that they are what they are not and never can be while earthly breath is in them, namely, artistes. I told one of them once that a good song should be a work of fine art every time it was sung; hie answer was a vacant stare—a big one, too." "Pray, get your breath, Mr. Sefton, get your breath," here put in Miss Foster, with an arch pout upon her dainty mouth. "Ay, ay," responded George "just so, but I tell you I have seen 60 much of this canti lose patience. There are a lot of people who make an idol god of the stave and they fall down and worship it. It never enters their pates that it can at best only be a finger post to the composer's feel- iog—that it is but a row of dry bones until the spirit of life Is breathed into it by a living soul. You know I don't believe this sort of people ever really enjoy an oratorio; they wilfully take the Stone and cast away the Bread. I find the best way to enjoy a performance is to quietly pon- der over the words at home, to get your mind filled with the dramatic feeling—the pictorial spirit—to bother little with the note-book, and attend well to the orchestra. Keeping hold of the vital intimacy between recit , air and chorus; the performance will then impress you, as a whole, with pano- ramic vividness, sequence, and power, and yen then come away inspired and helped for the turmoil of the morrow. " I agree with every word you say," responded Miss Fos- ter, "you must give a lecture. Get all the savants, entice, and learned perple to come and hear you. lam sure every one of them will be converted right off." At this quiet joke, a mixture of fun and satire, George laughed, saying—"Well. well, I dare say there will be some thing to say on the other side." But now the fiddles are tuning, the conductor's baton is uplifted, the second part begins.

Any man who is either sordirunsympathetic, or dirty in , his habits, and who is addicted to burglary, murder, and other recreations of the kind, is a human hog. The great objection to the human hog is that he is not edible. It is calculated that if all the human hogs_ now at large were worked up into sandwiches, the rest of the human race could be fed free for 997 years and three days. SPRING CHICKEN.—The chicken that seems never to have had a beginning, on account of the great age exposed by its toughness. It is a common thing to say that a boarding- house spring-chicken is so called becalms your knife springs off it, and because the only way to cut it up is to freeze it stiff and then go to work at it with and axe and chisel. It was believed by the ancients, according to Herodotus, that every chicken belonged to spring, jest as violets do, and that diners were fooled because they didn't compel restaurateurs I to put the year of every hen's birth on the hen, and guaran- tee it, like they do wine. Then, if a man living B.C. 8 got a chicken branded B.C. 2 it would be his own fault. It was once thought that a spring-chicken would make an effective bomb, and the experiment was tried without success. The powder failed to burst the spring-ch'ckeu. But the S. C. has always proved a great engine of war as a solid shot. CAT.—An animal with four legs, one tail, one head, and nine lives. Although the cat has but one head, he naturally seems to have about half a dozen when singing "Come into ! the Garden, Maud S." on a balmy summer night beneath; the throbful stars. The cat and the bootjack will never lie I down together, because they are alien to each other. Thei bootjack is a hand-made bird that flies through the air asl iwift as a falcon, and never hits a cat in the same place' twice. Sometimes cats have holes made in their ears. The proper way to make holes in a cat's ears is to start at one end and force the instrument right through the cat's head to the other ear. Then the cat won't trouble you anymore. If you put a cat in a bag, and take him off a long distance from your house, and let him out to lose him, you will find him asleep by the stove on your return home. When you put a cat in a bag, you should place a stone in also, and throw the whole business into a pond or river. And then when you return home you will not find the cat asleepby the stove. PARROT.—A feathered biped which utters articulate sounds at the wrong time. This creature is the only known rival of the B flat cornet. The parrot usually travels alone, and humanity is unanimous in the opinion that Nature did her prettiest when she ordained this thw. The parrot usually inhabits a large iron cage. It sleeps upside down, like a bat, and at incoherent intervals. It feeds on crackers and cheese and human fingers and old hair-cloth and spring bonnets and silk dicers and other dainties of that general nature. The parrot has frequent wrestling matches with the English language, and always collars the gate-money. The parrot is not mentioned in sacred history. No respectable prophet would acknowledge acquaintanceship with the par- rot, for these birds are imbued with the spirit of objurgation. Boys learn to swear, but parrots swear by nature. In com- bination with a monkey, a parrot can do much toward imitating the great nether gloom of the hereafter. The countenance of the bird has a Semitic cast, but his is mis- leading; for he is more like Pharaoh, in that he constantly hardeneth his heart and maketh it lively for those who cannot find straw to make bricks and kill him with them. Don.—A quadruped reuarded by man as the most in- telligent of the brute creation. There are many brands of dog, and each dog seems to be a specialist. The pointer points, the setter sets, the bulldog fleas, and chases Sir Romeo while the moon is sailing down the purple vault of heaven. Some dogs will watch your house, others will watch your beef-steak as it is broiling on the fire, and wait long and patiently for a favourable opportunity to secure it. One dog likes to remain in the house all night, while another wouldn't stay in the house for anything, but delights in stealing out and running up and down the yard all night barking with might and main. It is a popular satire to assume that through the sophistry of the knight of the shambles the dog ultimately becomes sausage. But this is probably a campaign lie. The dog is naturally a nomad, but nomad dog.

The thoughtna gaze, tneupturised---•—" She reflected that the rhyme which most readily GIo. curred was nose," and that was not precisely *what she meant. So she confined herself to more thought- pictures, and found them sufficiently satisfying. By a natural instinct, which, however, she could not quite interpret, she forbore telling her sister Alice—her only companion—of the rendezvous, and when the heavy morning had past, when the toilet had been made with quite unusual care, and Miss Julia Jeffer- son had stepped out on what she firmly believed to be errand of life or death to her, our strong-minded friend had a sudden sensation of faintness, and closed her hand tightly on her cotton umbrella, J-- square was reached at last, and sure enough, Miss Julia, gazing up hastily, with emotion, could perceive a gentleman, tall and well-proportioned, but well within the twenties, awaiting her approach. Another half-minute, and the two were standing Lee to face; the gentleman had stretched out a hand, and had given a welcoming smile. Miss Julia's heart sunned itself in its warmth, and she had already placed the handsome young stranger at one side of the domestic hearth to which she assigned her maiden self. "Miss Jefferson," he began, (he certainly had a beautiful voice), "I do not know how you will regard this unwarrantable intrusion on your time, but I could find no other way of getting an interview." "Speak not of that, Mr. Carthew," said Julia tenderly, "when the heart is the guide—" "My dear Miss Jefferson, how wonderfully you anticipate me. Let me cut a long story short. I met you and the young lady whom I have since learned is your sister, at a picture gallery some three weeks ago. It was a case of love at first sight," (" Oh, those intuitions I" sighed Julia, blissfully). I gathered your name and address from the secretary of the society, who chanced to know you, but in spit* of all my efforts could get no farther. What could I do (Poor fellow," thought Julia, "what indeed? ") Her charms, her—" , "Her! "shrieked poor Miss Jefferson, in an awful note of exclamation." You mean" . . . And then the truth flashed upon her, and she broke out, for the first time perhaps since her childhood, into bitter and uncontrolled weeping. The stranger's utter astonish- ment speedily gave place to a sense of the mischief he had unintentionally done, and with kind words and the most delicately formed apologies that he could offer, he endeavoured to soften the bitter- ness of the blow. For a time poor Miss Julia was not to be consoled. Her castle had been but of a day and night's growth, but it had been boldly built and bravely furnished, and now it had tumbled like a pack of cl!.sds over her desolate head. At length she stood quiver- ing with shame, but pale and collected, before Mr. Carthew, and the words came slowly: "Forgive, sir, a foolish woman's fancy. You wish to know my sister, and if I hear well of you I will try what I can do for you both." She was as good as her word. The happy court- ship ran quickly through its course, and, though Julia had Boomed to make such a request, Alice's lover kept the secret of the interview in J— Spare; Miss Julia went back to her Sociology,amd constructed a theory of Society from which marriage was con- spicuously absent. But when a small baby came to the wedded pair, and had the name of Julia bestowed on it, she changed her tune a little, and began the first chapters of a "Political Economy for Children," iu which she intends that Julia the Second shall have I. ?borough grounding,

—Sluti,eTere. I have an old engraving of young Master Cupid, sallying forth he the pride of the morning, with his trusty bow and quiver. He looks just what he is. the most pert and wic- kedly whimsical creature conceivable. Sometimes, if it snit his humour, he consents to please his voteries and trot in respectable fashion and in irreproachable traciLgs, but presently his humour changeth and he kicks his s,;angled leathers into bits, and now—whit a rumpus and a riot ! Away goes be with the power of a god and the antics of a madman, He meets the grandest "masher" or most sedate proper man in town; he pulls his toughest arrow and tumbles him a somersault right over his crown in the mud, and capers round him fiddling on his bow while he sprawls or be slyly pokes his nose round the corner, takes aim, and ;away flies home his sharpest spike, he laughing most con- sumedly at the shrieks and torments of his victim. If you attempt to remonstrate he will probably laugh or jeer at you, adjust his thumb to his nose for thirty seconds and whirl away in a polka gallop. He delights to scatter to the winds the schemes of wise people, and send dismay and confusion among the high and mighty. He is in ecstacy when he brings a King Cophetna to the feet of a beggar maid, or tumbles a coronet into the lap of a ballet girl. The odder the prank the more to his liking; to handcuff in steel a short fat man to a long lean woman—to net them march- ing in the street cheek by jowl, in the unalterable and blissful conviction that they are of the same exact girth and of identical height would so delight him that after such a feat he might unstring his bow and cover his sheath for a short holiday Ah, truly, truly, without navies and armies he rules the wide world o'er, "King of kings, and Lord of lords." As he lists, he tips his shafts with the angry sting of the wasp, or the soothing honey of the bee. Now, our friend Mr. George Sefton had come to consider himself quite dart proof to any love nonsense, and to hold in some contempt all who proved otherwise. It is ivy business here briefly to narrate how the little David of the bow and arrow slew this Goliath. I shall be a faithful scribe and detail all that he chose to communicate, and the reader may rest assured that nay story shall be true... .

George -Sefton had worked 'himself up to a position of high responsibility ha a large cotton-mill. He was a man of grave years. He was so good a fellow that a long time ago he had discovered and realized that he was but a dunce on God's planet, and at this point he took the turn in grow- ing wise. Faults he Mid, like every other created mortal, and herein lay some of his wisdom, that he knew it. Fair judging and straightforward in business of strict probity, true as steel ha friendship and virtue, frank and transparent to friends, and of generous instincts to all. He quietly doled more florins in a year than some of his station did in a lifetime. A detester of those low jokes and petty con- ceits of some men in respect to their relation of women— such in broad charcoal are the outlines of George Sefton's character. I said he had grown wise. There was one subject on Which it may be said, however, that he had grevrn foolieh ; he had once in his life been in love, or thought so; and Pendenis like had lived to marvel at himself, and be thankful it did not end in a wedding, but since then he had skated over the frosts of a dozen winters, and his wounds had long since healed. If love's plumet had at that time sounded the range and depth of his heart it had grown to be almost as a faded memory; fully to know him- self again, Ile was in need of a re-awakening, and before the remaining half of the present week had run its course he was strangely destined to this experience. Be now believed himself to be a philosopher in these matters and that love was nine-tenths an imagination. His theory was that given three or four sensible girls of good taste, homely, and good housekeepers, it was immaterial which be took to wife; it was simply a question of weigh- ing and posing a nice calculation between them. Though he would not for the world advocate wedding for money, he had a sneaking feeling that his friends Alackloom and Skicqwill, whose wives both managed the house and paid the bills, looked very contented indeed.
A tender conscience is an inestimable blessing; that is, a conscience not only quick to discern what is evil, but instantly to shun lt, as the eyelid closes itself against a mote.

_ THE KHARTOUM EXPEDITION. KORTI, SATURDAY.—One of the Nile boats on its way here has capsized 17 miles below Korti. Among those on board were two newspaper correspondents. All the occu- pants were saved by the pinnace of Her Majesty's ship Inflexible, but the higgege was lost. The navigation of the river is daily becoming more difficult, owing to the shifting of the sand. The arrival of the boats is thus delayed. KORTI, SUNDAY —The field telegraph is now in working Order: The Engineers' under the personal supervision of Lord Wolseley, have been making experiments in felling trees with gun cotton, the object being to ascertain the quickest method of obtaining timber for fuel for the steamer. The experiments were very successful. The natives came in to-day in large numbers, bringing produce and cattle, and a regular nsareet was held. The chief products of he coun- try are dates' salt, wheat, cotton, and cattle. A church parade was beld this morning, which all the troops attended. Mr. O'Neill officiated. WADY HALFA, MONDAY.—S:applies are being collected at ,Xeroeko with a view to sending them to Abu "lamed if necessary. - Koren, Moteretv.—The last detachment of the South Staffordshire it,giment has arrived here, along with two companies of tho, Susaex Regiment. From Debbeh to this place the Ree is covered with a long line of boats. Whalers are daily arliviog. An hospital has been erected hero in a shady spot, and is ready to receive any cases of sickness. Most of the Men who are ill are suffering from the effects of very hard rowing. KORTI, TDESDAY.—Four sections of the heavy Camel Corps reached Kerti leeday. Christmas will be celebrated in camp with as much fstivity as the circumstances will Permit. Double rations and a gratuitous allowance of tobacco will be served out to the troops, and various amuse- ments are being prepared for tbe evening, which all the tifficere, from the tieneral downwards, will attend. The camp is to be li.r,titerl up with huge bonfires. • WADY HALFA, TUESDAY.—Sir Evelyn Wood and Colonel Fraser started southwards to-day, Et.iYP !lAN DEBT.

CAIRO, SATURDAY.—At four o'clock this afternoon the reply of the Egyptian Government to the claim of Ger- many and Russia to representatioe on the Clime of the Public Debt was delivered to the Russian and German Dip- lomatic Agents. It is to the effort that E:typt cannot single handed change the Law of Liquidation, but as Austria and France haversupported the demand of the two Empires, and Italy has stated that she sees no inconvenience in acceding to it, it is only neceseary to corns to an understanciLrgab rut the proper mode and period of cirrying it into effect. Egypt will accordingly have great pleasure in associating herself with the demand of Germany and Russia as soon as an understanding between all the signatorien of the Law of 'Liquidation has been establisl,ed. It is believed that the German and Russ:an Diplomatic Agents will verbally .express to Nubar Pasha their dissatisfaction at the above reply. CAIRO, TIIESDAY.—In diplomatic circles it is believed that Germany and Russia will reiterate their demand for representation on the Caisse of the Public Debt, at the same time asking Egypt to give an unconditional consent for herself, and to undertike to elicit a reply from those Powers who have not consented.
- - CHRISTMAS DAY ON THE NILE. Konn, THURSDAY, 3.40 P —Chistmas is being kept as -a complete holiday in the camp. Early in the morning there was a grand church parade, which was attended by

4(teen hundred troops. s Koun, THURSDAY, 10 P.R.—Before the camp-fire concert 'was inaugurated to-night Colonel Swains, on behalf of Lord Wolseley and Sir Redvers Buller, read the following tele- • gram, which had been received by the Commander-in-Chief from his Royal Highness the Duke of Camorid.ge and the Marquis of Harlington :—" Our united best wish,s to your- self and troops at this festival season. May Success attend your efforts." This message was received with cheers The festive proceedings were opened with great eclat. THE MAIIDI'S PRF.PARAIIONS FOR FIGHTING, - Cam), WEDNESDAY.—A telegram front the Mudir of Dongola of yesterday's date announces that a Bedouin has arrived there from Orruittrman, which plan he left 15 days - ago. The man, after being a prisoner there with the Mandi's uncle, was sent with a letter to Mohammed-el-Khair, the Mandi's Ameer at Berber, stating that in compliance with the latter's request for reinforcements in view of the ap- proach of the English the Mabdi had despatched seven corps to Berber. The Beduin adds that Khashmil Moos, who was sent by General Gordon to Shendy, has returned to Khartoum with troops and boats. THE POWERS AND EGYPT.

come to an onderatand:ng to tacitly regard the proposAls of the British Government ,ith respect to Egyptian finance as settled in the event of England expressly demanding an answer.

div.p: FRANCE AND CHINA.

PARIS, SATURDAY.— The Ndtional of this evening publishes a despatch from Shanghai stating that China re- cently made some conciliatory overtures to M Patenotre, the French Ambassador, who was, however, instructed by M. Ferry to reject them, as a-ms alone must now decide the dispute between the two countries. WEDNESDAY.—Advices from Pekin published by •the Torop3 state that the Board of Censors has proposed Sentence of death on Maki-en-Chang, Li Hung Chang's secretary, whom it holds responsible for the Tientsin Treaty. It is, however, believed Hitt Li Hung Chang will intercede on his secretary's behalf and be able to save him,

div.head: VIENNA BANK FRAUDS.
div.p: THE VIENNA BANK FRAUDS.

VIENNA, SATURDAY.—The satch of Kufflea's residence and Jsuner's office lasted until nine o'clock yesterday even. jog. At the former two boxes containing papers were seized, audio the cash.lx,x, which up to the present had not been opened, ZOO florins in clsh were found, together with a pocket.book containing acceptances. Altogether acceptances to the amount of 2000,000 11 wins have been found at Kuftlar'a house. KulllA's bookkeeper was eximihed this morning with a view to ascertain particuLr3 concerning his employer's business. ANOTHER B INK TRAGEDY IN VIENNA. . .

VIENNA, MONDAY.—Joan Lucas. chief of the securities department of the Giro and Casservenin Bank, and brother- in-law of Dudley, a superior official of the sune institution arrested last week week on the charge of embezzling 166,000 florins' has committed sui,,ide. It N stated that he was lin- pelledto this act by the reproaches addressed to him for neglect of his duty. THE UNITED STATES. NEW Yuan, SDNDAY.—There are indications of a grow- ing determination to press for retaliatory measures against German exports in view of the continued prohibition by Germany of American Pork, the recently pronounced hos- tility against Americ‘n petroleum, and the threatened adoption of a discriminating tariff favouring Russian oil. A NAVAL FIGHL-400 PERSONS KILLED AND IV DUN DR P.

Naw YORK, WEDNESDAY,—lfitelligetlee recdved here from Panama states that an engleurnent between the Go- vernment steamer Ecuidouan and the rebel vessel Hualoh has been fought off Los Cruzilas. The latter vessel cap- tured the Ecuadouan, and it is said that 400 persons were killed and wounded. Another Government vessel subse- quently succeded in recapturing the Eculdouan from the rebels. It is stated that there have been more encounters on land between the forces of the Government and the rebels. SIEAMERS IN COLLIS ON. FLUSHING, SUNDAY The Harwich steamer Ipswich, while coming last night from Antwerp, ran down the Eng- lish vessel Stanton, lying wind-bound at anchor off this port. The latter sank, but her c ow, with the exception of Captain Brown and the mate, were saved. The Ipswicb, which sustained serious damage, returned to Antwerp this morning. TREATY WITII SPAIN.

MADRID. MOND—AY-..-A-COOrd-i-Dg t; ';-Cieclgration signed tO•day by the British Minister and the Minister for Foreign Affairs, the Spanish Government will present to the Cortes a draft law authorising the granting to England of the most- favoured-nation treatment, as soon as the House of Corn. Mons has agreed to the extension of the le. scale of wine duties from 28 deg. to 30 deg. England will abandon the idea of the mixed commission stipulated for in the protocol of last year. The definite treaty will not be negotiated until 1888. THE GERMAN ANNEXATIONS IN THE SOUTH PACIFIC.

BERLIN', MONDXY.—Official information confirms the re- port that the German flag has been hoisted at several points of New Gninea and the Now Britain Archipelago. It is ex- plained that this step has been token in order to place the Garman settlements and commercial stations in that region under the protection of the empire, in accordance with the wish expi eased last summer by German subjects interested in the matter. THE STATE TRIAL AT LEIPSIC. LEIPSIC, MONDMl.—Judgmant was delivered to-day in the Anarchist trial. Reinslorf, Rupsch, and Kuchler were sentenced to death, and Holzhauer and Bachmann to ten years' penal servitude. Solingen, Rheinbach, and '1 oller were acquitted. On the minor counts sentence of 15 years' penal servitude was also p3ssed on Rheinsdorf and of 12 years on Rupsch and Enchler, super- seded by the death smtenee. but this is, of course, A BURMESE TOWN SACKED. Gnarl-a, MONDLY.—It is rumoured that the Burmese town of Bhamo hoe been sacked and THE GERMAN ANNEXATIONSPUIaue d b Kakhyens. MELBOURNE, TUESDAY.—The Hon. James Service, Pre- mier of Victoria, has invited the Governments of the other Australian colonies to unite in protesting against the Ger- man annexations in the Pacific. THE SOCIALISTS IN AUSTRIA. _

• PESTII, TUESDAY—A Socialist printing press was dis- covered and seized yesterday by the police in an apartment occupied by a woman in a house at New Pesti'. Numerous Socialist papers and manuscripts were also seized on the premises. A compositor named Franz Spielman and the woman who had let the apartments were seized. THE BOERS PREPARING FOR HOSTILITIES.
CAPETOWN. SATURDAY.—A numbff of armed Boers are leaving tha Transvaal for the border, the President vainly endeavouring to stop them. FRIBTING IN ASHANTEE.

CAPE COAST CASTLE, DEC. O.—A. body of Ashantees at- tacked Mansua on November 12, but were repulsed. Their leader and 40 other members of the party were taken priso• ners, and will be detained pending the decision of the colo- nial Government. The new King of Ashanteo will be crowned after Christmas.

div.head: GFNERA.II NEWS.
div.p: GFNERA.II NEWS.

------- The sale of the Syston Park library, which concluded on Saturday, has realised a sum of £23,000. The Rev. H. Ward Beecher declares that the statement published by the Pall Mall Gazette that he was to succeed Minister Lowell is "ridiculone." The ancient parish church at Deane, near Bolton, was for- mally re-opened on Monday by the Bishap of Manchester ' after being restored at a cost of £2,400. A large spinning mill at Dundee, owned by Messrs. Morison, Buchart, and Anderson, was completely destroyed by fire on Monday afternoon. The loss is stated at nearly £40,000. The second mate and boatswain of an American ship were remanded at Birkenhead, on Saturday, charged with murdering a seaman whom they are alleged to have syste- matically ill-treated. At Chester, on Saturday, Mr. R. Briscoe, contractor, was fined £lO for having neglected to furnish the water bailiff of the Mersey with information as to the intended removal of a quantity of dynamite. The Leicester magistrates on Saturday committed for ti cal a young man named Renfreee described as a private tutor, on several charges of defrauding tradesmen by offering worthless cheques in payment for goods. At a Conservative meeting at Radcliffe on Saturday, the Hon. A. F. Egerton, M.P., moved a resolution expressing hearty approval of tbe action of the Conservative leaders, which action "had resulted in the passing of the Franchise Bill, with the prospect of a representation of the people in a complete and equitable manner." MERSEY SHIPPING TRADE.—The total amount of ship- ping. steam, and sail launched during the 5 ear now closing from the Mersey shipyards is about 45,000 tons, or 2,000 tons in excess of last year. The principal buikiers have at present a satisfactory number of vessels under construction, but the prospects ot trade for next year are not very favourable. Of late the inquiry has been mainly for sailing ves.ele. MURDER IN LONDON. At the Central Criminal Court on Monday, a youn,,,t barmen n tined Horace Robert Jay, was sentenced to dead, for the murder of Florence Ellen Kemp, a young worn ,n with whom he had lived for some time, and whom he suspected of .a preference for another man. Jay cut the woman's throat, and afterwards attemp- ted to take his own life. The defence set up was insanity. A LIFE ASSURANCE CASE.— The trial of the action brought against a life assurance company by a Mrs Lotinga to recover the amount of a policy effected on the life of her husband, a Sunderland money lender, has ended in the dis- charge of the jury without their agreeing to a verdict. The contention of the company was that the deceased man was, contrary to the representations made at the time of the pro- posal for assurance, a man of intemperate habits, and further that he had committed suicide. The evidence was of a most conflicting character, and the bewilderment of the jury will surprise nobody. THE PROPOSED REFORM OF THE HOUSE OF LORDS.—Tne following letter is published as having been addressed by Lord Rosebery to a large number of Peers :—'Lansdowne House, Berkeley-square, December 18, 1884.—My Lord,—l venture to ask you, if you are favourable to the general prin- ciple of the reform of the House of Lords (without pledging yourself to any particular method or to any views of mine), to be so good as to communicate with me, so that concerted action may be taken in the matter. Perhaps, too, you may , be able to communicate the names of other peers who are favourable to the idea.—l am, dm., ROSEBERY. ' THE Twee, OF ELLIS FRENCH.—James Ellis French, late head of the detective department in Ireland, has, on a third trial, been convicted of conspiracy to procure the commission of unlawful acts. He was sentenced to two years' imprisonment. Mr. Justice O'Brien acknowledged that the prisoner's position was one which had exposed him to a good deal of attack and animosity, but in passing sen- tence he said that the verdict of the jury had his unquali- fied concurrence. This termination of a wearisome case should have an appeasing effect on the irreconcilable party in Dublin ; but it must be remembered that with many of them agitation is a profession. LIBERAL MEETING AT MOSSLEY.— The Liberals Of Mossley held a meeting on Saturday, on the occasion of the formal opening of a new Liberal Club in that town. The chief speakers were Mr. Leake, M.P., Mr. Agnew, M.P., and Mr. W. Summers, M.P. Resolutions were adopted expres- sing confidence in the Government, and thanking them for , having, in the face of much opposition, passed the Fran- chise Bill and introduced a bill for the redistribution of seats. Each of the hon. members referred to the scheme of proportional representation, and expressed the opinion that it was impracticable, and that the Government plan would best secure the proper expression of the will of, the people in Parliament. ATROCIOUS MURDER AT WINDSOR.— A murder of an atrocious character was discovered at Windsor, on Monday, in a low neighbourhood, known as Victoria Cottages. A married woman, named Maria Shill, aged thirty-two' had been missing since Friday, and her husband, Joseph Shill, who went away about the same date, returned on Monday morning, but almost immediately went away again. The deceased was found lying under the bed, with her skull 'smashed in by some heavy, blunt instrument, and had evi- dently been dead some days. The bed was covered with blood, and the doctor who examined the body found a severe contusion behind the left ear. The body has been removed to the mortuary. The husband, who is somewhat deformed, was employed by Mr. Sharp, tailor, of Windsor. He was on Monday night arrested for the murder, at Egham. It is said that marks of blood were found upon his clothes. The Windsor Coroner held an inquest on Wednesday. The evi- dence showed that the accused had killed the poor woman j by repeated blows on the head with a heavy iron weapon. A verdict of "wilful murder" was returned, and Shill was committed for trial. CONSERVATIVE MEETING AT CHORLEY.— Colonel Stan- ley, M.P., and Sir R. A. Cross, Ml'., were present on Mon, day evening at a Conservative meeting in the Town Hall- Chorley. The former, in moving a resolution endorsing the action of the Conservative leaders in recant controversies, said the party had no cause to regret the position they oc- cupied on the reform question. He thought the Liberal and Conservative leaders had joined in an honourable attempt to solve that question, and if Parliament would address it- self in a business-like way to , the arduous though not im- possible task of next session a settlement equally creditable to both sides would be reached. Sir. R.Cross, who secon- ded the resolution, said it would have been a national dis- aster if affairs had been So managed as to allow a general election to take place on the enlarged franchise without redistribution. That danger now was averted by the safeguards which had been obtained by the Conservative leaders. A FAMILY DROWNED IN THE BITER DEE Early on Saturday evening a number of persons residing at Queen's Ferry, on the Flintshire side of the river Dee, engaged a boat to convey them across the river to a pablichouse called the Ferry Inn, immediately opposite, where a usual Christ- mas draw is held in the evening. At the hour of ten o'clock —the hour for closing—the parties left the premises to re- turn borne, and, after entering the boat on the Cheshire side, nothing of note happened until they had proceeded some distance. One gentleman in the boat suddenly re- marked that his feet were wet, and as soon as he had spoken these words water was perceived to be rushing in from a defect on one side of the boat. The boat filled so rapidly that it sank in a moment, and all the occupants struggled in the water some time to save themselves. Howevee, nine gentlemen succeeded in reaching the ferry, some of them swimming while the others held to the oars. A man named Robert Jackson, his wife, and chill were drowned. The stories of a few of the survivors regarding the occur- rence are of a thrilling character, as the night was very dark. FIRE IT WINDSOR STATIdN.—A fire, caused by an explo- sion, broke out about three o'clock on Saturday morning in the parcel-office of the Great Western Railway Station, at Windsor, but was prevented from spreading to the body of the building. The parcel-office was, however, burnt out, and a number of parcels destroyed, but the ticket-office close by was not damaged. A thorough inquiry Woe instituted , by the railway officials and the police into all the facts con- nected with the fire and its origin, and an examination was carefully made of the remains of the burnt packages in the luggage-room. These inquiries and the evidence obtained by questioning the various claimants who applied for lost parcels during the day have placed it beyond doubt that the fire was not due to an explosion, as was at first sug- gested.. What it may have originated in cannot be stated, as there is no evidence forthcoming on this point, but the officials of the Great Western Railway at Paddington in- cline to the belief that it was accidental. As to the sup- posed infernal machine, the wheels which were found on the floor of the parcels office are now proved to have been part of the winding apparatus of some fishing rods which were consumed in the fire, and which had arrived from Birming- ham on Friday addressed to a local tradesman. The bottle of colourless fluid supposed to have been an inflammable of explosive liquid has turned out after examination to be horse medicine which had been consigned tO the railway company for carriage to a customer by a Windsor veterinary surgeon. FAIR TRADE AND THE AGRICULTURAL DEPRESSION.— At a recent meeting of the Norfolk Chamber of Agriculture a resolution was passed asking her Majesty's Government to appoint a Parliamentary Committee to inquire into agri- cultural distress and its effects upon trade. The Chamber has received the following reply:—" Mr. Gladstone has had the honour to receive your letter containing the terms of the resolution which was passed at the recent meeting of the Norfolk Chamber of Agriculture. In reply, I am di- rectea to say that after the recent and very exhaustive in- vestigation made by the Royal Commission which was ap- pointed by the late Government, Mr. Gladstone cannot hold out hope that an inquiry into agricultural distress such as is advocated by the Chamber will commend itself to her Majesty's present advisers unless it can be shown that it would not do mischief to the cultivator of the soil by en- couraging expectations not likely to be realised."-In a letter to a Salisbury correspondent, Mr. Bright discusses a recent address by a Protectionist farmer to the South Wilts Cham- ber of Agriculture. The right hon. gentleman remarks that it would be as reasonable to expect increased prosperity to far- mers from a rise in the price of foodstuffs following the impo- sition of a duty on foreign wheat as it would be to anticipate an improvement in trade by greatly raising the poor rates, and SO enabling paupers to become better customers of manu- facturers and tradesmen. Mr. Bright continues:—" If land is not worth rent it should be, and will be, rent free. If land is paying rent which it will not yield, the question is one between the tenant and the owner." Writing to a Hackney Liberal, Mr. Bright, referring to a quotatien by Lord Dun- raven from a speech of the right hoit gentleman at a Cob- den Club dinner, says, "I have never attended a Cobden Club dinner. So much for Lord Dunraven's accuracy."
