div.head: EXAMINER. TURDAY. DECEMBER 27, 1884.
div.p: THE EXAMINER. TURDAY. DECEMBER 27, 1884.

HUGH KENNEDY was committed for trial on Monday at Bnry on a charge of unlawfully wounding Rose Stevens, his sweetheart. The prisoner attacked the woman with razor and tried to cut her throat, but fortunately only succeeded in inflicting a wound upon her forehead. A ward in connection with the Macclesfield Infirmary, de• signed for the reception and treatment of cases of sickness in children, was oper ed on Tuesday by the Duchess of Westminster, who was accompanied by the Duke. The latter, replying to a vote of thanks, said the illnesses of chil- dren appealed most powerfully to the heart, and he con- gratulated the town upon the acquisition of so useful a branch of its Infirmary. WRECK AND Loss OF THREE LIVES. —'The Ann, of Banff, was wrecked on Thursday morning on the Tarlair rocks. .She was owned by Mr. Donald MacDonald, of Thurso, and was 23 tons register. She is supposed to have been manned at the time by the master (Mackay) and another man and a boy. None of the bodies have as yet been washed ashore, but the vessel's boat has been picked up about half a mile west of the wreck. THREE CHILDREN BURNT TO DEATIL—A fire, supposed to have been caused by a spark from a grate in a workshop, broke out at an early hour on Tuesday morning on pre- mises in Montague-street, Whitechapel, occupied by a man named Isaac Zernaman, who with his wife and five children lived in two top rooms of the building. The flames spread with great rapidity, and only two of the children could be rescued. Three, aged 16 years, 13 years, and seven years, were burned to death. MURDER OF A RUSSIAN SAILOR. At Birkenhead, OR Tuesday, Ferdinand Korlynen and William Ranscher, re- spectively boatswaie and second officer of the American ship J. T. Chapman, were charged with the murder of a Russian sailor named Johnson, whilst on a voyage from Valparaiso to Liverpool. The evidence of a seaman who was on board the vessel showed that the prisoners had bru- tally ill-treated Johnson from the time of leaving Valpar- aiso, and on one occasion they tied him up in the rigging for several hours. When released b wee in a dying con- dition, and expired the next day. The prisoners were re- manded until Saturday. CRUELTY TO CHILDREN:A Glasgow magistrate has dealt very properly with a wretched married couple named Macdonald, who had been earning a livelihood by "singing" in the streets of Glasgow. Their four children, whose ages ranged from ten years to sixteen months, were obliged to follow their parents in all kinds of weather, and the hus- band, widi brutal frankness, said that their pitiful appear- ance aroused the sympathy of the public, and brought in more money than he could have earned bir` Singing alone. Owing to prolonged exposure the children have suffered severely in health. The magistrate spoke strongly of the cruel and unnatural conduct of Macdonald and his wife, and sent them each to prison for a month. SHOOTING A CORPORAL --Late on Monday- night two troopers of the 3rd Hussars, stationed at Leeds Cavalry Barracks, had a quarrel, and one of them, Corporal Clements, threatened to shoot the other, Private Shepherd. The latter reported this threat to his superiors, and an escort was sent to arrest Clements. When required to surrender, however, he pro- duced a heavy six-chambered revolver, and fired in quick succession four shots, one of which wounded Corporal Marner in the thigh. Clements then ran out, but was stopped by the guard and handed over to the police. Marner was taken to hospital, where the wound, which is severe and painful, was dressed. The prisoner was on Tuesday remanded by the Leeds magistrates. DISGRACEFUL AFFAIR IN WATERFORD.—An outrage of a shocking character was perpetrated on Menday morning in the neighbourhood of Lisniore, county Waterford. About four weeks ago Mrs. Hillier, a lady far advanced in life, the wife of Colonel Hillier, ex-inspector general of police, who resided near Lismore, died, and her remains were laid in the family vault. The deceased was apparently well liked and respected in the locality, and her funeral was largely at- tended. On Monday morning someone passing by the place found that the vaults in which the body was interred , had been broken open, and a closer examination showed that the coffin had been removed. The news soon spread, and on seatmh being made the body was discovered in a river some 130 yards away, having been dragged along the inter- I vening distance and pitched into the water. No reason is I assignable for the outrage. The lady was married but two ' years ago. It required nine or ten men to convey Mrs. Hil- lier's coffin back to the tomb. It may therefore be supposed that an equal number took part in the outrage, and the police oneht not to be without hope of getting information which will put them on the right track. MR. HLADSTONE'S BIRTHDAY.—A London correspondent says :—The newspapers are early in the field with their references in anticipation of Mr. Ciladstone's seventy-fifth birthday next Monday, and their reviews of his long Par- liamentary and official career. I believe the only mem- bers of the present House of Commons who took the oath I at the meeting of Parliament which succeeded the passing of the Reform Act, when Mr. Gladstone was first returned, are Sir Harry Verney and Mr. Christopher Talbot. Three remain out 658. Sir Harry Verney's legislative career has witneseed some vicissitudes, but Mr. Christopher Talbot's experience is unique, he having represented the county of I Glamorgan nearly fifty-five years. He was returned at the general election of 1830. There are few examples of this in our modern political history, and I can recall only two which nearly resemble it. Sir Charles Birrell represented Shoreham from 1806 until 1862, and the Hon. Henry Cecil ' Lowther sat for Wtatmoreland from 1812 until 1867. Mr. Talbot is the senior of Mr. Gladstone in the House of Com- mons by two Parliaments. THE SKYE CROFTERS.-.-A conference under the auspices of the Highland Land Law Reform Association was held at Anderton's Hotel, London, on Tuesday night, when Mr. John M'Pherson, of Elendale, and the Rev. Donald M'Cul- him, of Waternish, conveyed a message of Scotch crofters to their supporters in England. The meeting was large and I enthusiastic. Mr. MacFarlane, M.P., presided, and Sir I George Campbell and Mr. Fraser Mackintosh, members of Parliament, were among those present. The delegates from I Skye delivered addresses, giving graphic descriptions of the condition to which it was alleged the crofters had been re- I duced by the lairds. They expressed themselves as hopeful! that the struggle in which they had engaged would lead to the reform of the land Laws. A resolution was carried unani- mously declaring that the oppressed condition of the crofters, and cotters of the Highlands and islands of Scotland was I discreditable to the nation •, that the conference deeply 1 sympathised with the people in their struggle for social emancipation, and pledged itself to afford both moral and material support towards effecting such changes in the land laws as would enable them to live on their native soil under equitable conditions; and that, pending legislation, a bill for suspending evictions should be passed. THE CHANNEL TUNNEL SCHEME.—Sir E. Welkin presided on Tuesday at the ordinary general meeting of the share- holders of the Submarine Continental Railway Company, and explained the present position and future prospects of the Channel Tunnel Scheme. He stated that:it was intended in the next session to ask Parliament to read a bill for the further prosecution of the works of the tunnel, and referring to the assumption on the part of many that the opposition of the. Government had arisen from a desire to conciliate Germany, and the suggestion in high quarters that with a tunnel under the Channel England and France ought to be and must be one country, Sir Edward remarked that the Submarine Company did believe that a friendship between England and France meant the peace of Europe and the pac•fication of the world. Dealing with the question of what the Government had gained by conciliating Germany, he said it would be found from the papers that Prince Bis- marck bad been "very considerably drawing wool over our eyes." He contended that equally with the promoters of the Nicaraguan Canal his company was trying to carry out the tunnel works as "trustees for all mankind," and if they were opposed it would be by the same people who had op- posed the introduction of gas and of railways. EXTRAORDINARY CHARGE OF CONSPIRACY AT CHESTER. —On Monday Stevens was charged on remand at Chester with having performed a bogus marriage ceremony. The prosecution, which is undertaken by the Public Prosecutor, had not closed when the court ad- journed.—On Tuesday Edward Warburton, cowman, said he and Pugh were working together, and witness was jok- ing with him about the affair. Pugh said, "I am not mare red." Witness replied, "People say that you are married ;" and he said "Time will show." Ellen Harris, mother of the prosecutrix, said her daughter would be 21 years of age in August. In October Pugh and Mary told her they were going to be married. Pugh wanted the wedding to take place at Shocklach, but Mary preferred• Chester. Witness then detailed bow Mary and her brothers and cousin and the prisoner Pugh left for Chester for the marriage, and how Mary returned with a wedding ring upon her finger. Wit- ness thought they were legally and properly married. Three weeks afterwards, from what she heard, she pressed Pugh for the marriage lines. He said he had not got them, but would go to Chester and bring them back with him. As he did not, she and Mary went to Chester and saw Stevens. Witness told him she would go before a magistrate and in- quire more into it. At the conclusion of the evidence both prisoners made statements. Pugh's statementin several im- portant particulars corroborated the evidence given by pre- vious witnesses against Stevens. Stevens, on his part, said he was only acting as agent for Pugh to obtain information as to the steps necessary to be taken before marriage. Noth- ing which could in the slightest degree be taken for a mar- riage ceremony took place. The magistrates announced that both prisoners would be committed for trial.—On Wednesday morning, at the Chester City Police Court, before the Mayor and other Magistrates, this Case, so far a 9 the police court is concerned. was concluded. The Mayor said there was power to commit both the defendants to the Sessions, but under the circumstances R would be better that they should be tried at the assizes. The usual bail was accepted. AN IMPORTANT ENTERPRISE —For some time past remark- able reports of the wonderful efficacy of a Temedy for the cure ' of pain, have been made public in America. Australia, and el,evrhere. Of late, cures ry this remedy have been brought to light in England and on the Continent. Investigations show that the article referred to, St. Jacobs 011, is endorsed by representative men of the United States, Canada, Austra- lasian 0 lollies, and other countries, as possesssing, in fact, most astonishing properties tor the cure of rheumatism and other painful ailments. In Calcutta. India, and at Chri,t Church, New Zoalend, also, it was awarded the Dfplomas of Highest Merit and Gold Medal., as a pain-curing and healing remedy. The sole proprietors of St. Jacobs Oil are The Charles A. Vogeler Company. Baltimore, Maryland, GALA., who have blanches in various parts of the world and have recently opened a Great Britain Branch, at 45, Farrington-road, Lon- don, where Chemists and Druggists will be supplied with this great German Remedy for the cure of Pain. The house an. nounees as its conviction, that there is notbing unmerearMile or unprofessional in advertising meritorious goods, of a menleal or other nature. Therefore, they will avail themselves of the advantages of the public pr se, as a medium for making their remedy known. Tne price of St. Jacobs Oil is 25 lid per bot- tle Parties unable to obtain it from their chemists will re- ceive it, post paid, by sending 2s td. to the London address above given.-114vt.

NOTES BY THE WAY. At a meeting of the committee of the Lancashire Associa- tion'called to consider the recommendations of the Football Association regarding professionalism, it was decided to give support to all the recommendations with the exception of the one relating to the residential qualification, which the committee of the Football Association propose shall be from October 6 last. The committee of the County Association consider that it would be uniair to give this case a retro- spective application, and will bring forward a proposal at the forthcoming conf,rence to fix the residential qualifica- tion from the date of the adoption of the rules. The pro- posal is important to these clubs, many of whose players have joined since the beginning of October, and, if the amendment of the Lancashire committee was adapted, would thus be eligible in the same way that the Scotch players of other clubs are. The leading football players of North and South played a Rugby match at Blackheath on Saturday. The game was of a most exciting character, and ended in a victory for the Soath by a single try to nil. The following Association matches were contested in Lancashire, on Saturday :—Blackburn Olympic beat Bolton Wanderers by three goals to one; Great Lever and Darwen played a drawn game, neither side scoring ; Park Road beat Astley Bridge by one goal to nil ; Burnley beat Accrington by two goals to one • Halliwell beat githeroe Low Moor by five goals to one; Bagley and Clitheroe played a drawn game, two goals each ; Church beat Witton by two goals to one ; Preston North End beat the Corinthians by three goals to one ; Padiham beat Manchester by ten goals to nil; Darwen beat Darwen Old Wanderers in the third round of the Eng- lish cup tie by four goals to two. ' •

On Saturda:v, Old Forester beat Excelsior in the London Cup competition ; Old Westminster boat Clapham Rovers ; Glasgow beat London; Barnes and Upton Park played a drawn game; Dumbtrton beat Vale Leven; Battlefield and the Pilgtims played a drawn game; Third Lanark beat Clyde; Glasgow Rangers, in the Scottish Cup competi- tion, beat Arbroath; the Old Carthusians beat the Old Etonians ; Walsall and Notts Forest played a drawn game; Netts County beat Derby Midland. In the National Cup competition (second round) the Druids and Newtown played a drawn game. In the Birmingham Cup competition Aston Villa beat Wednesbury ; St. George's beat West Brom- wich Albion ; Walsall Swifts beat Burton Wanderers, and Wolverhampton Wanderers played a drawn game with the Notts Ranger; Ayr beat Kilmarnock; Cambuslang beat the Edinburgh Hibernians ; Edinburgh Wan lerns beat Ed- inburgh University; Derby County beat Lockwood Bros. at Derby.

A young man named Paul was before the Birmingham magistrates on Tuesday, charged with having attempted to obtain from manufacturers large quantities of goods of all kinds by the false pretence that he was the agent of a Cana- dian firm. He was committed for trial.

..--...- ..... _ At Douglas Bridge, in county Tyrone, a farmer named Brien has been killtd by one of his labourers named Don- na], who, in a quarrel supposed to have arisen through jealousy, stabbed him in the back. Donnel is in custody. A young man named William Monk was arrested in Whitechapel, on Wednesday morning, whilst attempting to C mmit a burglary. January sth, the coroner intimating [het he had meanwhile directed a post-mortem examination. Mrs. Hewett, the touacconiet, who is the princip el witness in the nice, has given but a smell portion of her evidence. She will be able to prove that no words passed between the young woman and her murderer before the blow was struck, and it will anquestionably appear that the deceased was awakeeed by the man entering the window and removing the table from beneath it, that she sprang out of bed, and was immediately stabbed by her assassin, who escaped by the window and dropped on the pavement, having been in the house barely a minute. It will also be shown that the deceased and the prisoner were for several months engaged to be married, and it was pertly on account of a complaint by young Marshall as to the girl not being acquainted with domestic duties—a consequence of her being employed in her father's shop—tbat she went to learn household work In Mrs. Hewett's service. At that time, five weeks since, when their aff sirs ran smeothly, Marshall expressed to Mrs. Hewett a hope that Laura would speedily learn hew to keep a house in order, and Mrs. Hewett replied, "I will keen her, Fred, for a year, and then she will be fit to he your wife." It was after this that the prisoner's jealousy began to make him trouble- some to the deceased and her friends, and their actual breach of engagement dated back only a few days. The Press Association learns that the Treasury have decided to take up the prosecution in the case, and the friends of Marshall have engaged a solicitor, who will instruct Mr. Geoghegan as counsel. The pence have not yet succeeded in recover- ing the weapon with which the murder was committed, and they believe it has been thrown into the Thames. It appears that the accused entered a coffee shop on the river bank, near the scene of the murder, as 80OR as the place opened at half past four a.m., and twe hours liter the crime was committed. The so-called dagger which the accuPd used to carry had been shown to the deceased and her half sisters, and the latter described it as a stiletto seven inches long and half an inch wide. The body was inspected on Teesday afternoon by Dr. Coleman, surgeon to the Royal Arsenal, who is of opinion that the stab was indicted when the girl was standing, and not when she was asleep in bed.

EARLESTOWN WANDERERS V. LIVERPOOL STANLEY.—The , Earlestown Wanderers achieved a high honour on Saturday I afternoon, when they succeeded in defeating,the Liverpool Stanley team in tbe second round of the competition for the eleyerpool and District Challenge Cup. The match WAS played on the ground of the first named, off Wargrave-road, Earlestewn, and as there was no other match in the district there was a very large attemlance of spectators. Having won the toss, the visitors chose to play uphill and against the wind in the first half. The Wanderers kicked off, and Immediately made an attack on the Stanley goal, and amid the cheers of the supporters of the home club the latter scored the first goal four minutes from the commencement. The Stanleyites appeared roused by this sudden reverse, and they had the best of the game in the first half. When ends were changed at half-time the score stood—Stanley two goals; Wanderers one. As the visitors had the ground and wind in their favour in the subsequent play, it was thought en the resumption that they would easily dispose of their opponents. The Wanderers, however, not only held their own, but assumed the aggressive. The game was fast 'and even for some minutes, but the Stanleyites soon manifested signs of being "fagged out." After twenty-five minutes' play the Earlestonians scored a second goal amid loud cheers. On the game being resumed, both goals were in turn endangered, but the Wanderers had the best of the play. About five minutes from the call of time a scrim- mage occurred in the front of the Stanley goal, and the home players again sent the leather between the uprights. This success created the greatest enthusiasm. In tbe re- maining few minutes the Wanderers played a good defen- sive game, and when time was called, the Earlestown team retired the victors by three goals to two. The Wanderers' team was as follows : T. Champion (captain), goal; Selby and W. Lord, backs; R. Johnson, J. Lowe, and W. Allison, half-backs; J. Shaw and W. Shaw, left wing; W. Dale, centre; J. T. Thompson and F. Knowles, right wing.

No signs of blood have been found on the pri- soner, with the exception of the mark of a recent graze on the right wrist. MAGISTERIAL EXAMINATION OF THE PRISONER. At tha conclusion of the ordinary business at the Wool- wich Police Court, on Monday, Frederick Marshall, aged twenty-one, labourer, was brought before Mr. Balgny, charged with having caused the death of Laura Wilson, by stabbing her in the breast with some sharp instrument, at 14, Beresford-street. The accused, a young man of middle size, rather spare build and gaunt features, seemed rather scared in expression and untidy in dress. He listened attentively to all that passed, but said nothing. Mrs. Hewitt gave evidence in accordance with the above facts. Being asked if she had ever seen the accused before, she said she had found him in her coal cellar three weeks•ago. Witness now became so nervous and coafused that the , magistrate intimated that he would postpone her sfurther evidence. Mary Ann Wilson, sister of the deceased, said the priso- ner had known Laura eleven months, and had been hanging about the place ever eiace courting her. But being found lately in Mrs. Hewitt's cellar their father forbade him to pay his addresses to Laura. Last Friday prisoner met her and asked witness to ask Laura if she intended to keep company with him. Laura said "No," and she told him so. Then he pulled something out of his pocket and said he would swing for Charley, their mother's second cousin's son, who was also paying his addresses to Laura. On Saturday night prisoner met her and Laura, but Laura would not speak to him. Ou Sunday night witness again saw him two doora off. He asked if Laura was in. Laura saw him from the door at a quarter past twelve. Witness saw him again near the house. This witness's further evidence had also to be postponed owing to her want of composure. A police-constable then deposed that be went early that morning to the prisoner's house at Plumstead and arrested him. When he told him the charge, the accused said, "Nobody saw me do it. You suspect me because I carry a ' dagger.' The policeman asked him what he had done with , the dagger, and he replied that he did not know, he was so confused. The prisoner was thereupon remanded tillyextMonday. THE INQUEST. Immediately thereafter an inquest was opened before Mr. Carttar, coroner, at the Town Hall. The sister of the de- ceased gave evidence of identification. Mrs. Hewitt was then examined shortly, and gave the same evidence as be- fore the magistrate, with the addition that the deceased lay moaning on the floor while assistance was fetched, Before,

WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnithtly meeting of this Boar i was held on Wed- nesday evening in the Worktcmse. Mare were present— Messrs Greening (chairman), lireadbent, Blackhurst, Mackie, Brown. Appleton, D.rlyshire, Harrison, Hunt, Jno. Houghton, William Houghton, Grange, Humphreys, lid- shall, Rev. G. F. Robertr, Gibson, Jeans, Owen, J. C. Sutton (clerk), and R. Sat on (assistant clerk).

div.head: AN IRREGT/LAIIITY.
div.p: AN IRREGT/LAIIITY.

The minutes of the previous m-e-eicr;g having been read Mr. BLACERCEST called attention to the fact that at the previous meeting a minute of the House Committee, recom- mending the adoption of plans for structural alterations to a window. dm., had been passed. He had reason to believe that that proposal had not gene legally and regularly through the books, and in fact that it had teen totally irreg- ular. He wanted to know who had ordered those plrns to be done, and whoever had done it without the order of the Board, ought to be made to pay for them. He had been told by Mr. Jolley that the alterations would only cost £4O, but he thought they would more likely cost £BO. First of all, however, he wished to know if the thing had been regularly and legally pissed by tl‘e Board—The CLERK having explained that he was not at the previous meeting, and also what had been done with regard to that particular matter, said he thought it ought to be gone into again de nova—Mr. BELOADEENT moved that the minutes be passed with the exception of that one referring to the window Mr. DAREYSHIRY seconded this proposal.—Mr. Buowx said the Howe Committee did not admit having been to blame in the matter, and contended that they had done nothing that was irregular.—Mr. JOLLEY said lie was glad that the matter had come to light if it were only that it eased the conscience of his friend Mr. tilacklauret.— The motion of Mr. Broadbent was then passed, it being understood that the House Committee would again con- sider the question of plans.

div.head: COST OF FAILMINg.
div.p: THE COST OF FAILMINg.

Dr. Mactint, referring to a statement showing the ex- penditure in connection with the Union Industrial schools for the half year ended September, which was submitted at the previous meeting, asked if any namber could tell them how it came that the profits on the farm at the Industrial School were "nil." The question of farming profits was of the very greatest importance, and he was curious to know whether this result of their farming was due to the ex- travagant rent, their management, or to the rates and taxes. MEXII3ER said they did not pay ar,y rent and still could not make their farming pay.—The CLent said *hat he him- self-bad advised ee superintendent of tip, school that it would be better tAun the accounts for the farm on for a whole year, as for one half year the'-3 was scarcely anythiog but expenditure, while the other half year the prOlite Cattle, in.—Dr. MACKIE said he Wda klad that hey had got that ex- planation, as it was very undesirable that it should co out to the public that they could not make their farm pay with no rent to pay.—The subj, ct then dropped.
THE SCHOOL COHEICTEE.-THE NEW CLOCK.

The Rev. G. F. ROI3SETS moved the adoption of the School Committee's minutes, which centained nothing of importance besides a recominepdatioa that the school dormitories should be provided with doors. He (Mr. Roberts) explained that these doors had been struck out of the original plans by the Local Government Board, bat owing to the draught which was caused by the want of doors the doctor recommended that they be put up.—Mr. DARBYSEtIRE, in seconding the adoption of the minutes, said ha should like to know from the Board whether they would not think it suitable to have the new clock at the schools made on the new system of numbering the hours up to 24. He thought that might be done at the earns cost, and he saw that the authorities at Greenwich were ehout to adopt the system.—Dr. MACKIE said that system was purely an astronomical arrangement, and had nothing to do with workhouses, goaLs, or private houses. It was not for the Warrington Guardians to set an example of counting the time by 13 and 21 o'clock. (Laughter.)—The subject thin dropped, and the minutes were confirmed. A GIFT.

It was stated that Mr. Cromptos, Marliet-place, bad pre- sented • a lOi to be divided among the children of the school, so that each child might have a• threepenny piece. =On the motion of Mr. DARBYSHIGE, it was agreed that the thanks of the Board should be tendered to Mr. Cromp- ton.

div.head: FAVOURABLE COMPARTSON.
div.p: A FAVOURABLE COMPARTSON.

The CLERK said that in compliance with a request by Mr. Appleton he had prepared a statement in which the amount of out-relief twenty years ago was compared with that of the present year. In 1864 for the June quarter the amount. paid by that Union was £1,316 Is 51, against £BB9 19.3 lid for ,the same quarter of 1884; for the September quarter of 1861 was paid £1,413'101173, as against £991.1.4s 11d for the -same quarter of 1881. The total for the September half. year of 1804 was £2.729 12s, and that for the same half. year this year was £lB9l 14s 101, showing a decrease of £837 17s 21 (Hear, hear.) The out-relief in the March half-year of 1864 amounted to £3,074 10s 41, as compared with £1,955 15s 3d for the sime half-year of 1884. In 1864 £lO5 9s 3d and £lO9 was expended in two weeks of the December quarter, and in the corresponding weeks of 1881 the expenditure was £72 3s 10.1 and £6B Oa 3d respectively. (Hear, hear.) He (the clerk) said that when they took into consideration the great increases of population and the great fall of out-relief there seemed to be a remarkable change sornewhere.—Mr. APPLETON said he could not understand how it was that the poor rates bad increased. although the out.relief expenditure had been so much re-- duced.—Mr.linwr said it was because of the expenditure at the county asylum—Mr. APPLETON thought it would be better to have a statement of the cost of indoor relief to supplement the other statement —Dr. MACKIE also thought it would be advisable to have a full and comprehensive statement. —Mr. Denimuntw-attributa a good deal of the

div.head: Tne tit would
div.p: Tne tit would

decrease to the better administration of the out-door relief, and Mr. BROA.DBENT was also of the same opinion—Thu CLERK pointed out that there were now many charges on the poor rate which did not exist 20 years ago, such as the charges for highways, school fees for non-pauper children, vaccination and registrars' fees, dm. The county rate also 20 years ago was under £2,000, but had been £l,OOO of late years.—After some further discussion the suggestion of the clerk that he should deal with the whole subject in his next report on the estimates was agreed to and the matter dropped.

THE VACCINATION cans. The CLERK read a copy of a letter which the Local Government Board had sent to Mr. A. Forster, of Earles- town, with regard to his complaint as to the clerk appearing before the magistrates in the vaccination cases. The letter was to tt.e effect that there had been nothing out of erder done.—The letter was then read, after which the matter dropped.

• THE HARRIS' CASE. With regard to the above case, the particulars of which we gave in our report of the previous meeting of the Board of Guardians, a report by Mr. Caldwell, relieving officer, Newton, in which he set forth the particulars, was read The CLERK said he would advise the Board to pay that portion of the account (MO Os 4d) which had been sent in by the Newton Commissioners, which had been incurred after the notice given to the Board of Guardians by Mr. Brierley, clerk to the Commissioners, had been dealt with by the Newton Relief Committee. This portion of the account amounted to about £22.—A warm and protracted discussion then took place on the subject. several guardians contending that the Board ought not to pay any portion of the account, as the patients had been sent to the Warrington hospital by Dr. Watkins, medical officer of the Commission- ers, before any application of relief had been made to the relievieg officer.—Mr. JEANS said he most decidedly:objected to the payment being made, and if the order was rustled he would on his own responsibility test the question.—Ulti- mately, it was decided that the facts of the case should be submitted to the Local Government Board and their opinion asked. THE CATHOLIC SCHOOL CHILDREN. The Cmenusteer said that the majority of the children at the schools were catholies, and it was only right that they should attend their own place of warship, but un- fortunately all the officers refused to go to the Catholic church, and therefore they had no one to take charge of the children, lie suggested that they pay someone to take these children to cherch on Sundays—The Rev. G. F. ROBERTS said them was the difficulty that the Catholie chapel was about two miles from the schools, and it was therefore not like sending them to some adjacent place.— Dr. MACKIE said the priest would perhaps take charge of the children if be were invited.— The CRAIRMAN said they paid the priest £lO a year for the seat rent for the children. —Mr. HARnisON said they could not Expect the priest to be reeponsible for the children. If they made the £lO itato more he might undertake to bring them—Mr. PARBSSHIRB thought there ought to be some responsible person in charge of the children, as if any accident was to happen somebody would be very blameable.—The CLERK explained that for- merly the person who drilled the children used to take the Catholic children to their place of worship, and be eugges- ted that some similar assangement might again be made.— Ultimately the further consideration of this matter was re- ferred to the School Committee. The meeting then ended.

CONFESSION OF MURDER.—A young Frenchman has its - limed the authorities at Moscow that he is guilty of the murder of Sarah Beaker, the young Jewish girl. The guilt of Mironovitch and 13:z ik, who have ‘.lready been'convicted of this crime, is thus placed in doubt. A NEW YORK THEATRE BURNT BOWN.—A ftre broke out at the 'Theatre Comique, New York, on Tuesday, which soon assumed considerable dimensions. Notwithstanding the efforta made to quench the flames, the building was ultimately burned down. The loss is estimated at 61.75.000. DEFININet BRICIEBATS.—Professor Johnson was one day lecturing before the students of mineralogy. He had before him a number of specimens of various sorts to il- lustrate the subject, when a roguish student, for sport, slily slipped a piece of brick amsmg the stones. The professor Was taking up these one after the other, and namiag them. "This," he said, "is a piece of granite; this is felspar," &c. Presently he came to the brickbat. Without betraying any surprise, or even changing the tone of his voice; "This," he said, holding it up, "is a piece of impudence." Who can tell the value of a smile? It costs the giver nothing, but is beyond price to the erring and relenting, t4te sad and cheerless, the lost and forsaken; It disarms malice—subdues temper—ttirnshatred to love—revenge to kindness—and paves the darkest paths with gems f sunlight. A smile on the brow betrays a kind heart, a pleasant friend, an affectionate brother, a dutiful son, a happy husband. It adds a charm to beauty, it deco- rates the face of the, deformed, and makes a lowly woman resemble an angel in paradise.

div.p: THE EXAMINE,
SATURDAY, DECEMBER 27, 1881.

MI. W. CROSFULD, J.P., the Liberal can- didate for Warrington, has now completed the series of addresses he has been giving to the electors at their various annual Ward Meetings; and it is very gratifying to find that the high opinion that was formed of him after his first address in the. borough has been more than sustained. He has dealt with various topics in a manner at once so frank and intelligent as to confirm the impression that he thoroughly understands what he is talking about, and that he has nothing to conceal. Mr. FRANK ROBERTS, at a recent meeting, expressed the popular verdict when he said the more the electors saw of him the better they liked him. Singular as it may seem, although he has had so much to say on so many subjects, those who are under- stood to be his opponents find it difficult to raise objection either to him or to his opinions. They are not usually what Dr. MAcicus calls "dumb dogs ; " but, in this instance, if thought struggles within them it does not find fitting utterance. Here and there, there is a solitary sound—it is as the voice of one crying in the wilderness, and the burden of the cry is that Mr. CROSFIELD is a stranger to Warrington. This terrible fault, if it be a fault, is one which, it is satisfactory to think, is growing "fine by degrees and beautifully less." Nay, we are not sure, if it may not be said that, like Sir GILBERT GREENALL'S political budget, there never was much init, and that it has now disappeared alto- gether. At any rate, Mr. CROSFIELD has received a "stranger's welcome" ; and if he goes on as he is doing—putting his strong common sense side by side with his oppo- nent's uncommon nonsense—there can be no question as to his being returned by a large majority at the next election. It is suggested by way of apology for "the old man of the sea" which the Conservatives of Warrington so unwillingly carry on their backs. that he is riot the first man " nearly eighty" who has been returned to Parliament. True; there is Mr. GLADSTONE for instance, but there," as BYRON says when comparing "Don Juan" to "Joseph," "all likeness ends be- tween the pair." The world has produced one GLADSTONE only—a giant in intellect at seventy-five; but it is in the usual way of things for the mediocre individual when "nearly eighty" to shift, as SHAKESPERE has it, "into the lean and slippered pantaloon" when all is "second child- ishness and mere oblivion." Sir GILBERT certainly tells us that he is " growing. younger," but this may be taken, ' under the circumstances, as one of the signs of his peculiar condition. He is far advanced towards the last stage, and in this respect, and this only, may he be said to be "an ad- vanced politician." It is awkward, of course, for the Conservative party in Warrington that they should be hampered by the chikikh whim of the old man ineloquent to stand before the people as a candidate in these stirring times; but it is something that they are not wholly without thought for the mor- row, seeing that they have named his succes- sor whilst he is yet upon the scene, They are, we suppose, quietly making up their

'minds to accept the defeat which stares them in the face, at the same time training their second champion for a bout to come off no- body knows how and nobody knows when. In this unhappy predicament, the leaders of the. Tory party need not be surprised if they find that there are men within their ranks who refuse to be jockeyed in this way, and who, rather than thrOw their votes away, will make up their minds to be on the winning side. Working-men' Tory or Radical, have no fault to find with aCaucus which gives them a voice in saying who their candidate shalt be; but they do object to a "mariner" $O " ancient ' that he has forgotten how to steer, if he ever knew; or to another helms- man being thrust upon them without their being taken into account in the slightest de- gree. They perceive that Mr. CROSETELA in submitting to the Caucus acknowledged the sound principle of the rule of the ma- jority; and that in his sp eches, without fawning and without flattery, he has de- monstrated that he is earnestly seeking to secdre the greatest good of the greatest num- ber. Who could listen to or read his address on party organisation without feeling that be looked upon "the machine" as a.necessa7 and legitimate means to a noble end? The " 200, rightly elected, means all the differ- ence between representation and mis-repre- sentation—between the united action of a great party, and the miserable inttiguing of a petty clique. Mr. CROSFIELD was not less clear and soul-din the interesting speech he made on war and its relation to the working•classes. He showed how easy it was to get into a qaarrel, and how difficult and costly it was to get out of it when once a Go- vernment had resolved to let slip the dogs of war, pointing the moral, like a wise man, in the pregnant suggestion that, as the end was, usually, the meeting of statesmen in a Coun- cil Chamber, in most cases it would be well if the end were the beginning. Parliament wants reinforcing with a large body of men with views of this kind men who ade- quately realise that "the greatest of Britisfr. interests is peace ;" and, holding firmly by that conviction, are prepared to resist the in- cessant pressure of that over-represented class who are engaged in what Lord DERBY happily described as "the gunpowder and glory business." Mr. CROSFIELD has been not less lucid in exposition of his views on the- Franchise Bill and the Redistribution Bill; in this, as in other respects, being in marked ctontrast to Sir GILBERT GREENALL, who, so far as may be gathered from what in cour- tesy we will call his speeches, is no more aware of the existence of these great measures than he is of his having, when in the House of CoMmons, persistently voted against pro- posals for the ettension of the franchise. A is not sufficient for the Liberal candidate fdt Warrington that the Lords have just now bowed their heads to the storm; he,would so alter the terms upon which they live and move and .have their being that they should in the future be powerless to • raise such a storm. Looking ahead, Mr. CROSFIELD sees that reform of county government cannot be far distant, and, having mastered the subject himself, he rendered a service to thoughtful men when he went into details as to the points that would hive to be dealt with, and the necessity there was for setting straight a large number of crooked things. In his latest utterance Mr. CROAJELD traced.the improve- ment in the condition of the people since the- , Reform Bill of 1832 in a way which showed how much he his at heart the interests of the I toiling masses of his countrymen. -He can- take a lesson from history, but he belongs in I matters of reform to the living present " rather tan the .1 dead p ist ;" and has, we do , not dori:)t, a useful land henourable career before hitn a tne future member fur War- rington.

FATHER CIIRIsTMS is said to be '6 not a bit like Christmas " unless he comes to us ac- companied by Jack Frost ; and as that keen gentleman, with the icy finger upon his lip," has been with us curing the past week, there can be no ground for complaint on that score. The young and strong take pleasure in being out in the cold bracing air, espe- cially when, with winged feet, they can fly across the frozen ponds; but to the old and ailing a rapid fall of the thermometer some- times means the difference between life and death. Some of our readers may have noticed, as we did, that following upon the ;cold weather of a few weeks, there was a large extension of our obituary notices. The ill- fed and ill-clad are of course the first to suc.:- cumb ; and this, brings us to the suggestion that those who would help their needy neigh- bours cannot do better at this time of the year than see to it that they' do not suffer from cold. A spare blanket or a spare coat given with a word of goodwill may be the means of bringing comfort to many a home. There are few in the receipt of regular wages —to say nothing of the rich—who are not in a position to help the less fortunate in one way or another ; and we are quite sure that Christmas Cheer will be all the sweeter when it is enjoyed with the consciousness that the recipient has seized the opportunity of giving , cheer to another. Indiscriminate alms-giving j is of course to be deplored at Christmas as at I any other time ; for it has been demonstrated jby a long series of observations that it does I more harm than good. What is needed,- where there is no special knowledge of par- ticular cases, is a little patient preliminary in- quiry, or it will be found that right things have got into the hands of the wrong people. The honest poor, who, " despised, endure temptation and distress," are a class wholly , apart from the idle and thriftless, and, as they they are not in the habit of either complain- ing or of obtruding themselves, those who , would know them and be helpful to them must search thr-m cut. It need hardly be I said that we do not countenance such momen- tary cheer in such cases as comes of I giving a glass of intoxicating liquor. It lis, it may be granted, an easy and convenient way of slowing a generous I disposition; but it works untold mischief at this season of the year. It may be that false pride stands in the way of giving a few coppers, when there would be no hesitation in offering a friendly glass ; but it should be remembered that an accumulation of pence will be found to be much more valuable at the end of a day's round than an accumula- tion of liquor —not excepting the case even. when the liquor holder has got "more than he can carry." The late POSTMASTER- GENERAL showed himself exceedingly anxi- ous that postmen at Christmastide should not be rendered unfit for their important, duties by the mistaken kindness of those who desired to " treat " them; and we wotild urge upon all who revere the memory of Mr. FAW.. CETT to give the matter thought and carry out his wish. The principle is cne which .is capable of a wide application; and, looking, back upon many festive seasons, we are pleased to think that there is less tippling than of old across the shop counter. THE Vein OF RUNCORN.—Sunday last was the 39th anniversary of the Rev. Canon Barclay's entrance upon his labours in Runcern as vicar, and at the close of the morn- ing service the bells of the Parish Church cent forth a merry peal. Speciail music was rendered by the choir at both morning and evening service. RUNCORN Gas COMPANY.—An extraordinary meeting of the shareholders of this company Was held at the gas works on Monday under the presidency of Mr. W. Hayes. There was a very large attendance. The business was to consider the bill to be laid before Parliament to enable the company go raise additional capital to construct new works and for ether purposes. The bill was unanimously approved and adopted. WIDNES CRI7RCII OF ENGLAND TONTINE SOCIETY.—The balance sheet of this teciety shows that the income of the society during the past year had been £247 2s 10. There had been £77 13s 10c1 paid to sick members, and £l4 in death claims, whilst various other expenses amounted to £6 fie 10d, leaving a balance of £144 to be divided 1 amongst 146 members. L balance of £5 4s 23. is carried forward. TRE Pawn OF BREAD IN FRANCE.—The Standard Paris correspondent states that the amount of the proposed, duty in France upon corn and flour will make the cost of bond in that country dearer than it is in 12 countries of Egrope, in sise of which there are no duties, and in the other six the duties are lower than they will be in France: It is estimated that the effect of the tax will be to increase the expenditure for a workingman's family of four persons by about £2 lOs per annum; and yet there are people in Ude country who advocate putting a tax on wheat. Rl:wow Penises CRURCH ASSURANCE SOCIETY.—The annual meeting of this society was held oneldonday even- ing, when a dividend of Ll 2s was paid to each member. The Rev. Canon Barclay presided and delivered an address on thrift. The vicar was re-appointed president, and Messrs Sohn Brundrit and William Whittaker the trustees. The other officers were appointed as follows :—Mr. William Sut- ton, hon. treasurer ' • Mr. John Littler, secretary ; Messrs Charles Pownall and Walter Brown, auditors ; Messrs John Yates and James Moores, stewards ; committee : Messrs John Wilson, James Littler, Peter Wright, Richard Hemp. son, William Rhodes, William Houghton, James Mort, John Rathbone and William Pownall. Lockwood, Messrs. John Ash- ton, Mclntyre, Aaron, Lewis, Wallington, Stokes, Derby- shire, Warburton, Neild, Knowles, Weir, R. Ashton EL Linaaer (clerk), W. H. On Tieesday morning, Robert Hughes, aged 64 years, who lived with his son at Halton, died very Innexpecte.dly. Father and Bon are employed at the Weston Chemical wilts, and on the way borne on Monday evening, the deceased complainedmi a difficulty in breathing, and he had to stop several times in consuptenca. On arriving home, however, he partook heartily of supper and retired to rest at half -past nine. Next morning at six o'clock, when the son went to awaken him he Found him lying in bed quite dead. Dr. Carruthers had attended the deceased on several occasions for Chronic bran- chi,ia and weeknene of the heat, and undentke circum- stances the coroner thought an inquest unnecessary. Tnu HOME Iron Tuape.—The iifeleesness of the Eng. lish iron market in the last week of the year is a matter which will cause no surprise. Even in the most prosperous years the business men casts away cares of toil for once at a time a Testive rejoicing. This 'year, ho,wever, many a enenufacturer and merchant will not be able to do this with a mind entirely at rest, for the 'past year has been any- thing 'b -at a good one. Tim unemployed workman also, who Las been made to fail the pinch of hard times, will look 'with a feeling of nneasirrecs to the future. Still, tbo re- teetion will come to many that the year now almost be- Lind Is>. In;ght I,Asre lih/Oft worse- All, however, will look with renewed hope—for there ate of a turn of the tide—to the new year.—lron. BEGGING IMPOSISRS AT BUNCORN.—Before Mr. C. Ileynolds and Mr. A. Thomas, at Runcorn -Petty Sessions' on Monday, John Ford was broueht up in custody charged with making a false statement for the purpose of obtaining relief. About nine o'cleck on Saturday night the prisoner applied at the police station for a ticket for a night's lode. logs, and informed Police Clerk Wallace that he had only 23 in his possession. The officio searched the prisoner and found 73 secrwed in his fele whereupon he took him into custody.—Superintenclent Leah said 'he had received an in- timation from the Workhouse that the wards were full, and that they could not receive vagrants. It was usual for tramps logo direct toe lodging-house, leave the whole of their money there, and then go to the police station and say they were penniless.—The prisoner explained to their Worships that his own trousers were in pawn, and a person had given him the pair he was wearing. Redid not know there was lTd in the pocket.—The prisoner was sentenced to -seven days' hard labour.---TWO men, who gave the name Of . IMansorl Thomas' were charged at Runcorn Petty Sessions Ott Monday with begging.—lt appeared that on Saturday afternooe PC. Egerton was on duty at 'Sutton in plain .clothes when he saw the prisoners go to Hallwood Farm amd present a letter, and they were given something. They wished to kiss the hands of Miss Savage. Subsequently they met the constable on the' round, presented him with a 'letter, and kissed his hands. The letter, read as follows':— Thin man is a native of Palestine, the Holy Land. He ,cannot speak English. By treating him as a stranger in a strange land, with kindness, you will serve God. He is a Christian in a humble devout way." Egerton took the pri- soners into custody, anden one prisoner be found 68 lland on the other Is 11-1. He also found two letters exactly like the ens handed to him.---Superintendent Leah said the prisoners were dressed 'in a peculiar fashion, and created alarm wherever they went. One of the prisoners had in- Isrmed the officer that -he was Jesus Christ. He carried a -stack in the form of a cease, while the other prisoner had carved on a stick he :possessed the word Palestine. The 'men pretended that they could not speak English, and were •utaisble to understand the evidence that had been given. 'Superintendent Leah said when they were arrested they 'spoke English, and stated they bad landed in Liverpool 'from Palestine.—The prism:ere were made to understand tbat if they would go to Liverpool at once they would be liberated, and during the afternoon they were taken to the railway station, given tickets, and placed on a Liverpool train. -SAD DROWNING FATALITY AT RIINCORN.—A DANGBROUS afire:sr.—At the Burial Boardroom, Cemetery, Runcorn, on Monday, Mr. T. J. Ridgway, 'coroner for the honour and fee of Halton, held an inquest on the body of Charles Jones, which was recovered from the Old Quay Canal on Saturday mornieg in an advanced state of decomposition. The de- ceased was 31 years of age, and, lived in Nelson-street. He was a chemical labourer at the works of the Runcorn Soap and %Alkali Company, where two months ago a fatal accident occurred through the opening of the door of a chemical chamber ever which he bad control. About eleven' o'clock on the night of the 25th November Jones left home to go to the flat Annie, lying in the Old Quay Canal, in order to .do some work for his father-in-law, and to take a loaf for the boy who was on board. There was a dense fog at the time. At the bridge, Ellis Clark, dock watchman, met the. deceased, and about five minutes afterwards whilst speaking tort ilatrean and his wife, who had lost their way, he heard a.scream. lieearoceeded in the direction of the sound, bet All was nuiet. Next morning deceased's hat and the loaf were:found fleeting on the water, and the canal was dragged withcut result.—Mary Hannah Joust, wife of the deceased, stated that her husband Is rd been in low spirits since " the job "at the Runcorn Soap and Alkali Works. He was dis- charged by Mr. Wigg. He was alweos very steady, and -was to'have eruplooment at St. Helens the first week in the new year.--t Ellis Clark, 27, Canal-street, dock watchman for the Bridgevrrter Navigation Company, in answer to the aioroner, said flatmes were veley careless and often left the bridge open, when it was very easy to walk into the water when the weather WaS.bad. lie was the watchman for about half a milesof docks and the yard, and he was not instructed to look after the bridge, but he .ssede it part of his duty to do so. The bridge was closed on the night in question. --By Mr. W. Randley (foreman): There was a lamp just ' against the bridge.--Several jurymen spoke of the danger of leaving the bridge open, and Mr. Kay (juryman) said titan used to be a lad to look after the bridge, arid he had a but and everything necessary on the spot.—The foreman said it was important that the bridge should be tended.— The Coroner said although the matter diki not come within the scope of that inquiry, he should take upon hie:mei( to write to Mr. Meadowcroft, as the bridge mig.ht be the cuss of an accident at some future period.—P.o deposed to recovering the body, He added that the bank was vary dangerous, as it eloped down to the canal. He was of opinion the deceased had crossed the bridge in cafety and then lost his way, and slipped down the bank into the water. ..The Coroner : It all shows that this is a dangerous place, Whetd a watchman would be a great benefit —A yerdaet of foga towned was returned.

BANKRUPTCY PROCEEDINGS.—The adjourned public cc- &ruination at Thomas Mather, of Weston Point, near Run- corn, bricklayer, and formerly a grocer, was fixed to take place at the Warrington County Court on Someday. The ' debtor was present, but no creditors put in an appearance. Mr Ridgway., official receiver, expressed himself satisfied with written answers given by the bankrupt to a number a of questions, and the examination was then declared Con. eluded.

THE QUE.EN -SICK AND BIM= SOCIETY, RUNCORN. nit society which is held at the Queen's Hotel, Waterloo- road, has just concluded the year's operations, and a divi. deed of £1 es iv has been paid to each member. Mr. Davies is the president, Mr. Coleburn, secretary, and Mr. John Miller treasurer. At the annual meeting, Mr. Thomas Williamson, who was the chief founder of the society, was presented with a silver pencil case for the manner in which he had fillet his octal position. The object was to raise funds towards the erection of a temper- ance hall at West Bank, and there was a good attendance of nen withers during the afternoon. At four o'clock the company sat down to a knife and fork tea prepared by Bro. W. Hodgkin/ion. Subsequently an enjoyable entertainment WWI given, The proceedings were under the direction of Bro. ASSAULTING A WIDNES WATCHMAN.—Finsh Brown, a youth, was summoned to Widnes Petty Sessions, en Wed- maJay, to answer a charge of aeeaulting Richard Aepinall. —eAspinall is the watchman at the copper works of Messrs. He denied the accusation, and also produced evi- dence that he took no part in the attack.—The Bench Inflicted a One of hand costs, 14s. ATTACK OS A R:71400/DS BEERNOOSS KEEPER.—Before Mr. Henry Reynolds and Mr. John Brun'drit, at the Run- corn Police Court on Wednesday, John Grattan, a boatman, WAS charged with assaulting John Bassett, the landlord' of the Lamb and Flag beerhouse, Halton-road. He was, however, set upon by the prisoner and his emu- panians, and severely handled. A warrant was issued for the apprehension of the prisoner, who was the only man , known, and on Tuesday he was arrested by P.C. On the previous evening P.O Smith observed the woman enter several shops and ask for assistance. If her demands were refused she cursed in an alarming fashion, arid was very violent in her actions. The officer, therefore, apprehended her, and she was now sentenced to 14 dame bard leboisr.—Mr. Brundrit remarked that begging was much on die incr.as,. In the town, and the bench were de- termined 'to stamp the evil out.— —Peter Leather appeared under a warrant for not sending his child regularly to school.—On the evidenoe of Mr. Bowyer, the attendance offices, he was fined Sc. Truer FROM A WIDNES PAYINDROCER'S SHOP. At Widnes Petty Sessions on Wednesday Mary Stewart, a mar- ried woman, living be euttori'a-lano, who appeared in the dock with a child three weeks old in her arms, was charged with stealing a pair of elastic tame, the property of Mrs. Jamieson, pawnbroker, Anne-street, West. About seven o'clock on Saturday night, Maria Jones, assistant to the prosecatrix, saw the prisoner loitering .about boots which were hanging ineble the Shop door. Subsequently the boots (produced) .were missed. and P.S. Strickland went to the house of the prisoner's husband and found the stolen boots there. The prisoner alleged that the articles were her hus- band's, but the husband did not know whether they were his or not. In answer to the charge the prisoner said " all right." She was 'convicted. . Sperm , AND CO.'S RUNCORN ALMANAC—The first edition of thiemelnable almanao is now in the hands of the publishers. Ift counting a mass of useful local and general information, a largenuantity el highly readable matter, is profusely illustrated, and fin me altogether a volume which ought to find its way into every household. A new and the chief feature in the book is a historical sketch of Runcorn, which all persons interested in the port will read with pleasure. The social, ecclesiastical, and commercial phases of the town has undergone since the year 916 to the present time are described in an attractive way. The account also includes an interesting reference to the Board of Commis- sionere, and the reprint of an interesting old directory. The almanac, which is published at a penny, reflects great credit upon thee enterprising firm whose name it bears. Tun TICHDORNE CLAIMANT AT WIDNES.—At the Widnes , Police• Court on Monday, before Mr. J. Brock, George Hold- I hie, known to the pigeon-shooting community as George ' I IL Fowler, ,Fowler Millfield Inn, Appleton, Widnes, applied for a . , special license to sell beer on his recreation grounds on 1 Tuesday.—Mr. Lewin asked why the special license was wanted.--Applicant: It is the occasion of a pigeon-shooting match between Sir Roger Tichborne and myself.—Mt. Brock : Sir Roger Tichborne ?—Applicant : Well, the Claimant —Mr. Brock : Does he go pigeon-shooting ?—Ap- plicant: Yes.—Mr. Brock : Anything to make money.— Applicant: I shot with him before his first-trial.—Mr. 'Break : I think there is a great deal of cruelty—abominable cruelty—connected with this" sport."—Applicant : Well, 'that just depends, sir, how it is carried out. I believe there is a great deal of cruelty connected with some matches.— Mreßrock : We hear of a great deal of cruelty which is ve.y authentic.—Applicant : I know; but it is not so when it is properly carried out.—The application was granted.-- On Tuesday afternoon a pigeon-shooting match took placo between the Claimant and Mr. Fowler. There were not many spectators present, although the weather was all that .4ould be desired. The birds were supplied by Mr. Draper., 1•2 of Belton, and were shot at 31 yards rise from five traps. Mr. Edwardson, of Widnes, attended the trap machine. 'Considering (as "Sir Roger " said during the afternoon amidst much laughter) that he has had no practice for ten leers, he shot very well, hitting 12 birds out of 21. After his tenth shot, when his score stood at five, he killed Aix •Virds in succession, but he failed to hit the last four. Mr. 'Fowler killed 16 birds, and so came off victorious by four. ' At noon the Claimant was met at the railway station by a ,curious crowd.

A WARNING TO WIDNES PDBLICANS.—Before Mr. J. Brock and Mr. H. Gaskell, jun.' at Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, Wilbraham Wood, landlord of the Grapes In, Victoria-road, was charged with having supplied in. ting liquor to P.C. Prior whilst on duty, without the consent of his superior officer.—Mr. J. 0. Swift, of St. Helens, elefended.--,P.S. Strickland and P.C. Prior gave eel- dence.to the effect that about ten o'clock on the night of the 18th inst. the constable and Mr. Thomas Edwardson, mineral water manufacturer, Simm's Cress, met near the defenthnt's house. The constable observed that it was -cry cold, and Mr. Edwardson asked him to have a drink. The 'ovation was refused, but Mr. Edwardson having entered the public-house, the constable followed. Mr. Edwardson ordered a pint of beer for the officer and a glass of beer for himself, and they were quietly consuming the liquor in the bar-room, when Sergeant Strickland appeared lon the scene. To the sergeant Mrs. Wood admitted that 8-e ueo supplied the cor-sta3le.—ln his address to the Bench, Mr. Swift drew attention to the fact that for 13 years tha defendant had been in charge or public-houses in Widnes.and not the slightest complaint had been made against him. He contended that as the defendant bad not sold nor given the liquor to the constable, ne offence had been com- mitted under the itet.—Thomas Mlerardson deposed that when the constable eigcred the room tke "drinks" were on the table. Mrs. Wood stated that when she supplied the liquor she bad no idea it was for a polieeman.—The Bench considered the case proved. Mr. Brock remarked that the drink was pra.ctically served to the constable, whose discre- tion appeared to have been overcome by the cold. As this was the first case against the defendant he would only be fined 5s and costs, Us. rublicans could apt be too careful wbst they did.

div.head: DREADFUL EITICIDeAT RUNCOZN.
div.p: DREADFUL EITICIDeAT RUNCOZN.

Wifliam Ashbrook, landlord of this Millstone Inn, Mill- street, Runcorn, committed suic;de in a very determined manner on Fiiday night last week. Far a fortnight pre- vious Ashbrook had acted somewhat strangely; he appeared to be brooding about some matter, and showed a groat disin- clination to converse with the members of his own family. On Friday night the members of the Tontine Club, of which he was the secretary, had to meet at his home to receive their dividend, but at 7 o'clock, before the time fixed for their arrival, he left the house. As he did nut return the box in which he kept the "club money" was broken open, and it was discovered that there was between £ll and £l2 short. Ashbrook could not be found and about ten o'clock his step- daughter, Ann Ellis, went to a drawer to fetch some tobacco, when she came across the following letter:—" December 19th, 1881. Dear wife, Amen! I write these few lines to say , that I cannot meet the club members as I have used their , money and I am in debt. Yon must put my children in the workhouse. You have been a good wife to me and I have been I think a good husband to you, but we must part. I have male my peace with God. I hope he will forgive me for what I have done. You will lied my body in Anderton's tub. God bless you and my children, and I remain your affectionate husband, W. Ashbrook." John Ellis, brother.in- ltw, landlord of the Forester's Arms, Canal-street, and several other persons at once commenced a search. They obtained access to Andertou's yard, but there was nothing whatever suspicious about therein tub. About eleven o'clock however, his dead body was found lying in a pool of blood in Andetton's pig stye, and Dr. Robinson and the police were sent for. In his throat were five wounds, no doubt inflicted by a small open penknife, which WAS found on the floor be- neath him. His clothes were very wet, and it is thought that he had endeavoured to drown himself in the fain tub, but had failed, and retired to the pig sty. An inquest on the body WO9 held at the Police Court on Monday, before Mr. T. J. Ridgway, the coroner. Evidence bearing out the above narrative was given by Ann Ellis, John Elps, and P.C. Disley, and the jury, of which Mr. W. Handley was foreman, returned a verdict that the deceased committed sui- cide whilst of unsound mind.

div.head: CHRISTMASTIDE AT RUNCORN.
div.p: CHRISTMASTIDE AT RUNCORN.

To the great majority of the people Christmas is only another term for abundance of the necessaries of life, a few of its !wearies, and a general geniality of spirit. In Rune corn the tradesmen take the fallest advantage of the joyous etesson. and their shop windows are made attractive by I bright:tinted paper, green fo iage, and a skilful arrangement of their wares. On Tueelay evening, "show night," the shops were all ag'ove witk gaslight, and the streets were thronged with persons of all ages and all sexes, and the 'scene altogether was one of brisk animation. Naturally the establishments of the butchers, with gaily decorated carcases of cows prime porkers, and well fed sheep ; but the game dealers' display of farmyard fowl, and plump par- tridges and fat pheasants, attracted the most attention. I Amongst the butchers Mr. J. dough's, Church-street, Mr. Savage's. High-street, arid Mr. Medley. High-street, had some splendid beasts cut up, while Mr. S. Yarwooch Church- , street, had an extensive stock of genie, dm. Mr. W. Mellor, ! grocer, Chtirch-street, had his windows set out in a very attractive fashion, and the game may be said of Mr. Byrne , and Mr. Blair in the same locality, and Mr. J. 0. Jackson, in Bridge-street. The extensive frontage of Messrs Unsworth ' Bros.' establishmentovas brilliantly lighted with gas jets, and their great variety of goods were displayed to the fullest advantage. Messrs Boyden and Coventry. Church-street, had decorated their places of business. Mr. Handle, Bridge- street, Mr. R. Morris High-street, and Mr. King, Bridge' street, had disposed their bright drapery goods in an attrac- tive manner; while the stationery goods out Christmas presents of Mr. Humphrey, High-street, had not been lees successfully arranged. On Christmas eve, and until late in the morning, the choirs of the different places of worship went about the town singing seasonable hymns and merry carols, while several brass bands also made the night melodious with music. On Christmas day the railway station was closed, and the town wore a very quiet aspect. Below are particulars of a few events:— RMSCORN Permit Cflunca.—The interior of this sacred ledifice was beautifully and appropriately decorated for the Christmas season. Twining the massive stone pillars was a wealth of holly leaves and evergreen of various kinds, and on the walls were texts formed of green leaves. On the south wall was the promise "There shall come forth a rod out of the stem of Jesse," while on the west side were the words "Rock of Ages." The chancel presented a very pretty appearance. There was some tastefully executed trellis work on the east wall, and shields bearing ecclesias- tical devices adorned the chancel arches. Ivy leaves and , holly bordered the pulpit, the panels of which were tilled ' with appropriate emblems, whilst the font was artistically decorated with flowers and mosses. The evergreens, &c. were eupplied by Mrs. C. Flazlehurst, of the Trange, Mr. S. B. Chadwick, J.P., Mt. J. L. Wigg, and Mr. H. Linaker, Aston Hall. Aah- But they have asked Flint and Denbigi..—Mr. Nor. man : They have asked but not before they got hold of oar £l,OOO. They 'evidently thought a bird la the hand worth two in the bash.—Mr. Norman Whether that is so or not I think we htve a perfect right to have this thing properly settled.—Mr. R. If we i do not get a' reply the matter &told. go on further.—The Chairman : You 'would repeat the. question 2—Mr. Speak- man: Yea, I should.—Me West Itlgton : We have asked a clvtnoestuanTann-weretrght to have-s civil aaswe,. W•ter to the Mayer a once.—Mr. Aaron: Write to his master at ; once.—The Deputy Clerk: Send a copy of the correspond- ence to the Mayor.—Mr. Norman: I move that. —Mr. Weir: I second that.—Mr. IValliogton supported the motion. The town clerk's letter was au insult to the clerk.—Mr. Speak- man moved, and Mr. Mclntyre seconded an amendment that the question be repeated to the town clerk.—Mr. Nor- man's motion was carried by 8 votes to 6. FINAMCR.—Mr. Randley presented the report of the Finance Committee, who recommended the payment of au- -1 counts amounting to £1 200. WARRINGTON PARISH CHURCH.

DEDICATION OF TWO NEW BELLS. On Christmas eve an interesting service took place in the Parish Church. Two additional hells having been recently given, one by the family of the late Mr. W. C. Jones, of the Elms, in his memory, and the other by the Rev. W. Quekett, MA., rector, to complete the octave. Christmas eve was chosen as the day appropriate for the interesting ceremony. At eight o'clock the choir marched in procession to the organ, and the service commenced by the singing of hymn 203, A. and M., then followed shortened evensong said by the Rev It W P Montgomery, curate, after which a special hymn composed by the Rev. Canon Bell, rector of Chelten- ham, was sung to music by Sir J. Stevenson. The curates then left the choir stalls and followed by the churchwardens, who left their pew to receive the bells, stood immediately before the belle in the chanceL The Rev. Montgomery said it devolved upon him .end his fellow curate to dedicate these bells in the absence of the rector through serious illness. He knew it lay near the rector's heart to have himself per- formed this service, and, as it were, completed the work I which would always resod as a memorial of him to all future generations, viz , the restoration of the church and the building of the spire. Tnis last gift would complete the work which the rector had undertaken. Before formally dedicating the belle, he could not but feel and express his regret that the rector was not with them. But as they were aware their rector was seriously ill and he commended him to their prayers. He thou4ht it was somewhat appropriate that the bells should be dedicated on Christmas Eve, reminding people as they called them to worship of the birth of Jesus Christ. Perhaps that night they would carry their thoughts to the tinkling of the sheep belle on the Juicean hillside on the first Christmas Eve when the birth was announced to the step.] herds. May those bells ever ring out to them the sweet message that Jesus Christ is born to save them. The rev. gentleman touching the bells then said—" We dedicate these bells to the glary of alini.thty God and the use of this Sburch for ever ;.' aol, addressin4 the churchwardens, said —" We present on behalf of the Rector these bells to you for the uso of this church, of which you are the custodians as representatives of the parishioners." Hymn 223, A. and M., was then sung, after which a c)llect was said and the blessing pronounced by the Rev. J. iVeller. The choir afterwards sung some carols, and Mr. W. S. Weode, the organist, played two voluntaries. The bells are from the foundry of Me3srs. Mess and Stainbeck, and weigh respectively 15 cwt. and 5 cwt. The church bells were suitably decorated by the following ladies r—Mrs. Quekett, Miss Ryles, Misses Bargees, Miss J. Allen, Misses White, Misses Buckton, Misses Robinson, Mrs. Franeomb, Miss Kidd, Miss Cassidy, Miss Holley, and Miss flinde.

div.head: WARRINGTON BLUE COAT SCHOOL. DISTRIBUtION OF PRIZES. .
div.p: WARRINGTON BLUE COAT SCHOOL. DISTRIBUtION OF PRIZES. .

The distribution of prizes to the scholars of this institu- tion took place on Tuesday evening hi the presence of a considerable number of visitors. After the children, whose appearance was very neat and cheerful, had sung three anthems, Mr. I. CHARLTON PARR, delivered the prizas. In doing so he said that not only did the children receive valuable and useful presents, but they had also the 'satis- faction of feeling that they had pleased their masters, and they had the approval of their ewn consciences in the feel- ing that they had done their beet. Education well ' direct's' was an inestimable boon and a great pewee for good, but education without correction, or wrongly directed, might not only be productive of little good, but of consider- I able evil. In these days of secular and technical education it was a satisfaction to old-fashioned people like himself to turn to a good old foundation like the Warrington Blue Coat Schoel. (Appl au se.) There they had religious teach- ing, and high moral principles were inculcated iu the boys and girls, who were taught their duty to their God and their neighbour, and were receiving a sound and practical education to lit them for a career of usefulness in the world. (Hear, hear.) To educate children without religion was to deprive them of what should be their guiding star through life, and what must be a source of inestimable comfort to them to the close of life. The care and attention that had been paid to the children was evidenced by their happy, healthy, and intellectual faces, and it was a great proof of the care and management of Mr. and Mrs. Rose (master and and mistress), who were to be congratulated on their efforts. He must heartily congratulate Mr. and Mrs Rose on the creditable examination that the children had passed. He then press nted the prizes which consisted exclusively of books. —Alderman DAVIES, who rose to propose a vote of thanks to Mr. Parr for attending to distribute the prizes, said that he thought it would be interesting if he told of some of his recollections of that school. It was founded in /an, and he had no doubt was brought about by the determination of the Englishmen of that day, who, having gone through what be weuld call the fire of the Cromwellian period, had a strong religious feeling in their breasts. These men determined to assist others, and at that time sprung up in various parts of the country the foundation of Blue Coat Schools. He thought that the world had grown rather better since those times, and had grown better amongst the children, as there was not now the same tyranny exercised by big over little boys as was formally the case. He was glad that such tyranny had decreased. They (the children) were to be the men and women of the next generation, and the education they now received was the seed that would hereafter bear fruit. If religions education was not fostered they would live to see the day when England would degen- erate. The Church had exerted herself much to make things better than they were, and if religious feeling was not maintained a most undesirable revolution might take place in this country.—The vote of thanks was heartily recorded to Me. Parr, and cheers were given for Mr. and Mrs. Rose. A miscellaneous programme was rendered by the scholars in a creditable manner.

DRAM OF THE EARL OF INEORTON.—OR Wednesday morn- ing intelligence was received at Wentwotth Woodhouse of the death of the Earl of Morton, brother of the Countess Fitzwilliam. The late earl has been a representative peer of Scotland since April, 1859, and was elected to the present Parliament. He will be succeeded by his eldest eon, Sholto aeorge, Lord Aberdour, who was born lo 1844, at Dalalahoy.

div.head: OUR LONDON LETTER.
div.p: OUR LONDON LETTER.

LONDON, THURSDAY. The immovable hold which Christmas has obtained upon the British public is testified to by the appearance of the Lon- don shops throughout this week. All the windows are fall of " Christmas presents ;" there is Christmas decoration ever/where, and the butchers' shops are once more blocka- ded with grossly fat beasts. The late Mrs. John Spratt must have had a particalatly merry time at Christmas, revelling in the monstrosities, which, in obedience to sup- posed taste, butchers produce at this season. The Esquiruaux might get along very well just now; but, regarding the average meat-eater, there must be an enormous amount of waste on the butchers' bills at Christmas time. To breed beef, and mutton, and pork till a pennyworth of lean is hidden among an intolerable quantity of fat, is, however, one of the traditions of the trade not to be borne down by consideration of reasonableness. A butcher whose Christ- mas show presented an average admixture of lean and fat such as at other seasons are seen in a well fed beast, would feel himself disgraced. It is said that another Christmas usage, ttiacof sending Christmas cards, is dying out, though the assertion is not borne out by a glance at the shots win- dows. There seem this , year more Christmas caids than ever, and an increase of skill, taste, and ingenuity bestowed upon their manufacture. Nevertheless, society has declared against Christmas cards, perhaps not without a shrewd re- cognition of the regularly increasing trouble in dealing with an ever widening circle. The thing to do now is to obtain a special design, the simpler the better, and Moo. in the Dame of your friends, send the cards Abroad with '' the com- pliments of the season," or wishes for h ppy new year. Certainly, as yet, this inrovation has made no difference in the aggregate sale of the aiticle. The best known among the manufacturers tells me that he has this year, with satis• factory results, invested more money in the production of Christmas cards than during any previous year.
