It is curioua the difference of opinion between the Germans and the English on the merit of the great singer. It is now many years since Madame Joachim faced a London audience, bat even then her husband had attained the rank in public favour which be has always known how to keep. Rumours of a great repu- tation preceded her ; but her success was " a success of esteem." She had tleought better of the British public, and left the island very angry, said she would never revisit it—a threat which so long as we pessess Patti, Nielson, Albani, Marie Bone, Leo., seems to leave the public not in- consolable—and did all she could to prevent her husband's visits. Happily she could control her own movements better than his. I think he has almost as many triends., and indeed almost as many relatives, in London as in Berlin.

THE FAIR TRADE QC/MID/Z.—The following leaflet, about to be circulated in the agricultural districts by the Cobden Club, is written for the Club by the Rizht lion W. E. Baxter, M.P. :—" A Catechism for Fair Traders." 1. Is it true that the labouring chases are better off now ithan they ever were before in times of commercial depres- sion ? 2. Is pauperism declining ? 3. Is the volume of our trade actually increasing, although manufacturers and merchants are still suffering from that over-production which deceived SO many people a few years ago as a sign of great prosperity? 4. Are the manu- facturers of industries of other coantries, say the United States and France—where a Protective system prevails—not in a far worse state than ours? 5. Have both these nations virtually lost their shipbuilding and ship- owning trade to our great gain ? 6. Is more tonnage turned out in the yards on the Tyne than in all France? 7. Have the American cottorfspinners and weavers been driven out of neatly all the markets of the world by unprotected British manufacturers ? 5. Have wages in New England fallen 40 per cent in ten years ? 0. Are the working classes in many American manufacturing towns at this moment not presenting every sign of poverty and wretchedness ? 10. In all countries under the protective system is not the commercial depression greater than in this country, and in- creasing ? The only reply to each of these questions is " Yes !" and the answer is conclusive against any change In our laws, except that which would give us a free break. fast-table, and abolish all duties on food of whatever kind.

It is a point in which they are more interested even than in the Coleridge scandals, sal, by the way, I hear that a settlement is at band, and that though the plaintiff is not yet married he will be shortly. The other litigation is the test action that is going to be brought, to try how far railway companies will be supported in relying on conditions printed in diamond type on the backs of tickets limiting their liability. The judges who refused to .. . . allo- - • ' "

tow a plaintiff leave to appeal in a Cas.e. which they gays 10 favour of the defending company have been strongly criticised. The question is one of great importances. All travellers are interested to know whether companies caS protect themselves in cases of gross unpunctuality, result.. ing is appreciable loss to their customers, by printing a little sentence on the back of a ticket, and thus showing that their servants were not gui!tv of wilful. misconduct. hear a case is selected upon which the facie will be very clear. Indeed, the Prosecuting Association will be ems. harassed with the wealth of their seltcticn, and then the qaestlon Arilt go up to the House of Li rls. It is not thought likely that two judges will again ref Li Se the plain- tiff leave to appeal.

_ LY.11.4. DrILNICENYESS.—Jobn Murphy, labourer. was braught before Mr. Norris at Lymm Police Court on S Lturday, on a charge of being drunk and disorderly. He was fined 7s and costs, or seven days' imprisonment. Culusruss —I he festive season was observed in the usual manner at Lymm, but the village was a Itttle quieter than has been the case in former years. The local baud turned out on Christm is Eve, but the waits were few and far be- tween. Yesterday there was a good many vi4itors, scd one or two youngsters ventured on the ice at the dam.

DISASTROUS COLLISION AT SEA. TWO VESSELS SUNK. A disastrous collision occurred off the Eddystone Light- house on Thursday morning, resulting in the foundering of a Norwegian barque and a steamship of nearly 1 200 tons, with a cergo valeed at between £60,000 and £70,000. The Chelydra was a screw steamer, and belnnesd to Sunderland. She left that port on November 20, 1883, with a cargo of coals, baund for India. Going down the English Channel an accident happened to her machinery, and she put into Plymouth for repairs. After arriving at Tuticorin, about fifty mks north of Ctylon, she discharged her cargo and sailed for Singapore for orders, and thence to Manilla. In August last she sailed for Japan, where she took a cargo of rice for Bremerhaven. All went well on the homeward voyage until Thursday morning, when foterteen miles from Eddystone Lighthouse, she Was run into isy the Norwegian baeque Holstein, bound to Newport. The ha quo foundered within a quarter of an hour. The stesmer went dawn in 40 minutes. The Chelydra's crew of 28 took to their boats, and were picked up five hours later. The barque's crew of 15 took to their boats with the intention of making for Plymoutb, but have not since been heard of. They had no provisions with them. ANOTHER Accormr. Early on Christmas morning a steamer and a barque came into collision in the English Channel with the result that bath vessrls sank. The steamer Wee the Chelydra, 1.1413 tans, W. Wynne master, owned by Mr. Cuthbert Hutchin- son, Sunderland. She left Hirgo, Japan, with a cargo of rice for Bternen. She carried twenty.seven hands and One passenger. She made Uahent on Tuesday at midnight, aed on Christmas morning was proceeding up channel, the Eddystone being about 14 miles distant. It was a clear starliglat night. About 3-30 :the look out men on board the steamer sighted a large barque coming down channel, ap- parently intending to pass the Chelyctra on the port side. When the vessels were almost within hailing distance the barque came right across the bow of the steamer. The shock was very heavy. The steamer's port side Has cut into about midships to the depth of sev.n • feet, and when Captain Wynne, who was in his cabin, came on deck he found the barque's bowsprit over hie ahip and the vase' surging round his quarter. He gave a hlaf turn ahead, starboarded his helm, and the two ships parted, the barque dissappearing. The Chelydra had a great hole in her aide, extending from the upper deck far below the water line, and the water rushed in with such great force that when the care penter sounded the well within a few minutes of the acci•; dent be found four feet of water in the hold. The crew, which was British, behaved well. A sail was passed over the hole, and two steam pumps-were kept at teork, but the water speedily rose to nine feet, and the Alp settled down. One of the lifeboats bad been smashed in the Collision, and the remaining three boats were safely lowered and pulled off. The cantain and mate were the last to leave the steamer, and at that time the, water. was level with the upper deck. Within a few minutes the Cbelydra went down bow first. At the time of the collision an elderly seaman sprung from the barque on to the steamer, bat he was frantic with fear. A quarter of an hour before the steamer foundered, a Ix a: from the barque came alongside with about fourteen men in it. The ca,ptain, who was one of them, said his vessel was the Alice Crockall, of Fleetwood, that he wage sure she would sink, but he did net need help, as he would pull for the lighthouse and the shore. He took aboael his boat the seaman who had get on to the steamer and then pulled away. Nothing has been heard of them since, but as a steamer was seen to pass the spot soon after it is expected tbat they got aboard her, and will be landed at an up-Channel port. . . THE LONDON BRIDGE EXPLOSION.—Workmtn are tn. gaged in repairs at Loadon Bridge, but the tide is unfavour. able for operations. They are protecting with iron bars the grating fixed on Tuesday over the gully holes. A body has been washed ashore near Rotherhithe, and lies in the par.:h mortuary. The clothing is said to correspond with the du.- cription given by Carter of those worn by one of the men to whom the Ariel wee lent. Carter has seen the body lying at the mortuary at R)therhithe, but has failed to recognize it. Photographs have been taken of the deceits ; but there was nothing in his papers to connect him with the- outrage.

WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT. SATTIRDAY.—Be(ore Aldermen Burgess and Mendley. DRUNKENNESS.-7ames Garretty, 22, Ship-yard, was fined 5s and costs for being drank and disorderly at the Wool Pack Inn on the previous evening, and 103 and costs for assaulting a man named Samuel Hughes, at the same time and place.—Thomas Taylor, labourer, was charged with being drunk in Bold-street on the previous evening; he was diemiased with a caution. Scernann.—Emma Janes, domestic servant, was charged on suspicion with stealing various sums amoanting in all to £2 45 3d, the property of Francis •Jesper, her employer.— The case was not pressed, and the girl was acquitted. MONDAY.—Before the Mayor (Alderman Harrison) and Mr. John Fairciough. penementearzes.—Mary Banks (18) was fined 103 and costs, cr 14 day', for being drunk at the police station on Satter- day.—George Parker, charged with being drunk in Mersey street on Saturday eveaing, was alloived to go on payment of is, the costs.—The following eases were also heard Wm. Bayley, fined 5s and costs or seven days; Thomas Wilkinson, charge withdrawn ; Catherine Ball, fined 53 in- eluding costs; Mary Walker, 55 and costs; Margaret Camp- bell, 53 including costs. Mrscremamons.—Patrick Dempsey and Michael Kenny were charged with assaulting Was. Foy; they were dis- charged.— Tobn Phcenix and Edward Smith, boys, pleaded guilty to damaging holly trees, the property of Mr. Buck- ton, on the 18th inst. Phoenix was sentenced to receive 12 strokes with the birch rod, and Smith to receive six.— Mabel Gandy was sent to prison for 14 days for using ob- scene language in Buttermarket-street on the 14th inst.— Thomas Hackett wds fined Is for allowing the chimney of his dwelling.houme to be en fire ; and emma Taylor, for setting the chimney of her house on fire, was ordered to pay the costs of the case, 3s. 61. TUESDAY.—There were no charges down for hearing. WEDNESDAY.—Before Aldermen Burgess and Chandley. DRUNELNNESS. Margaret Fleming was fined 5s and costs or seven daya for being drunk and disorderly in But- termarket-street ASSAULTS.—Micba3I Naylor was charged with assaulting a married woman named Fanny Williams. Both parties live in Edward-street, and the assault, which was of a trivet nature, was alleged to have taken place on the 13th inst. Mr. A. Browne appeared for the complainant, and Mr. Jenkins defended.—Mr. Jenkins, on behalf of his client, offered a public apology, which was accepted by the other side.—Thomas Gibbons was charged with assaulting his wife on the night of the 20th inst. Defendant, his wife, and his tnother-in-liw were coming from Grappenhall to Warrington, and a quarrel occurred when near the Cheshire Cheese. The chfendant "thumped" his wife. He now said that at the time he was elevated, and "somehow or other they got intermixed with one another" and he did assault her.—Alderman Chandley : YOU are a dangerous man to be mixed up with.—Prisoner: If it bad not been for my mother-in-llw there would not }lave been a bother.— Alderman Burro: Oh. you are suffering from mother-in- law. (Laughter )—Defendant was bound over to keep the peace for six months.. FRlDAY.—Bcfore Mr. John White, Alderman Davies, and Councillor Milner. THREATENING LANGUAGE.—Robert Barns was charged with using threats towards his father, Patrick Burns, on the 21st inst.—He was ordered to find sureties to keep the peace fOr six months. ASSAULTING A PUBLICAN.—John Connor and Richard Warburton were charged with being drunk wed disorderly in Battermarket-strect on Christmas Eve ; with refusing to quit the licensed premises of Wm. Humphries ; with as- saulting Wm. Humphries, and damaging a door to the amount cf £l, at the Lower Angel lon.—They were each fined £1 and costs, and were ordered to pay for the damage done to the door.

Joseph Hewitt (Eccleston), were each fined 5s and costs for drunkenness. For a similar offence the following persons were fined the amount stated :—John Kelly (Windle), 73 63 and costa; Martin Dudley (Windle), 7s 6d and costa; Edward Woods (Parr) 7s 6cl and costs; Timothy Barnes (Eccleston), 103 and costs ; and John Brannan (Eccleston), 103 and costs. Patrick Graham, Edward Garrity, Patrick McGovern, John -Garrity, William Read, and Jamas Scally, young men, resid- ing in Ercleston, were summoned fsr obstructing the foot- path in Liverpool-street on the previous Wednesday night. P.C. Cottam proved the case. Smiley was fined 7s 6d and costs, Wm. Read and Edward Garrity 50 and costs each, and - the remainder 23 6d and costs each. ALLEGED ASSAULT. An elderly man named James Flynn was summoned for assaulting Margaret Gormley. The parties live in Bold-street, Greenbank, and it was alleged that on Sunday afternoon Flynn dealt the com- plainant a blow on the face and kicked her about the shin. —The maeistraten, considering there was a doubt in the ease, dismissed the summons. MoNney.—Before Alderman Mcßryde and Mr. A. Sinclair. DRUNKENNESS.—A fine of 53 and costs was imposed on each of the following persons for drunkenness :—William Glover, William Atherton, Mary Dolan, and James John- ston. UNLAWFULLY Wouirmiro.—Thomas McHugh, a resident of Pocket Nook, who has been several timea remanded on a charge of unlawfully wounding Thomas McGlynn by striking him on the head with a poker, was again brought np.—Mr. R. W. If. Thomas, who prosecuted, stated that the injured man was still unable to appear, and asked for a further remand for a week.—The Bench granted the ap- plication, and admitted the prisoner to bail as previously. BREACH OF THE PEACE.—Michael Killigarf was sum- moned for committing a breach of the peace by fighting in Duke-street, Windle, and was fined 5s and costs. PITCH AND Toss.—Michael Bow and John Cain were summoned for playing at pitch and toss in Victoria-street, Windle, on the 14th inst.—Bow did net appear, and he was fined 23 8J and costs; a peralty of is and costs being Im- posed on Cain. CHIMNEY ON FlRE.—Robert Crelley, High-street, Eccles- ton, was fined Is and costs for having the chimney of his dwelling house on fire on the 18th inst.—Eliza Shaw, of Newton-road, was fined a like amount for a similar offence committed ma the 16th inst. OLD OFFENDERS —Elizabeth Tither, who appeared for the 84th time, was committed to prison ior a month for be- ing drunk and disorderly in Exchnnge-street, Windle, on Saturday night.—Mary Thotnpson was charged with being drunk and disorderly on the previons day, at Eccleston, and ' it being her 22nd offence, she was committted to prison for a montlL—John Crossby was also committed to prison for a month for being drunk and disorderly at Eccleston, on the previous day. It was the prisoner's 77th appearance. TUESDAY—Before Mr. W. Pilkington and Alderman Mcßryde. Bsoom.—Patrick Cushney, of unsettled residence, was charged with begging on the previous day and was com- mitted-to prison for seven days. BRUACH or THE PEACTL—Thomas Anders, of Eccleston, was charged tinder a warrant wt.!' committing a breach of the peace on the 13th inst. He was bound over to keep the peace.

Tan STRIKE AT LEIGII.-03 Monday, at Leigh, four spinners and a plecer were summoned for leaving work at the Mather-lane Mlin without notice. They bad been in. duced to cease working by the men on strike. Damages were laid at 103, and the defendants were each fined in the sum and costs. • The Vice-President of tha Peace Association has for- warded to the Premier an appeal for permission to be given to Mr. Wilfrid Blunt to lay before the Government his pro- posal to undertake a peaceful mission to the Mandi' and to obtain not only the evacuation of Khartoum And General Gordon's return to Don', but all the Government have announced as their o`.lects in the Soudan. FLISSuAr. or LOUD CHOLMONDELEY.—The funeral of the Marquis of Cholmondeley took place on Tuesday afternoon, at Kemal-green, the body having been brought up In the morning from Messingham. Norfolk, to London, whence it Was conveyed in a hearse drawn by four horses with plumes and feathers to the cemetery. The chief mourners were the Earl of Rocksavage (the present marquis), the Hon. Edward Gledwyn Arnold (sou-in-law), and Mr. Vera Cholrnondeley. Lady Marcia Cholmondeley and Lady E. Arnold arrived by Special train' but drove to Hyde Park-street, where they joined Lady Henry Cholmondeley and other ladies of the family. The burial service was conducted by the Rev. Foster Rogers, rector of Barrow. Cheshire. No wreaths were sent by any members of the family, as it was known tt.e deceased did not like the custom, but a few friends sent some floral tributes. The proposal of the Committee of the Council of the Royal Agricultural Society to include mongrel and cross-bred horses in the classes for Shire-bred stallions in the prize schedules of the society, under the classifi- cation of "Shire and Agricultural," was rightly de- scribed as a most retrograde movement, which would make matters ten times worse than they were before. We are quite at a loss to comprehend how such a pro- posal could have emanated from the society's executive. —Mark Lane Expresi. SUCCESS OF ANOTHER ENSILAGE EXPEIUMENT.—A silo, constructed in accordance with instructions given by the Rev. H. D. Rawn.sley, in a lectule delivered at Kes- wick last winter, on the estate of Mrs. Joshua Stanger, • of Fieldside, near Keswick, has been opened, and the re- sults have • given the greatest satisfaction to all con- cerned. , The silo in size is 13 feet long, 10 feet broad, and 10 feet high, and was made in an old building, of which three walls were standing. A fourth was built, and the whole covered with a skin coating of cement, the total cost being £9 10s., and it is conjectured that the silo will last for nearly half a century. The grass used was of the coarsest kind, so coarse that when pre- vious crops have been made into hay, the cattle often disdained to partake of it, and the quantity it yielded was generally calculated at about six tons. By the pro- cess adopted there are now about twelve tons of fodder, all of which is in excellent condition. The cattle ate it almost ravenously, and afterwards licked up the seeds and essential oils left. When the grass was put in it was carefully trampled down, and covered with about three inches of hedge clippings. Over these planks were placed, and heavy stones Tere made to take the place of weights. The care taken in this respect has resulted in there not being an inch depth of fodder rendered use- less, and it is almost impossible to have a better sample of ensilage. It will be seen that the extra quantity of food, without considering the quality, will have more than compensated for the outlay. CLEVELAND llonsts.—When the railways superseded the stage-coaches the Cleveland Bay began to fall into desuetude; but now that our street traffic in large cities is being conducted largely by means of huge omnibuses fitted with very complete brake power, the Cleveland Bay is the horse we want once more. There is now a demand for this particular stamp of horse which will absorb them quite as fast as they can be bred. The Cleveland Bay Stud Book contains a very interesting histtry of the Cleveland Bay breed of horses, or Chap- man horses as they were originally called, from the pen of Mr. Dixon, with which every lover of horses would be pleased. Mr. Dixen remarks that writers on the origin of the breed seem to have taken little or no trouble to collect informatien respecting it, but have complacently set themselves the task of showing that the Cleveland ,Bay was the result of an elaborate system of crossing, and that, strange to say, the very obvious theory that the breed was originally what is termed a pure one has, with one or two exceptions, been lost sight of. Mr. Dixon tells us that the Cleveland Bay breed was in a flourishing condition from 1851 to 1867, as may be gathered from the fact that in these years there was an average of nearly twelve brood mares exhibited at the, Cleveland agricultural Society's Shows, there being nineteen in 1860. After this date the ,breed began to decline on account of Shire and Clydesdale horses cord- ing more into favour, and from one cause and another— including the suicidal policy of using cart stallions to Cleveland mares—many agricultural societies eliminated the breed from their prize schedules. The Cleveland Bay is now a lighter horse than heused to be, and it will be the aim of the society to encourage breeding for rather more bone. Mr. J. B. Lloyd, in an article in the first volume of the Journal of the Royal Agricultural Society, gives an account of a Cleveland stallion he had purchased for him in 1827 by a friend in Yorkshire for his use in Gloucestershire. Of this horse he says:— "When Old Cleveland was at his full size he measured 16 hands 1 inches high, 91 inches round the pastern, 10 inches round below the knee, 21 inches round the arm, 151 inches round the knee, and 6 feet 10 inches round the girth. When measured he was in good condi- tion, but not what you would call full of flesh, and his legs as clean as a racehorse." ENSILAGE IN NORTH LONSDALE.—TWO silos have been recently opened in Furness. and have proved satisfaok tory to tho owners. The first is owned by the Lindal Moor Mining Company, who have the farm at Lindal-in; Furness, where some 40 milch cattle are kept. The grass, to the oxtent of 57 tons, was put into silo in July and August, commencing to fill on July 25th, most of it being put in wet; 46 tons were thus put in, and the re- mainder in August, the subsequent sinkage being but trifling. The mass was rendered solid in the silo. As the company fiad a lot of waste iron about the works this was moulded up into weights of feat. each, with handles left on. Boards were placed on the top of the grass, then the iron weights were placed on the top of these to the extent of some 1501 b. to the square foot. The temperature was tested daily; it was found to be the highest, 80 degrees, in August, and lowest in Nevem- ber, 73 degrees. The highest temperature was found nearest the top of the silo. When opened on November 28th two boards were taken off, and the grass was gra- dually CUL down as wanted for feeding until the bottom was reached. The quantity of food for one day's use is cut on the previous day, and it is weighed as taken out, in order to test the relative weights when put in anduiwlyn Psyiveritd %dor ensilage_ rt tho fen: rom o e dings, is anetfer r,suauy aid of this the ensilage Is brought within easy reach of the shippons. It is cut with a knife, and is almost as solid as a stone wall. It is of a colour between grass and hay, and emits a pleasant smell, resemb- ling that given off by barley when in process of malt- ing. When laid out for a week and allowed to dry it resembles sweet hay, both in smell and colour, and this leads up to the inference that there is:no reason why ensilage should not become as marketable a commodity as hay. It might be cut out in cwt. trusses, or blocks, and thus easily sent by rail. At present some of the cows have 351bs. each of the ensilage per day, whilst others have nothing but ensilage. The weights are still retained on the part of the silo not in process of cutting, and in another case one of two silos was opened. These were constructed in a barn on the premises by running a brick wall across, with a petition wall in, the centre, the inside walls being cemented. They are 10ft. 6in. and 10ft. 10in, square respectively, and 17ft. high. The grass was mostly put in when wet, and each layeeof grass Was salted. The principal objection to a silo of this kind is that the grass has to be thrown over this 17ft. wall, entailing much heavy work. Boards were placed over, and on tnese were bags of cobble stones, to the extent of 801bs. per square foot, and for the getting up and re- moval of these a pulley had been fixed above the silos. Evidently the grass had not been got in here as solidly as at Linda!, for the sinkage was considerable. It had to be renewed several times, yet the final sinkage prior to the opening was 6ft. The top layer was composed of rough grass and weeds cut from the sides of the hedges. When opened a very strong and disagreeable smell was given forth. The top grass was dark coloured, wet, and I warm. The pungent odour evidently had its effect upon.' the cattle, for most of them refused to eat it. Lower down the ensilage was better in every way, smell and colour improved, and after being exposed for a few hours the Cattle ate it readily, and continue to do so.

TRY DAILT INCREASE OF VARIOUS BREEDS OF CATTLE. —The Mark Lane Express publishes a carefully prepared estimate of the daily gain of the different animals in each of the cattle classes at the recent Smithfield show, and there is no more instructive lesson to be learned than this, more especially by those who are fond of dis- cussing the question of the battle of the breeds. In the Devon classes the steer eic hibited by the Prince of Wales, 539 days old and weighing 1,1671 b., is at the top of the list, showing a yin of 21.71 b. per day, the reserve steer in this class coming next with an increase of 2•131 b. per day. There is another proof that the older the beast the less it pays in the shape of profit, for as the animals decline in daily gain of weight as they advance in age, the oldest steers and heifers in some cases descending as low as 1.021 b. and I.oBlb. All this is in favour of early production and the slaughter of young cattle. Her Majesty's cup steer, which was 1,081 days old, only showed a gain of 3:561b. daily. In the Hereford class Mr. Child's cup steer had done the best work. In 601 days he put on 2191 b. per diem. The shorthorns proved themselves infinitely the best lot in the show in this respect, although the cup winner of Mr. Gorringe was not at the top of the tree. He put on 2.211 b. daily for 707 days, whileher Majesty's cup heifer put on 2.021 b. per day for 954 days, a remarkable performance. In the young steer class only one failed to reach 21b. daily, Mr. Gorrmge's commended beast heading the list with 2•491 b., or practically 21b. a day for 584 days, several other beasts coming close. A beast of Mr. James Bruce's put on 2.061 b. per day for 1,023 days, which, taken all round, is the best performance in the short-

_ horn classes. The Sussex beasts also did remarkably well, the top daily weigilt being the Ist prize steer belonging to Mr. Kirkpatrick, which put on 2•281 b. per day for 722 days, all the *animals in the young steer class showing remarkable weights. The cup beast, however, came down to 1•331 b., which he had put on daily for 1,422 days. Unfortunately there were but few red polled; but even these proved, what some people de- cline to believe, that a dairy race of cattle such as this is not a beef making one. The first prize steer, exceed- ing three years, put on 1•561 b. daily for 940 days, and the cup animal 1-261 b. for 1,439 days, a result which is by no means to be despised. Colonel Platt's first prize Welsh- man did little better than this—viz., 1-531 b. per day for 1,335 days. Strange to say, the Scotch polls do not come up to the other leading breeds. The cup winner increased 11311 b. a day for 969 days, and Mr. Egginton's commended beast 2.331 b. for 797 days, by far the best performance of the lot The cross-bred steers showed a general im- provement throughout, the highest weights being in the young class, where 2•371 b. per day was, reached, and ap- proached in several instances. The cross-bred animals in the young steer class stand at the top of the tree, with an average increase of 2.221 b. per diem ;the short- horns coming next with 221 b; the Herefords, 2151 b.; the Sussex, 2181 b.; and the Doyens, 118ffb. The cross-breds, too, equally stand at the head in the other two classes for older steers; but in these the Herefords take second place, although there is very little difference between this race, the shorthorns, and the Susses In each case the Devons are at the bottom, and the Sdotch polled last but one. BIRCH, de- signer of "Old London" at the Health Exhibition, gave a short address. Some of them, he said, would perhaps ask what "Old London" had to do with the Health Exhibi- tion. There really were reasons for it, and one reason was to show how their forefathers were housed and what sort of dw el lings they lived in, and what conditions of life and what sort of surroundings they had. 'that was the reason why old London street was first mooted. He was spoken to about it in the end of February, and the exhibition WalEl to - be opened in May, an that there was not very much time. rHe was commissioned by tha corporation of the city of 'London, and not by the authorities of the Health Exhibi- tion, and he was asked to give, if possible, a representation of Old Cheapside, and there were only two representations of Old Cheapside in existence. He could not say that he could turn out his original intention as he wanted to show the sanitary arrangements—or want of sanit try arrange- ments, and also the manner in which the streets were found In the time of their forefathers. On that point he had con- siderable discussion with the committee, his own idea being to have eoble pavement, but he could not get the commit- tee to agree to that. The chairman of the committee, the Duke of Chandos and Buckingham, wrote to remind him that the public had corns—(laughter)—and he had to give the idea up. He bad been a great many times to War- rington; but always at this time of the year. He ha 4 never seen Warrington in summer time, and of course Warrington in his mind had always been to a certain extent associated with ashes and cinders." But he knew several people who had come from Warrington, and they had shown to a certain extent what Warrington was capable of in regard to art. Be waanot only alludingap those friends of his, Mr. Elides and Mr. Harry Woods, but also to others who had come from that school. As the chairman had very 'wisely said. that a school of art should not necesearily turn out artists. There were other things to be thought of with regard to a school of art, other prospects to look forward to, and there was one thing especially connected with Warrington which always struelc him might be done. If they went to the museums of Europe, and to the museum of South Kensing- ton, they would there see the most wonderful collections of glass generally from Venice, and it struck him there was an opening in that direction which wou'd enable the Warring- ton School of Art to do a great deal of good. (Ap- plause.) The Cnatnmax said he was glad to inform Mr. Birch that the school of art had not lost eight of the glass manu- facture. He believed Mr. Beamont could inform theni that the Museum bad applied to the department to lend them samples of glass, which would be mada available for the pupils who came from glass works (Hear, hear.)
Mr. BEAMONT then -moved, and 'Alder, man CIIANDLEY seconded, a vote of thanks 0 the Chairman, and it was car- ried by acclamation. The CHAIRMAN having briefly re- sponded, the proceedings terminated.

div.head: MANAGEMENT OF POULTRY.
div.p: THE MANAGEMENT OF POULTRY.
FABLE POULTRY AND PREgERVED-EGB AT BIRMINGHAM.

The cross-bred classes were well filled, and contained many remarkable specimens. These were shown in. couples, instead of in pairs, but this we hardly think an. improvement; in fact, as we explained last week, we re- gard the pair system a§ by far the preferable plan, for. ' then the sexes can be compared side by side. however,. in the cross-bred classes eouples were preferred, and. thus there was a class for a couple of cockerels and. another for a couple of pullets. In the cockerel class there were 17 pairs shown, of which eight were killed. Some very large birds were I exhibited, two couples of which weighed upwards of 171bs. The winners were all Brahma-Dorkings, except one, and that was a. Dorking-Brahma, so that these tem breeds had it all their own way. This shows the extreme folly of throwing all breeds, iuggledy-piggleby, into one class„ as there can be no doubt the Brahma-Dorkings are not the best class for table purpoies. There may be size, and on that account the cross be popular, but for quality of flesh and distribution of meat a cross in which the Game and Dorking are employed is to be pre- ferred. The winning pair weighed 171b5., and was pro- duced from a dark Brahma cock and a silver-gray Dorking hen. These were very large indeed, but we have seen plumper ones. The second only weighed 151bs. 10oz., and had a decidedly coarse appearance. These were the same cfassas the first prize couple. The third were from a darkßrahma cock and a coloured Dorking hen weighing 151bs. 40z. These were better in colour hen, and flesh, but showed heavy thighs, inherited from the father. The fourth were the heaviest of all, turning the scale at 171bs. 2oz. They were from a coloured Dorking cock and a dark Brahma hen, and• were first-rate in shape very plump, but spoilea by lumps of yellow fat. But share, this they must have been first, and the cross shows that in using these breeds the Dorking should be the male parent. Another nice -couple were exhibited, bred from a,white-legged game cock and a"-silver-gray Dorking hen. These only weighed 101bs., but were very good indeed in quality. Another pen, bredj from aLa Fleche cock and black-red Game hen, were spoiled by dark-coloured flesh. • =

•In the class for pullets there were 19 pens. The win-1 ners here were dark Brahmas—silver-gray :Dorkings, weighing 14 lbs. These were very plump and of capi- tal colour. Second were of the same cross, ;but] weigh- ing 220 z. less, and, although well made and plump, were coarse. Third were a cross—and, we think, a good one —from a Latleche cock and a black-red Game hen. These weighed 11 lbs. 120 z., and were plump:with good- coloured flesh, but the skin was . coarse and wrinkled. Fourth came from a black-red Game cock—Malay hen cross. These were plump and of good, shape, weighing • 91bs. toz. • The flesh was yellow also, but this is always to be expected from Malays. Other good couples were exhibited, chiefly Dorking-Brahmas, and the only other one we need to mention is a cross between a Plymouth , Rock cock and a silver-gray Dorking hen. :These were I beautiful in shape and very plump, weighing nibs. 20z., , but the pullet was spoiled by a crooked breast. These cross-bred classes, it must be admitted, have not taught us as much as we had hoped. "

div.head: PRESEAVED EGGS.
div.p: PRESEAVED EGGS.

For the Preserved Egg competition' thirty-four lots had been sent in. These were in pbssession of the com- mittee from August 15th last, sufficiently long to test any system, especially as a portiorl• of it_was during the hot weeks of August and September.SVery many methods had been adopted; sense of which were entirely new. And it is only fair to state that eggs pteserved on the system which secured the prize last spar did not compete. First was given to 'eggs preserM in lime- water and cream of tartar. These.were very good in- deed, and quite fit for table purposes. This system is a very simple one. Second went to eggs rubbed with butter and packed in salt. These were also good. Eggs kept like one of the lots which won second at the Dairy Show in October, and at Birmingham last year, were not awarded even a highly-commended card. From this it will be seen that the old method of lime-water succeeds best of all, and though the awards at the Dairy Show did not support this, yet the experiments made by Mr. Tegetmeier did. SFASONABLE HINTS. "

Preparations should at once be made for the next hatching season, by getting the hatching boxes ready, as these will soon be required. We prefer these boxes made singly, as they can be more easily cleaned out and re- moved. The size of each box should be 12in. square, and 15in. high, consisting. of back, sides, and top, but no bottom. The front must be divided into two portions, the bottom part across the front, and three inches deep, to be a fixture; and the upper part to form a door, hinged, and to open outwards.. The bottom can be covered with wire netting, as a preventive against rats. When a few holes are put in the top for ventilation, the box is complete. Sprat's Patent make and sell these hatching boxes at a reasonable price, about as cheap as they can be made at home.

div.head: COTTAGE GARDENING
div.p: COTTAGE GARDENING

PRUNING Faurr Mgrs.—This will engage the atten- tion of all gardeners for the next three months whenever the weather is favourable. The most suitable weather is that which admits of the ground being dry under foot, either from the drying effects of the wind or the action of the frost, as either will render it More agreeable than its being in a wet, sodden condition, though the air may I net be quite so agreeable. Intelligent gardeners allow I themselves to b; guided in their operations by the weather, and are consequently rewarded more bounti- fully then those who conduct their work regardless of the elements. Young apple and pear trees will not re- quire much pruning if they have been attended to during the summer, unless they are trained against a wall, as we sometimes see them nailed to that of the dwelling. Older trees are in many instances benefited , by it if judiciously managed. But those that may have ' been replanted or nndergone root disturbance are best left alone till the following year. When large trees are taken in hand, there are two or three rules by which the operator should be guided. He will direct his attention first to all those branches that grow inwards, and secondly to those that intefsect each other. Should the tree appear crowded, some of the most ill-shaped of the remainder may be moved. All pieces too thick for the. knife should be taken off with the saw, and in either case the cuts must be made obliquely, as flat ones encourage , the wet to rest on them, and so cause canker. Every ' , cut must be made close to the parent branch, as nothing I looks more unsightly than pieces left several inches long, which invariably die back their full length. In each case, where the saw lias been ysed, it is of importance that the knife should be used to dress the surface of the cut, and so give it a neat appearance, leaving each one , when completed slightly convexed. Applying the knife is not solely for the sake•of appearance, but to correct an important defect left by the saw. It will be observed I that the surface of the cut, after the saw, will be un- usually rough, which in that condition will act some- thing like a sponge—always sucking water placed in contact with it—so that in time the wet is conducted into the branches. The knife smooths the surface' and the cells soon close, so that wet cannot enter. For large wOunds we like to apply a dab of lead colour paint. The advantages claimed for this winter pruning are that more light sun is admitted amongst the branches remaining, and consequently a better ripening of the wood and dis- position to form more and stronger flower buds, as well as much finer fruit. •It is evident that whatever has been moved from a tree, the roots have that much less to supply with food, which allows so much more for the remainder, amongst Which it is certain to be distributed. Trees against thevrall are usually pruned in the summer or early autumn by shortening the shoots to about 61n., which induces the formation of flower buds at their base, and• the winter pruning is confined to moving the wood above the flower bud. Pyramidal and bush trees are treated in a 'similar manner, but the young growth at the end of every main shoot is left longer at thd summer cutting, and is seldom shortened in winter. THE Faciwr GARDEN.—Any alterations contemplated in this department should be taken in hand during (Wen weather. These•will 'consist of improving the form of the beds, the formation of some new ones where none ' are already existing; laying fresh edging to the borders or beds, as well as replacing turf where it has by some means been damaged beyond recovery. Should any of these alterations involve the necessity of taking up some or all of the plants in the beds they are more likely to be preserved if laid in-rows °lithe surface of the ground with soil from the surrounding ground packed firmly round them. To make holes to lay them in at this time of the year would be to invite the water to accumulate round the roots and destroy them. It will be, therefore, obvious that we avoid that by packing them on the sur- face. Should severe weather ensue they can be pro- tected by some kind of covering, though as a rule they are considered quite safe. When they have been packed in short litter moderately dry, or bracken in 04 similar condition, as well as cocoa nut fibre and leaves, they have been found more vigorous than their confreres that have been left undisturbed. THE WATEOW.—The boxes that usually stand outside the window, if not already planted with bulbs, as many are in the habit of doing, may have a dwarf shrub or two placed in them. Some also, rather than see them naked, insert a few pieces of evergreens at odd times. It is, however, best to have two sets of boxes, and plant one lot with bulbs and a wallflower or two, and stand them in a suitable place till the plants that have been there all summer are destroyed by frost and require moving, when they may be replaced by the winter ones. The unused set can be repaired and painted, so as to be ready to go back again when the time comes.

div.p: PRESCOT.

TEIIPBRAME MENTING.—The fortnightly meeting of the Church of England Temperance Society was held on Mon- day in the Houghton-street schoolroom. A service of song entitled" Christie's Old Organ," was given by the females attending the 44 unday schools assisted by a few members of the choir, the solo parts being well sung by Miss Waine, Miss Spencr, Miss Welsby, Mr. J. Heaps, and Mr. J. Welsby. Mr. E. Baylis presided at the piano. DAMAGE BY &mum —Dining the storm which raged on Friday night and early on Saturday morning the sails of tbe mill situated in Warrington-road were blown down. They fell on the roof of a house occupied by Mr. J. Drownbill, 'irronfounder, and penetrating the roof broke several articles of furniture. This is the second time that an accident of this kind has occurred this year, and will be a great lose to Mr. J. Rigby, who rents the mid, owing to the stoppage of work. The damage to the mill is estimated at £250. ENTERTAINAIANT AT WdlaraN.—Mr. William Bennett gave his literary and mueical entertainment in the Whietota School-room on Tuursday week before a large and fashion. able audience. Mr. Bennett's programme consisted of hum- orous and dramatic recitals from English and American authors, interspersed with songs, and was the same perfor- mance which he gave at Prescot. During the entire per- formance Mr. Bennett kept his hearers interested and highly amused. Amongst the audience were the Rev. J. Moore, vicar of Whisten, and Captain Willis, who both expressed themselves highly delighted with the enjoyable entertain- ment Mr. Bennett had given them and their friends.

div.head: BOARD. OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: BOARD. OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of this Board was held at Whis- ton Workhouse, on Wednesday, under the preshiency of Mr. J. T. Hall. The other members present were the Rev. J. Barnacle, Messrs. R. Leigh, W. B. Longton, T. Dobell, T. Sadler, W. Gerrard, W. Newsome, W. Birchall, W. Tyrer, J. Leatherbarrow, H. Hulme, E. Sydere J. Lowe, J. Jackson, W. N. Meadows, J. Kenwright, J. Griffith, J. Agnew, J. :fisher, W. Swift, and H. S. Hartley (clerk).—The Work- house Master's report gave the number of inmates this week in the house at 470, as compared with 449 last week, and 464 in the corresponding petiad of last year. The vagrants relieved numbered 44, as against 53 in the corres- ponding period of last year. The Clerk was instructed to acknowledge wltia thanks the receipt of various publications for the use of the sick and of Christmas preeents. sent to the House by gentlemen and ladies in ,the neighbourhood.— The Clerk reported the election of Mr. Wea, Ely. Kershaw, timber merchant, as Guardian for the township of Ditton. The sum of three guineas was voted to the clerk for ser- vices rendered in connection with the election.—The Clerk reported the receipt of a letter from the Local Government Board, enclosing a communication eent to that body by Mr. Brewis, town clerk of St.. Helens, on which tba observations of the Guardians were requested. The letter en- closed" stated that at a meeting of the Health Committee of the Borough of St. Helens in the course of the consideration of matters relating to the Infectious Diseases Hospital, it transpired that from time to time since the establishment of the hospital pauper cases had been received iato the institution, and the question arose whether in such cases It was not rather the duty of the Guardians than that of the Council to provide accom- modation, and that if the Corporation did receive such cases the cost should be borne by the Union Authorities.—The Chairman said that he supposed that the casea were sent in by their own medical officer.—The Clerk said that he was not aware that any cases bad as yet been sent to the St. Helens hospital. It was a matter of regret that the Si. Helens Cor- poration did not in the first instance think it right to ap- proach the Guardians on the subject. The Guardians ,had never been asked by the Corporation whether they were will- ing to pay for any person's maietenance in the hospital. It was no duty of the Guardians to preserve the public health, but if it woe shown to the satisfaction of the Guardians that a person in the hospital was a pauper, it would be a matter of arrangement between them and the Corporation as to the payment for maintenance.—lt was decided to leave the ques- tion of replying to the communication received to the Clerk. Messrs. Cammack and Company wrote offering to send to ths House a quantity of mineral waters for the use of the inmates on Christmas Day. The offer was accepted. —Mr. Fairclough was appointed assistant relie7ing officer for Rainfoni. There were 29 applications for the office, and five candidates attended before the Board.—This was all the buziaeas.

WARRINGTON Sea-0U OF ART.
- :DISTRIBUTION. OF PRIZES.

ThA animal distribution of prices to students of the above school took place in the Lecture.room•at the Museum on Monday evening. The chair was occupied by Mr. John Rylands, chairman of t,be committee, and there were also present Alderman Chandley, Rev. S. Witkinson, Messrs. O. Birch (London), E. Brewtnall, C. Broadbent, W. 8. arp, J. Ellison, W. Beamont, W. Owen, (hon. secretary and treasurer), and others, there being a large attendance. Be- fore the distribution took place some business was transacted. The t easurer (Mr. John Ellison) read the statem nt of ac- tivities, from which it seemed that the balance in band from iset year was £4B Is 2d; subscriptions, £l7 18s ; fees, 1951 9s ; the removal to the new school had cost £49 218 a 101 ; and the total expenditure (including the balance of £l5 1289 d) had been £417 13s 3d. The balance in hand on the prize fund was £lB Os 11d, and that on the reserve ; fund £33 Os Id.

The SECRETARY (Mr. Owen) also read the following re- part:—" The 30th annual report of the Warrington School of Art for the session ending 30th June, 1884." This session has been somewhat momentous inasmuch as the school has vacated the old rooms so long held in the Museum at a nominal rent from the Corporation, and has entered into possession of the new buildings in Museuna-street. The removal coming as it did in the middle of the session might have interfered somewhat with the students works and the May examinations, but we are able to lay before you a very satisfactory atatemeut of the results of the session. The number of students at once increased in the new building. The public day class increased from 13 to 29; the artizm class from 39 to 80; and the special class from 65 to 68; showing the largest increure in the artizan class which the school is specially intended to bandit. The total increase is from 117 to 177 (60 students.) The school smt to the annual examination at South Kensington 1,909 works ex- ecuted by 153 students, and nine 3al grade pr;zes were awarded by the examiners. At the second grade examina- tions held in May last in Warrington 49 papers were suc- cessfully worked, and amongst them 14 were marked excel- lent which entitled the students to a prize. Three students submitted seven works for the art teachers' examination, and of these five were acceptA. At the personal examina- tions held in May the same students proved successful in four.aubjects."

The &UMW; moved that this reDorthe passed. Mr. C. BROADBENT, in seconding this proposal, said thai all who had heard the report read must have been satisfied with it. It showed the very satisfactory condition of that new institution—or rather new in its present abode. He was rather quoting the knowledge of others who knew mote of the subject than he •did, than his own, when he said that that school of art, in the new building, and under thenew state of things, was answering all the best expectations of its friends, and that it promised to be one of the most useful and admirable institutions in WarrinAten, and one of which they should all be proud. (Applause.) The motion was then carried.

Mr.p.aap moved that the following gentlemen be elected to form the Committee of the School of Art for the ensuing year and until the neat annual meeting :—Pres:dent, the Right Hom Lord Winm Lneigh ; vice-presidents, Messrs John Crosfield, John Dun, James Matson, and S. Rigby ; committee. Messrs E. Brewtnall, C. Broadbcnt,S. Chandley, C. Chorky, W. Fell, H. N. Houghton' E. Milner, W. Sharp, J. Ellison, and R. Garnett, with Mr. Owen, as hon. sec. and treasurer.

lAlderman CIIANDLEY, in seconding the motion, said that i society was deeply obligated to Mr. Owen, not only for his pelt services as secretary, but also because he had very kindly nna.rtnk•n the re9p011811)1e orheo of trceourcr. Very great thanks were due to Mr. Owen for his disinterested kindness, and he (Alderman Ctiandley) hoped that at some future meeting he would have the opportunity of moving a very hearty vote of thanks to Mr. Owen. The Cnarnateu said it was perhaps an oversight that they did not couple a vote of thanks with the above reaolution, bat the motion having been passed. . Mr. BREWTHALL moved a vote of thanks to the secretary and to the retiring treasurer (Mr. Ellison). Mr. SHARP seconded this proposal, and the Ciesnietax, In supporting it, bore testimony to the services of Mr. Owen. The treasurer's duties, he said, were very valuable, brat be must say they were nothing like so important as the work the secretary had to do.—The vote of thanks was then caraled by acclamation. The CHAIRMAN then said he was extremely sorry to have to announce that Lord Winmarleigh would not be present that night He had got a letter from him on Saturday tv sty it would be impossible for him to come. He was sure they would regret as he did Lord Winmarleigh's absence, I and some of them would not know as he knew that Lord Winmarleigh had been one of the best friends of that insti- tution ever since it commenced. He had been a.constant subscilber, he had been their president for many years, and ' had taken an interest that never seemed to fail. Having , mentioned that he had received letters of apology for non- attendance from other gentlemen, the Chairman went on to say that it devolved upon him to take as far as he could Lord Winmarieigh's- place. He did not know that he had any other recommendation than the fact thit he also had taken a very great interest in the School of Art, and had done all he could for its success. They could not overlook the fact that while the prizes they were going to distribute that night really were-for work done under the superintend- ence of Mr. Thompson, a change heel taken place. While he did not want to take up much of their time in reference to that cha'nge, they might naturally suppose that the com- mittee had had a very anxious time of It, and naturally felt that such a change was a matter of very great importance. Mr. Thompson had been there for many years. They all respected him and some of them were very much surprised that he should have to leave. However, they did what they thought beat under the circumstances; they got the best opinion and advice they could and eventually they ap- pointed a new master and an assistant master. They looked with great interest to the result, and he was happy to say the result had been perhaps More favourable than they an- ticipated. The school had increased in numbers, and he hoped it would go on even to increased usefulness. How- ever. time would alone show how far that hope would be fulfilled. There were only one or two remarks he should make in reference to art, and one was thit he would remind them that a School of Art was not primarily intended to make artists. They had taken great credit from time to Vine to themselves on account of the fact that from the War- rington school had proceeded men like Fildes, Harry Woods, Warrington Woods, Edward Brewtnall, and others, who were more or less eminent artists, and naturally, too, they felt pride in it. But he would have them re- member that no school In the world would make eminent artists unless nature had properly fitted them to be- gin with. But art like everything else has its grammar and they professed to teach that grammar. Their teaching was principally of a technical kind and while they did all they could to improve the taste and educate the eye, and also gave that technical education, he believed it was out of their power to make artists even if they wished it. But that was no reason at all why if any of them really aspired to be ar- tists they should not do all they could to excel in art. If they did not excel as much as they wished to do he thought the attempt would be its own reward, for it would add very much to their happiness. He had been reading same remarks which Mr. Millais had recently made, and he spoke some- thine to the effect that he qeite believed that the eminent ar- tist was really like the poet—born not made ; and he had also men a curious remark by Mr. Phil Morris who was dis- tributing oriees at some school. He said the way to excel in art was very plain, meaning no doubt that it was really hard work ; but he went on to say that if they were not diverted by Slade professors and cuckooing audiences they would probably learn to admire and appreciate works which were directly inspired by nature. He (the chairman) thought that was very good, and he thought he knew what was meant. There were a number of men who wrote about art and praised up pictures which did net seem to have been inspired by nature at all, but by something else. He had seen pictures in witch he could see very little traces of nature, and when he found people writing up these pictures and speaking of them as perhaps being the best pictures of the day, he thought that they could not -do wrong by tak- ing all their inspiration from nature. (Hear, hear.) He had pleasure in inf irming them that they had amongst them that night Mr. Birch, the architect of Old London, which some of them had seen at the Ilealtheries. He be- lieved there was nothing more popular than Old London, which was most picturesque and most interesting. After they had distributed the prizes he thought he should ask Mr. Birch if he would kindly give them a little information about old London. (Applause.) He then proceeded to de- liver the following prizes to the successful students for the year 18834, vie : Passed in one subject and gained a certifi- cate :—A. J Allen, freehand ; Eliza Allen, perspective; C. Broadbent, freehand; M. Connor, model; Ada Cuppage,

div.head: EARLESTOWN.
div.p: EARLESTOWN.

Cantsl.3lAs Frommrits A Eanrarwrowtr Arm NEwToN. —The workmen employed by the .London and North- Western Railway Company at the Viaduct Waggon Works, Earlestown, have this year been allowed three days' holiday for Christmas. The works stopped on Wednesday night until next Monday; and such has been the case at the Vul- can iron foundry, and other smaller works in the neighbour- hood. At the printing works of Messrs. George McCorquo- dale and Co., Newton, the employs have only been stopped for one day—Christmas Day—owing to the great press of orders the firm have to complete within a very short time. It is expected that in each case the holidays will be the same next week.

CHRISTMAS FOOTRALL/NCI AT EARLESTOWN. —On Christmas Day, considerable interest was manifested in two football matches which were played on the ground of the Earlestown club at Wargrave Moss. In the forenoon, the Committee of the Club played a specially selected team of members who are not recognieed players. There was a large attendance of spectators, who were as highly amused at the antics of the players as they were interested in the various evolutions of the ball. The result of the match, a fairly even one, was a victory for the Committee by goals to one. In the afternoon, the first teams ofrthe Earlestown and Haydock St. James's Clubs met in a friendly contest. Some 500 spectators were present, and witnessed an exciting game, which resulted in a draw of one goal each. THE TIUFERANCE TONTINE SOCIETY. The members of the Earlestown Temperance Tontine Society held their first annual tea party at the Welcome Coffee Palace, Market-place, on Tuesday evening. Before partak- ing of tea the members met for the purpose of dividing the receipts for the past half-year, which amounted to over Lao. Thirty persons sat down to an excellent tea, which was well served by Mr. and Mrs. Jackson, manager and manageress of the coffee palace. At the subsequent proceed- ings the chair was occupied by Mr. John Crompton (presi- dent of the society). During the evening songs were given by Messrs. Thomas Gorse, Gearge Sumner, A. Allison, Hy. Warburton, Walter Duncan, and Mrs. Allison ; recitaticns by Messrs. F. Bagnall and George Warburton; and a read- • ing by Mr. George Clarke. It was decided to re-start the society early in January. Dream AT THE BIIIIAILIPAST TABLE. About half- past sight on Monday morning William Huhnee, 61 years of age, formerly employed as a fitter at the Viaduct waggon works, suddenly expired under circumstances of a peculiarly distressing character. He came downstairs from bed about eiv,ht o'clock in the morning, when he appeared in his usual health. He sat on a chair before the fire until breakfast , was ready, and when he attempted to rise he fell with his head against the fender. Two sons were present and they I , raised him up with the intention of taking him to bed. His wife in the meantime went for a doctor, but the poor man expired almmt immediately. It appears that for about twelve months previous to May last, he suffered from heart disease and was attended by Dr. Patterson. Shortly after his death Dr. Patterson examined the body, and gave a cer- tificate that the cause of death was heart disease. The death was notified to the coroner, Nvho has since intimated ; that he considers an inquest unnecessary. DISTRIBUTION OF CHARITIES AT NEWTON.—The an- nual distribution of what is known as the Poor Stock Clothing Charity in connection with the Dean Trust Charity took place in St. Peter's Schools, Newton, on Monday after- noon. The charity partakes of the distribution of clothing to old and iofirm persons, who have been born and are resi- dent in Newton, and who are not in receipt of pafochial relief. Applicants for the charity sent in their applications during the month of November, and these applications were subleonently considered by the trustees'of the charity fund. According to the condition and position of the applicants bundles of clothing were awarded to each, and the presenta- tion of these bundles took place on Monday afternoon, as previously stated. Nearly 40 persons received gifts, the parcels being handed to the recipients by the Rev. H. Monk, vicar of the parish. The parties thus receiving what might be termed a welcome Christmas present were principally widows and aged persons in poor circumstances.

THE S&NICEY CANAL: IMPORTANT AcrtoN.—We are in- formed on reliable authority that the London and North- Western ailway Company are taking important steps in regard to their Can.o, knOVn as the. Sankey Canal, which connects St. Helens, Earlestown, tic, with the river Mersey. It is Stated that they have issued circulars to several local authorities calling upon them to divert, during the next six months, all sewage and sewerage which runs into the canal at the present time. This matter will prove a serious one for the Newton Commissioners—and will require their im- mediate and careful consideration. Hitherto the sewage from the populous west-end of Earlestown, near the Viaduct Waggon Works, has been discharged into the canal, and as it will, accorning to the notice of the railway company, have to be tamed away elsewhere, after the next six months, a new echeme will have to ha considered by the Commis- sioners. It is stated that a considerable expenditure will have to be incurred to comply with the directions of the corn-

pany. Tna EARLESTOWN WANDERERS V. LIVERPOOL STAN- LET CUP TIE —The Earlestown Wanderers on Saturday defected the famous Stanley team by three goals to two in the Liverpool Cup competition. The Stanley team, how- ever, afterwards protested against the victory (which every- one present at the match thought was genuine and well deserved). The grounds of the protest were against the Earlestown second goal, which the referee allowed to be off- side, but urged that he was not appealed to by the Stanley umpire, though the latter avers that he did protest. It was also stated in the protest that the ground was one sea of mud, which made it impossible to kick with acceracy, and that the Wanderers' backs on two occasions fisted the leather to keep It from scoring, and once o'er an Eerlestewn forward hated it through the Stanley goal. The protest was considers lat a meeting of the com- mittee of the Association on Mondav, and it was decided' that the match should be re-played. This decision created a , bitter feeling in Earlestown agrinet Eke Stanley players and , the Liverpool Association. CHRISTMAS AT EARLESTDWIP AND NEWrON.— Christ- I rem passed without any observance of a special character. I Beyond the stoppage of all the works in the neighbourhood ; an the closing of the various places of business on that day there was nothing to denote that the proverbial season of joy and festivity was at hand. The shopkeepers, how- ever,. thoroughly over-hauled their stocks-in-trade, and ex- erted* themselves to giving their premises as bright an ppearntance as could conveniently be done. Amongst the tradesmen who so succeeded were Mr. Samuel Duncalf, grocer and provision dealer, Earle-street; Mr. Aohn Howe, grocer, &c, Market-street ; and Mr. Thomas Molyneux, " The Stores," Market-street. The butchers shops were well stocked with Christmas beef, mutton, ie., and among those who, made striking displays were Messrs. W. W. Owen, JI H. Pollard, C. Owen, and Nevitt. The poulterers ad fruitners were represented by Messrs. J. Riley and Dunn; and in addition to the shop- keepers mentioned Mews. Evans. and McClure, T. Clark, Haynes, and E.T. Evans might be named. In the forenoon of Christmas Day services were held at several of the cherches and chapels in the district, and were fairly well attended. The chief attractions of the day appeared to be the football matches played at NVargrave Moss. in the evening the streets of the town had a remarkably quiet and deserted ap- pearance. _

Sr. PISTERift Carmen, NEwrOsrt— This church was very attractively decorated for Christmas, and at the ser- vices held therein on that day the decorations gave the sacred edificia very pleasing appearance. Numerous sprigs of holly, with bunches of bright red berries, were suspended in prominent positions, while the chancel, pulpit, font, dm., received especial attention from the decorators. The ar- rangements were efficiently carried out by Mrs. Gillespie, Mrs Jones, and Miss Pearson, and thanks are due to these ladies for the gratifying result of their labours. Mrs Gil- lespie bedecked the font with a framework of evergreen leaves with bunches of berries at. the abutting points end angles. In the bands of the Misses Pearson the pulpit was almost hidden from view by the holly leaves and berries, which were artistically arranged round the top and down the panels. In each of the panels was a device of frosted wool on a red ground, and certainly the appearance of the pulpit was an evidence that great pains had been bestowed upon its decoration. Mrs Jones had charge of the chancel decoration, and she accomplished her task in a commendable manner. Beneath the window at the back of the chancel was a frame of wood, which was covered with frosted wool, bearing various emblems formed of everlasting fiewers. Below this, and just above the communion table, was the text in red letters, "The light of the world." In the chancel were also several sprigs of ever- greens, dm. PRIMITIVE METHODIST Ti PA.RTE.—The Primitive Methodists of Earlestown held their annual tea party on Christmas Day in the new schoolroom, Lord-street. The room had been attractively decorated with sprigs of holly and evergreens by Messrs. Pendrey, James Worsley, ton, and others, the decorations being interspersed with seasonable mottoeti. Each of the windows was bordered with evergreens) and from one of the gas standards was Sla. pended a large misletoo bough. About 100 persons partook of the excellent tea provided, and which was served by Miss Dickens, Mies Pendrey, Mrs. Kemp, Mrs Wm. Austin, Miss Clark, Miss Ellen Worsle7, Miss Thompson, Miss Susan Thompson, Mrs. J. Jones, Miss Sephtrn, Mrs. Speos- ton, and Mrs. Thomas Worsley. At the subsequent pro- ceedings the chair was occupied by the Rev. A'. N. Shim- min, resident minister, who was supported by Mr. lames Woods, school superintendent. In opening the meeting the chairman gave a short review of the past year. He alluded to the epidemic a fever in the town, and observed that many homes had been visited,. causing an amount of sorrow; Lut in the midst of cli there bad been streaks of light and loY• He spoke of their efforts to obtain better school accommodation and stated that with the support of the general public they had been enabled to accomplish the task of erecting those new schools. He sincerely thanked the public for the gen- erous support they had accorded them. Am excellent pro- gramme was subsetmently gone through. The choir of the chapel, under the leadership of Mr. W. Banton, rendered several selections of music, Mr. W. Austin presiding at tha harmonium. Dialogues, recitations, songs, dm., were givz.o by J. W. Austin, A. Morris, J. H. Woods, J. Potter, J. T. Banton, J. Edmonds, F. Dickens, Elizabeth Woreley, Massey, Ada Dinkins,. Lillie Worsley, Miss Dinkins. E' J. Stevens, Nellie Thompson, Rhoda Massey, Phoeba HaYege J. Potter, S. Thompson, A. Massey, A. Worsl-eA, J. Dinkins, Miss Woods, MiSS Massey, M. E. Whittaker, A. Clarke, M. Peers. In cent-1128km, a vote of thanks to the ladies who presided at the tables, and to all who had taken part in the getting up of the meeting was proposed by the Rev. R, N. Shimmies, aeconded by Mr, J. Woods supers intendent of the same', was carried hy scalsrastlon,

The purchase of diamonds by the peck is sometime* facetipuely alluded to; but it is a fact that gold is found by the quartz. "My daughter," said a pompous old gentleman," 700 must never listen to flatterers." "But papa," rejoined this young lady, "that is altogether impossible ; how can Ptall that they are flatterers unless I listen." _

Youthful question to a pa-rent at the British Musenm.: all the mammas, when they die, turn to mammies, do all the papas turn to puppies." The following conversation took place recently at a hotel: 1" Waiter!" "Yes, sir." "What's this 2" " It's bean soup • sir." "No matter what it has been, the question is—what is it now ?" IT'S NICE TO Be A BABY.—" I wish I were a baby," , murmured a bashful bachelor who was making his first call on a sweet young lady. "How ridiculous !" she exclaimed. • "Why do you wish so ?" "Because a woman can never- look at a baby without kissing it." Just as a country lover dropped on his knees and began popping the question, a poodle who thought the proceedings rather strange made a rush at him. With a remarkable nerve for a woman, the girl reached over, grabbed the dog by the neck, at the same time calmly exclaiming, "Go on, Georga- dear ; I'm listening to what you are saying." A Philadelphia convict has been granted a new trial be- cause—in the language of the judge—"his reason hal been torn up by the roots and judgment jostled from her I throne."

The politest man in town has been discovered. He WAS hurrying along Fleet-street the other night when another man, also in violent haste, rushed out of a side alley, and they collided with great force. The second man looked fierc.e. while the polite man, taking off his hat, said. "My dear sir. I don't know which of us is to blame for this violent en- counter; but lam in too great a burry to investigate. If I ran into you, I beg your pardon:. if you ran into me, don't mention it ;"" and he tore away at redoubled speed. THE EIAIIIIRST PART OF TRE WORK.— Is that brake hard to handle ?" a4ed a young man on the front platform of a Broadway car"bf the driver. "No," responded that person. "Is that whistle hard to blow ?" again interro- gated the youth. "No," gruffly responded the driver. "What is the hardest thing to do on a street car ?" "An- swering fc.ols' questions," relied the dr:ver. Going out poaching, a boy shot a bird, and another ran to secure ths trophy. Coming near where it ha.} fallen, he found a white owl so sprawling in the grass as to present to his view only a head with staring eyes and a pair of wings attached. Instantly he shorted in dlsmay, "We're in for ;t now, Jock—we've shot a cherubim l" When a young man i 3 paying attention to a girl, "hem a senor of duty—just to lease the old folks," it is astonishing how the least show of bad weather is suscient to- furnish him,with an excuse for not makkg his :periodical 'aall ; but let that same young man get to paying attention to a girl that he loves and the "old foils" disapprove of, and theme news vet was weather bad enough to keep him from going to see her.

A CIIIJEL Dl2...ll"PoniTsmr.—"TOl me, goad man," cried a farmer in a high state of excitement, rushing up to the ,station agent et a county village, "hasn't the train due. here at twelve o'clock ran off the track 2" "No," calmly. replied the netonisbed railway employe. "Hasn't she broke' an axle?" "No!" "Nor collided with another traiuet "No; bna why do yen ask? Have you friends on St " Oh, yea," replied the despairing man. "Well, you needn't be alarmed," cams from the innocent station man; "they're ` all right !" "Needn't be alarmed !" exclaimed the stranger, mapping his brow "well, I guess I need be. I've got wren sound, non-dyspeptic, eat-everything-they-can-get city cousins on that train, who expect to spend two months at my house, and if they're not blown up before the train reaches here, I lose all faith la the efficaay of prayer, that'a all."

ONE !—An _writer, treat. frig of Pompeii under the text that there is nothing new under the sun says that the bread baked yesterday at Naples is of the precise shape of the loaves found at Pompeii which were put into the oven nearly two thou- sand years ago. The coinage of that period differs little from the coinage of this, except that its workmanship is better. A gaming table then had a pair of dice, and a lady's toilet table a mirror and is,rouge-pot. "Small boys scribbled on the walls and playedwith balls and knuckle-bones and whipping tops. and marbles in the streets of old Pompeii as they do In modern Faris, Na- ples, London, or Berlin. There even are the pass checks which were current at the theatre where the people were assembled at the time of the eruption." Of one modern article, however, this writer could find no coun- terpart among all the matters recovered from Pompeii. There was no classic corkscrew4—Harper's Weekly. THE BAIRNS.—AII English clergyman and a Lowland Scotsman visited one of the best schools in Aberdeen. They wore strangers, r but the master received them civilly, inquiring, "Would you prefer that I should speer these boys, or that you should speer them yourself," The English clergyman, having ascertained that to." speer" meant to question, desired the master to proceed. He did so, with great success, and the boys answered satis- factorily numerous interrogations •as to the exodus of the Israelites from Egypt. • The clergyman then said he would be glad in his turn to `• speer " the boys, and at once began. "How did Pharoah die?" There was dead silence. In this dilemma the Lowland gentleman interposed. "I think, sir, the boys are not accustomed to your English accent; let me try what I can make of them." And he inquired, in his broad ScoAh, Hoo did Phawroah dee !' Again there was ade silence, silence, upon which the master said, "I think, gentlemen, you can't speer these boys; PH show you how Ido it." And he proceeded: "Fat cam to Phawroah'at his hinder end?" The boys answered promptly, " Hetwas drooned and, in addition, a smart little fellow conrmented, "(my lassie could hae telt you that." _ TEETOTALISM IN EARLESTOWN. Sir —lf " Disgusted Teetotaller," instead of rushing into print, bad applied to a "certain rev, gentleman" for proof of said gentleman's " Historical Fact," I have IRO doubt his stock of historkal knowledga would have been considerably increased, and that without disgust, except pe, haps at his own previous opinions. I will not attempt to give him a definite answer, but will adopt the convenieut mode of ask- ing him two questions on the same subject. First, if Christ was an abstainer where was the sting of thd people's remark that he was a winebibber? Second, during the life of our Saviour the Greeks and Romans, ever great drunkards, and • eta Jews, in this sin as in many others, were no doubt very ' much like their neighbours. Well, then, if "our great example" Wal an abstainer, bow is it He was silent on this question and did no command His followers to abstain? But instead we fled the Apostle Paul bids them be moderate ,in aU thins. A careful consideration of these questions may not lead to a satisfactory answer, tint will, I hope, .explode your cJrrespondent's dtsgust.—Yours, , MODERATOR.

CEIBISTIAN UNITY. Sir,—li ever there was a time when it was necessary for Christians to be united in all good works it is now. We have viewed with no little foleasure the increasing forms of charity which this season of the year brings into promi- nence. Amongst them we find the annual treats to aged people, which must be a source of pleasure to many, and in which all denominations unite in most parts of the coun- try. This is as it should be ; Christian unity cannot be better demonstrated than in united efforts of charity and love. But evidently the authorities of Sc. Thomas's Church, Stockton Heath, think otherwise. Permit me to lay before your readers the following facts, which ought to be kn.,wn. For two years pat a committee of Churchmen and Dissen- ters have provided a treat for the aged people of this neigh- bourhood which we have reason to know has been very- much appreciated by them. But this year, without a word of consultation with any of the said committee, some earnest (?) votaries of the church have taken toe matter in hand and announced th it they will provide in connection with the church a tea for aged peeple of all denominatons on the same day as before. Such a course of action, we 9uh. mit, is discourteous, unchristian, and unjust. Ills seeking to frustrate the true end of charity, and, farther, the in- terests of the Church by crushing dissent. Will it succeed? We answer no. Jalgiog from the history of the past it can- not. We are living in days of liberty and enlightenment which will not Buffer this. If it be for all religious denomi- nations, why are not other denominAtion3 represented on the committee? Let it be known that previously the vicar of the parish has been invited to be resent and take part in these gatherings, but has refused. But lam glad to know that the old cammittee is not dead. I hear they are In- tending, as usual, to give a treat to the aged poor, thou?h it will assume a different form to previous years. So that these earnest votaries of sectarian bigotry have not been so suectssful in drying up the springs of charity as they would desire. Is it not time that this spirit of Popish supremacy which some would arrogate to themselves should cease, and that the professors of religion should unite in all philan- throp.c and Christian enterprises ?
