div.head: FAIR TitADE.
div.p: FAIR TitADE.

Sir,—Permit nee to express my thank to your correspon- dent " Clifford Dix" for the clear, and to my mind truth- ful, remarks he made in his last two letters concerning the above question. Now we al: know that after all Fair Trade is, metaphorically speaking, nothing more than the old epir:t of Protection seeking for a reincarnation under a more seductive form, no doubt being led away by the notion that under such a favourable garb the country would accept it. But I am of opinion that the majority of intelligent workingeeen are too well cmviacsd of its real character to allow teemselves to become converts to such a theory sim- ply because a few selfish persons who perhaps on account of some ulterior motives find it convenient to profess to believe in such a selfish principle. eelfish I call it, because anything that tends to the prosperity of the minority at the expense of the majority is such. If we look back in our own history to the palmy days of "Protection," what did it do for the poor? Could their employers afford to pay them more than now ? Bat its advocates would no doubt here make the rejoinder that our country's mann. teetering industries were at that time in an undeveloped state, and consequently the system could not have a fair trial. This is all no doubt very true; but allow me to ask what is it now doing for the people of those countries whose Clovernmente still adhere to Protection. la not one of these countries are the people better off; nay, not as well off as in our own, with the exception of the United States. But her prosperity is not to be attributed to Protection, but rather to the fact that she is not burdened like onrs,dves,wi;ll a "glorious con- stitntio " which c)sts us millions upon millions annually to uphold. ee, after all we working men of England have the satisfaction to know that we, notwithstanding had trade, comp ire favonra Iv with our 01355 in countries where recip- rocity is upheld. lam therefore convinced that the people will have to look for some other remedy than the fallacious theory of Fair Trade before it will find a means of imerov- ing matters, and "Clifford Dix" toncbed the hey note of this at the end of his lest letter. Now, we workiagmeen are apt to be gulled by men who profess to have our cause at heart; but as seou as they secure our votes and get M.P. appended to their names they sink into political oblivion, and we seldom Lear any more of the premises made us. Nay, even worse than this, they perhaps array themselves against the interests of the ye! y eaea FRIDXY.— tiaouid represent, and. as ic were, kicking the tinng from under their feet this has helped them up.—l am yours, (tee •
LOT [EKI:
AT BAZAARS.

Sir.—ln your issue of Saturday last you gave your readers your personal opinion upon lotteries. This question, if raised at all, would be far-reaching, and extend even to the Stock Exchange and to speculation in commercial life. Our laws of what is right ought to be baeed nvm the ques- tion of what is fair and (coal. Can you define a distinction beween a draw for a Liverpool lottery ticket and a draw for a Belgian lottery ticket? If the law of En-tend weeld commit the speculator in an English lottery Licket to the del,radation of itrrisonment, why should the aame law per- mit thousands of foreign lottery tickets to be circulated . _

through this country continually ? Is it because we are blinded by a frac, but none the less unfair trade policy ? It =ay be I;vv, but is it justice, is it fair 2 The fact is, there ,is a great deal in the law of this country which is unfair, and there ar,, to few persons who have the moral courage to speak or write about the unfairness which exists. Any point of advar.tage in argument is usually plssed by with- out comment, out this is contrary to the way in which we Should act if our esire is to get at the truth. Let facts be at once admitted and truth prevail. The Mayor of Warring- ton as I understood his remarks, did not intend to convey

, the impression that nambling was legal under the present law, but intended to point out the difference in the moliveir •which ao' nate and the purposes which are aimed at by the ,difierent parties, and this is the real point to keep in view. You surely do not m-an to tell me that if I went to a Wes- leyan &mar got up expressly with the object of raising money for new schools, and I there patronized the lucky bag with a full knowledge of its purpose, that you would say that I wati a rogue and a vagabond, Why, sir, the bare idea is enough to make ma laugh. In my opinion, a man is a rogue and a vagabond when he obtains other person's goads and does not nay for them; this is the man who ought to be imprisoned and not be allowed to escape through the , farce of a bankruptcy court. We have too mach narrow- ' caindednese and grandmotherly legielation, and too little of what is really nseful. When a man has earned his money he has a perfect right to spnid it as he chooses, so long as he does not injure or annoy his neighbour against his will. —Yours truly' FAIR TO ALL. Warrington, Dec. 23, 1984. [Our correspondent seems to have mi,apprehended the point of our remirke, though we thought we made it clear that it was not being " fair to all " to tine one person £l5 and costs, and let another go scot free for a breach of the ! law. As to what the Mayor Intended to convey, perhaps it will be as well to allow him to speak for himself.—En. Ex.]

and Dr. Bell are mentioned. SALE OF Won't —On Tuesday a sale of work was opened in the Wesleyan school-room, Penketb, by the Rev. J. McTurk. The sale of work had been got up chiefly by a congregational sewing class for the purpose of raising funds Lot the enlargement of the day school and the building of new vestries for the chain.l. The room was prettily deco- rated with evergreens and mottoes; and the stalls and Christmas tree were well furnished with a variety of useful and ornamental articles. Al stated, the larger portion of these articles were the work of the ladies' sewing class, of which Mu. It. Garnett was the secretary, and Miss Bost- wick the treasnrer ; amongst the other members being Mrs. D. Garnett, Mrs. Mainley, Mrs. Seed, Mrs. Watson, Miss Peers, Mrs. Todds Mrs. Winn, Mrs. Cook, Mrs. Wilkinson, &c. The stalls and Christmas tree were in charge of Mrs. Cook, airs. Mainley, Mrs. Wilkinson, Mrs. Watson, Mrs. Seed, Misses Bestwick, J. and A. Moses, Cook, Routledge, E. Hobson, Mainley, and A. Griffiths. A hymn having been sung and a p-aye: offered up by tha Rev. J. slcTurk, Mr. R. Cook expressed his pleasure at seeing Mr. McTurk pr. sent. He might just tell him that the sale of work had been principally got up not so very much for the amoant of money that should be realised by it, as in order that it might interest and cause the co-operation of everybody in the viTage, not only the gentlemen who were always flrst and foremost In work of that kind—(laughte-)—but also of the ladies. The ladies had been very busily employed, and they saw before them some of their handiwork. So for as ' he was concerned he was exceedingly delighted to sea such a splendid display as they had. The productions of the Sunday scholars and the young people in connection with that place of worship were particularly gratifying, bcause they could not too early begin to be useful and to do some- thing for the Lord Jesus. (Hear, hear.) They must record their deep indebtedness to Mr. Bestwicsk and to Miss Best- wick for their extreme kindness' the sewing meetings hav- ing for a considerable time past been held at Mr. Bestw:ck's. (Applause.)—The Rev. J. McTark, in formally opening the meeting, said he lid not believe that the work that had been undertaken there was simply for the gathering of money, but had been for the promotion of union amongst them. (App'anse.)—A vote of thanks was accorded to Mr. McTurk, on the moti in of Mr. Cook. In the coarse of the evening there was singing, Jrc under the leadership of Mr. Wet. son. We understand that the sum realized from the bazaar was over £33, and that a number of things were left unsold

Amongst those present were Major Litton, Mr. John White, J.P., Mr. Buckton, Captain Ridgway, Captain Thomson (Newton , Company), Lieutenant Bnckton, Sergeant-Major Fennelly, &c., dm—Major LITTON, in an appropriate address, regretted that their colonel was unable to be present, and said that letters of apology hal been receivel from several gentle- Men who were not able to attend the distribution. These gectlemem had, however, sent their prizes as usual, and they (the Volunteers) were much obliged to them for doing so Proceeding, Major Litton said that they had fewer volunteers this year than they had hid for several years previously. This year the strength was 536, as against 550 last year, and 578 the previous year. Re could only account for the diminution in consequence of there being a dearth of officers. That complaint did not apply to the 9th Lan. cashire Volunteers alone, but to the whole of the volunteer forces throughout the country, and also to the militia. He I did not know whether it was that the expense was too I heavy, or whether the rising generation of gentlemen were not made of the same pluck as the generation before them. He thought perhaps they were somewhat short of pluck, for they found the same thing appertained in regard to cricketing and other athletic sports, and that the young gentlemen of the country did not come to the front in these respects as they formerly did. Snrirsox TO YOCNCI MEN. —The Rev. John Yonge• pre.ich.d his monthly sermon to young men in Wycliffe Congregational Church"on Sunday evening, taking for his, text Proverbs xx, part of the 29th verse : "The glory of young men is their strength." The discourse, which was a very interesting one, was listened to with special attention. There was a good attendance.

A meting of the ward reptesentatives of the executive in connection with the Liberal Club, wa3 held on Monday night, Mr. Charles Broadbent presiding. Mr. Broadbent was re-elected chain- man of the executive, and Mr. F. A. Roberts, deputy- chairman. A manag.melt sub-committee for the year was elected, consisting of Mr. li,oadbent, Mr. John Crosaekl, Mr. Frank Roberts, Mr. Frederick Monk 4, M. John MO, Mr. C. S. Rargess. and Mr. W. Pierpoint. Arrangements were made for the holding of the annual meetiog of the General Council on the 19th or 20th January. It was also decided to send congratulations to the Premier on. Monday next, on the occasion of his birthday. The Parliamentary , Elections Redistribution Bill was considered and referred to I the managicg sub-committee for further consideration, with a recomniendation to watch its progress as regarded War. i rington. The rest of the business was of a private character

THE SARRICES.—iit Orford Barracks Christmas was ob- served right merrily. The various companies had dinner in the barrack-romns. and Colonel Thackwell, who he exceed- ingly popular with the men, visited each room and wished the occupants the compliments of the season. He was en- thusiastically cheered. 'The other officers who took part in the proceedings were Major H.miltoo, C aptain Richie, Lieutenant Orßrien, and Sergeant Majors Cope and Bailey. At dinner the usual loyal and patriotic toasts were honoured and tae repast, a substantial one, gave every satisfaction. The 6 arrack-rooms were tastefully decorated, that of B Com- pany, King's Liverpool Regiment, being about the most at- tractive. On the walls were placed numerous. mottoes. one wishing succees to Captain Richardson, and another to Lieutenant Scales, and the names of the various engage- ments in which the regiment has been engaged were also affixed to the walls. They were Egypt, Deltingen, Malplaquet, Blenheim, Peiwar-Rotal, itbmettiee, Mar- tinique, Dalbi, Lucknow, Niagara, Oudenarde, and Afghanistan. The barrack - room of C Company, King's Liverpool, was alio tastefully decorated. Sergeant Naylor rendered good service in the decorations, and willing hands were not wanting to make the barracks as attractive as possible. During the afternoon and evenidg a good number of civilians were hospitably received by the military, and (lancing was indulged in until about eleven o'clock. The best order prevailed, and -a most enjoyable day was spent. The sergeants recelved a number of visitors in their mess- reorn, and entertained them in a fitting manner. CAIRO STREET SUNDAY SCHOOL.— The annual scholars' party in connection with this sohool was held on Christmas Day. Tea wai partaken of at five o'clock by about ISO scholars and 100 teachers and frieuds. After tea an enter- tainment was given which included procession of Father Christmas, recitatioes, hymns, and tiuished with an effective representation by several officers of the school of Mr. Pil- chei's drama of " Joseph." The whole entertainment passed off very successfully, and the representation of the drama deserves the highest praise. After the entertainment was concluded, the room was left to the scholars for about an hour to enj sy various games, and at 830 the younger ones were sent home,. each being as they left, presented with an orange and an apple. The room was then cleared for dan- cing, and the teachers and older ones, to the lively strains of Mr. T. R. Ford, thoroughly enjoyed themaelves till 11 o'clock. During the evening the scholars of Mr. John Chalmers (a teacher in the school) presented him with a writing desk and an album as a small token of the high respect they have for him. The party was in all ways a • most thorough BLICC2S9, the whole passing off without the sligh'est hitch, and reflecting great credit on the officials. The schoolroom was most tastefully decoreted. PADGATE SCHOOLS —On Christmas morning the children at these schools attended divine set vice. At one o'clock in the afternoon to the number of 191 they sat down in the large school-room to an excellent dinner of roast beef, plum pudding, &c, there being present Mr. Derbyshire, chairman of the Echool Committee, Mr. Mines, the master, and others. After dinner sweets, which had been sent by Mr. Derbyshire and Mr. Lyttagoe, Sankey-street, Warring- ton, were distributed, and also biscuits given by Mr. Hough- ton, of Padgate. The children were each further provided with a threepenny piece by the kindness of Mr. Crompton, Market-place, Warrington. Suitable addresses were given by M. Derbyshire and Mr. Mines, for whom and for thofe who had, given the presents hearty cheers were given by the scholars. The afternoon was spent with games, &c, and in the evening an entertainment was given. It may be mentioned that a number of old scholars were present. BRICK STREET AND FRIARS' GREEN CONGREGATIONAL TEA. PARTY.—The annual tea party and entertainment in connection with the above, took place in Brick-strzet school- room on Christmas Day. After tea an entertainment was given by scholars and members of the congregation. The choir, under the leadership of Mr. W. Mountield, sang aeveral selections of music. A dialogue entitled " Circum- stantial Evidence" was excellently gone through, the fol- lowing taking part :—Misses Warburton, Barton, Lewis, and Burton ; Messrs Hazledine, Ifenshaw, Critchley, James, Rigby, and Wright. Mr. C. Furnies was deservedly encored for his reciting of " The Fireman's Wedding," Mr. J. Mounfield occupied the chair. On Friday evening the scholars' treat took place. After tee the scholars enjoyed themselves until about ten o'clock in games of varioue characters.

EMPLOYER AND WORKMAN.—At a Sitting of the Warring- ton County Court, on Satter lay, Hugh Jones, a Welshman, sued Richard Spann, wheelwright, Warrington, for the sum of 15s I3J, as wages due.—Mr. A. Browne, solicitor, War- rington, appeared for Jones, and objected tom set-off flied by the defendant. He said that his client was summoned before the maeistrates under the Employers' and Work- men's Act fo- £4, and the case was adjourned ; therefore he thought his Honour (Judge W. Wyane Ffoulkes) had no authority to act in that resinct.—His Honour, said that the proper thing would be to adjeurn the case until the magistrates had given their decieion.—Mr. Browne : The case was adjourned by the magistrates until you had deci- ded, so as to decide them—His Honour : It is the magis- , trates' decision that must decide me. The case was entered !in the!r court first.— the case was consequently Adjoarned, the counter claim being struck off.—On Monday morning I the case came on for bearing at the Borough Court, but I Jones did not appear —After hearing the evidence of Mr Sperm, who claimed £4 in consequence of Jores leaving work without notice, the Bench made an order for the Letter to pay damages equivalent to one week's wages. CRUELTY TO Aenue.es.—At the Borough Coart, on Mon- day, Charles Rigby, farmer, WAS charged with ill-treating a horse by allowing it to be worked whilst in an unfit state on the let instant, and Richard Cunningham, who did not ap- pear, was charged with working the horse.—Mr. A. Browne, solicitor, Warrington appeared for Rigby. Inspector Greanwell, of the R.S.P.C.A., said that on the day in ques- tion he saw Cunningham, Mr. Rigby's servant, working a grey pony that was excessively lame and was suffering from a bone spavin.—Mr. Robinson, veterinary surgeon, also gave evidence as to the animal's condition.—Mr. Browne said that the horse had only been purchased recently by the de- fendant, and it wee then lame. On the day in respect to which the charge was mole the streets were slippery, and it fell and thus increased its lameness.—Consfdering these circumstances, the Bench only fined defendant in the costs,. XI. 15.—A warrant was ordered to be issued for the appre- hension of Cunningham, who went to Ireland before the summons could be serve I upon biol.—Arthur Millwood, 'bus driver, was fined 10e. and costs, or 14 days, for savagely beating a herse attached to one of the 'buses of the War- rington Carriage Company, of which he was in charge, on the 9th instant —lnspector Greenwell proved the case.— The Mayor took occasion to refer to tha fact that the 'bases were sometimes excessively loaded, and s iid that steps would no doubt be taken to punish the offenders. DRAUORTS.—Mr. W. Strickland, of Leeds, on Monday evening played six games of draughts at once, against six of the best players of Warrington, he being so placed 33 to be unable to see either the board or the men. The Mayor (Alderman Harrison), who preehted, advised everyone to learn the game of dranghia. it being one of theme genus that aaaeiciee4 till Mind, It bed a tendenCY to Strengthen the memory very Materially, wag a tnoet interesticg game, and one that would teach them lessons from which they might draw comparisons and illustratieng io the (trainer/ events of i.fe.—Dr. Mackit reco nmetided draughts as a game peculiarly eniteble for the plainest homes, one in which a whole family debt Boon learn to engage, and one that was a long way remn`eed from those glen:ling and disre- putable games that were unfortunately mixed up with many public places.—Mr. Frank Dunne explained the method by which the game would be played. There were six boards, each square being numbered in retation. As each player made a move Mr. Dunne would call out the number of the square he moved from and of tbe equere be moved to Mr. Strickland, who would sit with his back to the players. Mr. Strickland would then notify the move he wished to make by calling out the number of the squares, as his opponents did.—After a very interesting game, which was watched with great interest by these present, votts of thank were pissed to Mr. etrickland and the chairman. WESLEYAN CIRCUIT QUARTERLY MEETING —lea quar- terly meeting of the Warrington Wesleyau Circuit was held on Monday. The proceedings commenced with the local preachers' meetine, at three o'clock, in the ministers' vestry, under the Rev. James McTurk's presidency. A large num- ber of local preachers assembled. The usual routine busi- ness pertaining to the department of sere ice in which the brethren were interested was traneacted. Two young men, whose term of probation was completed, having successfully paseed through the preliminary stages, were unanimously accepted as fully accredited local preachers. Tea was held at five o'clock, and about fifty persons set down to a repast, which was both season -able and enjoyable. Afterwards the general meeting of etewarde, leaders, trustees, and local preachers was held in the large room. Mr. Mc rurk occu- pied the chair, and there were present,among others, Messrs. E. J. Guest, Thomas B. Carter. Robert Gernett, Robert Cook, Edwin Richardson, J. Bennett, Wm. Bennett (2), W. Barlow, Isaac Hayward, ,L S. Green, W. Y. Lawton, Elwin Brown, Thomas Dutton, W. Silcoek. R. G. Ilensh all, James Summersgill, J. H. Oman ; Revs. G. E. Cutting and J. H. Jones. The previous quarter's minutes were read by Mr, T. B. Carter, and confirmed. The financial report_ was read by Mr. Guest, and deemed satisfactory. The numerical condition of the society was given by the Rev. ale rurk, and led to a conversation which was impor- tant in• its object and ultimate issue. Messrs. E. Guest and Edwin Richardson were elected circuit stewards for the en- suing year. Mr. Guest was cordially thanked for past ser- viced, and Mr. Carter, whose engagements would no longer permit bins to remain in office as circuit steward, was ac- corded a similar compliment.—Mr. Robert Cook, amid the hearty applause of the meeting, consented to fill the impor- tant office of circuit chapel secretary. Sanction was given to the introduction of the weekly offertory at Bewsey-road. A committee was appointed to carry into effect the general desire for the greater efficiency of raission work, and the better accommodation and convenience of the mission workers, regard thus being made to John Wealey'seft quoted saying, "Go to those who want you, but go to those who want you mesa" During the last quarter the new and coin- mod bus schocl in connection with Bold-street Chapel has been completed and is now used every Sunday, and some time in March next, the Sankey Bridges new chapel will be ready for opening by the Rev. Charles Garrett. Pro- jects are on foot for the further enlargement and consolida- tion of Weslevanism in the town and country pl ices of the circuit, and the ministers and workers are full of heart and hope. The meeting closed by the pronouncing of the Bene- diction by the chairman. OPENING .OF THE Cincos.—On Wednesday evening Mr. Harmston's handsome new circus was opened by a perfor- mance which was witnessed by the Mayor and Mayoress and a very large attendance of spectators. This circus, which has a high and imposing frontage on Sankey-street, is almost entirely built of iron, though resting on a brick foundation. The length of the building is 90 feet and the width 72 feet, and it is consequently capable of holding a large number of spectators. Inside it has a spacious, light, and graceful appearance, and its attractiveness is very much increased by the tasteful and ornate manner in which it has been fitted up. The Sankey-street end of the structure is app oprlated for the reserve and box seats and a portion of the promenade, the latter extending also partly along each side and over the pit. The opposite end of the circus is fitted up as a gallery which will, when filled as on Wednesday night, accommodate something like a thousand persons. Means of entrance and exit—an important feature of public buildings of this description—are amply provided by a cal:Reim:le eliding doorway opening into Sankey-street. and by two side doors, one on each side. The performance which was gone through on the opening night was worthy of the occasion and of Mr. Harinston's reputation as •a caterer of this kind of amusement. The programme was varied, and the bare-back riding, the acrobatic feats, and the wit of the clowns were all alike excellent. The remark- able somersaults on a bare-backed horse at full speed which were made by the son of the proprietor won the admiration of the audience, and were frequently and warmly applauded. Unusual skill in turning somersaults was also shown by another member of Mr. Harmston's troupe, who while per- forming these difficult feats held two sharp-pointed knives first at his breast and then at his throat and ears. The singular strength and agility of the Alfrano brothers was shown in a variety of striking ways; while the wonderful sagacity and training exhibited by four beauti- ful horses, when being pat through a number of evolutions by Mr. Harmston, won unbounded applause. An amusing part of the entertainment was the appearance of a trained pig in a perambulator, which, with a good deal more suc- cess than might have been expected from so iedocile an animal, mimicked the spoilt child, and afterwards still further suprised the audience by going through a number of performances. Towards the close of the entertainment Mr. Ihrmston carne into the arena and thanked the Mayor and Mayonns and the others present for their attendance, and expressed hie intention to do his utmost to please shore who might favour his circus with their attendance. He concluded amidst applause with wishing them all a " Merry Christmas." Mr. Hermston has aenouncal a specially at- tractive programme to be performed to-day (Saturday), on New Yearni Day, and also On :qtr.' nights nuliag the week'

BANK QUAY MISSION. The annCel gathering of the scholars and tea Chere of th.; Sunday school Connected with Bank Quay Mission, took place last evening and was a decided success. A substan- tial tea was partaken of, end subsequently Councillor J. Crosfield, J.F., presided at a Crowded meeting, at which a programme of singing and recitations was ably rendered by the children, addresses also being delivered by gentlemen interested in the work of the echoel. After a hymn having been sung and prayer offered up. Mr. W. Ford, secretary, reed his annual report of the work of the school. It stated that there was a marked increase in the number , of echolars, so that if it continued, as they hoped it would, additional accommodation would be required. The number on the books last year was 394, this year 450, an increase of 56. The average morning attendance of females was 80 and of males Pa, being a tot dof 178. There were 22 teachers' names on the register, the same as last year, one visitor, two superintendents, and two secretaries. The su- perintendents, Messrs .Dale and Ashley, deserved great praise for the manner in which they had performed their duties, and the excellent example that they had set both teachers and scholars. The male teachers had at- tended very well, but the attendance of the fe- male teachers had been rather poor in the morn- ings. Two children connected with the school had died during the year. The Band of Hope had been very successful. When they le irned that these who were striv- ing against the evil of drink were gaining the mastery their various agencies fer the promotion of temperance shoul4 take heart and put their shoulders to the wheel with increased ardour. If they did no the time was not far dis- tant when England would be sober as well as free. It was intended to have a band, for which purpose £22 3s 511 had been collected. A sum of money given to the singers at Christmas Eve had been kindly devoted to that fund. In concluding, the report encourieed the teachers to persevere in their labours, and thanked them for their past services The Chairman said that he had listened with great interest te the excellent report, which was a credit to the secretary and to the school. He was glad that there had been an increase in numbers over the previous year. Us would remind the children that they were much indebted to th 3 teachers for their services, and he- hoped they would make a point of at- tending punctually to their classes. When teachers gave their time and labour, the least that children could do was to be regular in attendance. He wished them all a" Happy New Year." (Cheers.)—Mr. Monks, Den., in a short ad- dress. gave some sound practical advice to the children.— Mr. J. Dale felicitously observed that their chairman hid been their Santa Clem; in providing them the treat of tint day. He also spoke of Sunday school week as a preparation for the church.—Mr. Ashley said that since the school had been erected good seed bad been sown and had borne fruit. He urged them to adhere to temperance-, and remarked that they were the pioneers of the Bend of Hope Union of War- rington, which was grewing in proportions very rapidly, and was making its influence felt. At the close a hearty vote of thanks was passed to Mr. Crosfield, who, after suitably replying, received quite an ovation as he paesed through the room, accompanied by Niles Dixon, who bad occupied a seat on the platform.—The following are Um officers for the ensuing year :—Messrs Dale and Ashley, superintendents •, W. Ford, secretary ; J. Halsall, afristant secretary; J. Dauber, treasurer; J. Monks, senr, visitor. The programme appended was gone through by the children, in addition to several hymns that were sung : Recitation by Ethel Teem, " Little maid ;" song by Martha Jane Monks, "I am Jesu's little lamb ;." recitation by Lizz;e Wade ; recitation by Harriet Tomson, " A kind little girl ;" reading by Jos. Monks, jun.; recitation by Emma Smith," Complaints of the poor ;" recitation by Willie Monks; recitation by Minnie Smith ; recitation by Nellie Wade.

WARRINGTON HARRIERS.—Abont 30Meernbers met at the Club-room on Saturday, and out of that number 13 took part in the ordinary club run. The hares, J. Waterworth and G Grenade were despetched at 3-16, and the pack, with J. Dunbelt as pace and J. Massey as whip, followed at 3-26. The trail lay along Kontsford-road as far as the Tannery At Latchford, and then turned to the left and crossed the fidds, with some good ditches to jump. and The!wall was reached. The trail lay through Woolston, and by the Old Quay back to Warrington-bridge, where the word was given to race for home. The result was that J. Massey cime in first, just behind the bares, at 4-58; W. Whitfield 2nd ; J. Green 3rd ; T. Grleave 4th ; W. Gleave sth ;G. Hands 6th; the rest close up. Distance run about nine miles. THE NEWTON' COMMISSIONERS REFORE THE HOUSE OF LORDS.—For some time past the Newton Improvement Commiesioners have been engaged in law proceedings with the County Justices of Lancashire with respect to the pay- ment of half the cost Of maintaining the Warrington and Wigan road, which passes through the Newton township. The Newton Commissioners contend that according to a recent Ant of Parliament the County Justices ought to pay one- half of the cost of maintaining the road In question, but this claim was disputed by the county authorities. An action was accordingly entered by the Newton Commis- sioners for the recovery of one-half of the expenses, and the c tse was duly heard at a quarter sessions. The verdict was in favou- of the Newton authorities on all the points involved, and they were awarded their costs. The County Justices, however, appealed against the de- cision, and the MO was re-tried in the Court of Appeal, b fore three jndees, a fortnight ago. The decision was again in favour of the Newton Commis- sionere—the three judges being unanimous in their verdict —and the county authorities were again ordered to ply the costs. The questions at issue are of a most important char- acter to all local authorities, and will affect several bodies. Stilt maintaining that they are in the right, the county just'ees have been advised lay counsel, it is stated, to appeal to the House of Lords lelainst the decision of the judges in tha Court of Appeal.. It is believed tbie course will be taken,.

THE OLI;EST liArTLWAY SHRVANT.—The death occurred on Thursday at Shildon, near Darlington, of John Glass, the oldest railway servant in England. Ha was engaged in the construction of the Stockton and Darlington ltailway in 1822, and continued in the service of that company for 62 years.

SUICIDE BY POISONING AT OLDHAM On Christmas Day a woman named Elizabeth Cocker, of Greengate-street, Oldham, poisoned herself by taking a quantity of oxalic acid. The deceased was a widow, and was in low spirits through thinking she could net support herself in the future. She was 57 years of age. SUICIDE ON CHRISTMAS DAY. Thomas Filburn, a jet worker. at 'Whitby, committed suicide on Thursday by banging himself. Ile remained at home to superintend the cooking of the Christmas dinner, while his wite went to church. Soon after she left be was found by his son sus- pended by the neck in the staircase. SCOTCH IRON TRADE.—A review of the Scotch iron trade shows that the past year has been inferior to that of the preceding year. The ',value of iron and steel goods exported from Glasgow in the year was £3,287,440, compared with £3,824,580 last year. The bulk of the slppmenls consisted of locomotives and sugar-crushing machinery. SHOCKING OCCURRENCE.—EmIy on Thursday morning a blind man, named John Fiskin, and his wife, residing at Hull, met wit, their deaths in a shocking manner. They had Wen drinking with a woman named Leak on Christmas Eve, and when going to bed OD "Thursday morning, about five o'clock, Fiskin and his wife fell downstairs, and sus- tained injuries which resulted in death. SINGCLkiI FIRE ar DARIVEZT.—The gas from a main in a thickly populated part of Darwen got ignited on Christmas night and set tire to a shop in Elikon-street, which was considerably damaged. Dirnmock's mill fire brigade and the corporation fire brigade played on the flames for two or three hours without effect, and at ten o'clock the main was broken in at another street, and water poured down i:. This risky ex- periment p-ored saccessful.

„ • FATAL RAILWAY ACCIDENT.--A railway porter named I William Everton was killed on Thursday at Leughborough, on the Midland Railway. 'use deceased and two other men went to Loughborough from Leicester to assist in collecting the tickets for the up mail to London. After the collection the deceased attempted to enter the guard's van-while the 1 twain was In motion but he lost his bold by some means and I fell on the rails. The carriages passed over his body, death being instantaneous. The deceased has left a widow and four children. SERIOUS FIRE AT NOTTINGIIAIS.—Soon after six o'clock on Christmas morning a police-constable named Jones saw smoke issuing from a Louse in Clam-street, Nottingham. He obtained an entrance and. found that a quantity of soot Thad fallen from the chimney and set on tire the furniture and flooring of a room. It was with difficulty that three men sleeping on the seemed floor could get downsta;rs, and four old people on the third floor were afraid to face the dense smoke. Jones, however, placed wet cloths over their mouths and pluckily brought down all four, includ- ing an old woman who- expressed a wish stay in bed, saying she would rather be burned there than face the smoke

GOLBORNE. TEMPERANCE LEcTuas.—On Monday night the Rev. W. A. Wickham, M.A., of •Wigin, delivered a lecture on the temperance question in St. Thomas's schools, Golborne, before a moderate audience. The rector Presided. CHRISTMAS-TIDE. The Golborne tradPsmen have mode great preparations for the season, and a friendly tivalry seems to have existed as to who shall make the best show. Shops in the principal streets are nearly al decorated. THE REP. J. T. Camal, Claremont Park, Blackplol, has received a unanimous invitation to become the pastor of the Congregational Church, Got borne, Newton-le-Willows, and will commence his duties on the first Sunday in Feb- ruary next. _ _ .

THE ELOPENZNT —lt is stated that the `f runaways " who playecisuch an important part in the story of last week have thus far kept from Golborne. The forsaken husbind understands that the pair tried to put up at a house in the district, but as the faithless wife happoed to be known to the inmates, they were quickly orderf d off. Goulding has already broken up bis house and disposed of his furniture amongst his neighbours,.

THE LATE.RAII:WAY ROBBERY—We and ,rstand that the police bave within the last few (bye apprehended a well- known Golborne man who is suppos,d to be connected with the robbery which took place at Golberno Passenger Station about May last, when SOM3 wearing alma wel was carried away. The, individual referred to has been about Lowton for some time, arid in a conversation lately be said something in company which led to his arrest the same night. A suit of clothes reported amongst the stolen pro- perty is said to have been found in he possession. The case will coma before the Newton magistrates to-day (Saturday). CONCERT AT LOWTON.—A concert promoted by the Low- ton Football Club for the benefit of W. Ashton, who, it may be remembered, bad his leg broken M the foothill field in a recent match, was held in St-. Luke's boys' school- room, Lowton. on Saturday evening, and was well patro- nised. Mr: W. H. Arnett presided. A number of dis- tinguished strangers gave their services, in addition te the local singers, Miss Yell (Lowton) arid Mr. W. Jackson, Gol- borne. Mr. Grime (Wigan) opened with a well executed pianoforte solo, and was succeeded by Mr. J. F. Williamson, whose contributions included "The- Skipper" add "The Old Brigade," the last mentioned being repeated. " Mag- gie's Secret" and Home by the River" proved accept ible items in the hand of Miss Fell. Mr. W. Jackson crested roars of laughter with 'The Runaway Musketeers," "Martha Box," "Awful Little Scrub," and "The Wooden Leg Brigade." At the end of the litter song Mr. Jackson contributed some verse on the football accident. A couple of trios (piano and violins) by Miss and Messrs. Barroclough (late of Lowton) proved very pleasing. Mdlla. Christine (Man- chaster) received a hearty reception in the well-known "Kathleen Movourneen." For her nest song, "I love my love," she was cheered to the echo. and replied with Sulli- van's sublime " Lost chord." Mr. Fidler oroved an accept- able singer, his selections being" The pilgrim ef leve " and " When Other lips." " Darby and Joan," as rendered by Miss Williamson (Sale> found many admirers, as did also " Daddy." As an encore song, she replied with "The Sham rock." The National Anthem concluded a most enjoyable eveninre. The accompanists were Mr. Grime, Miss 'William- son, and Miss Barraclough. We understand that in additior to the proceeds of the concert being handed over to him Ashton is receiving 3Os a week from the football club 2nd gratuitous professional services from Dr. Dobb.
